Hannagan Meadow at an elevation of about 9000 feet reported over 20 inches of snowfall.
Elevations above 6000 feet in Graham county had in excess of 1 foot of snowfall.
Over one foot of snowfall occurred on the higher elevations of Mt. Lemmon and the Santa Catalina mountains.
Three inches of snowfall occurred in Oracle and heavy snow also occurred in the the higher elevations of Southeast Pinal county above 5000 feet.
Heavy snowfall occurred at Kitt Peak at an elevation just under 7000 feet.
Heavy snowfall occurred in the higher elevations of the Santa Rita Mountains in Santa Cruz County.
Heavy snowfall occurred in the Chiracahua and Huachuca Mountains in Cochise County.
Three to six inches of snowfall occurred in the Oracle area.

Three to four inches of snowfall occurred in the lower elevation areas outside the Upper Gila River valley including Fort Grant, Klondyke and Highway 191 south of Safford. The mountain tops including Mt. Graham had in excess of one foot of snow with drifts up to four feet.

Heavy snow fell across all of Northern Greenlee county with 5 to 10 inches of snowfall along Highway 191 north of Morenci. In the highest elevations such as Hannagan Meadow, there was 16 inches of snow.
Six inches of snow fell at Kitt Peak at an elevation of about 6800 feet.

Heavy snow fell at elevations above 3000 feet in Eastern Pima County. Locations such as the far east and southeast side of the city of Tucson in addition to Vail and Corona De Tucson had 2 to 3 inches of snow. In the higher elevations of the Catalina Mountains there was well over a foot of snow with drifts up to 4 feet.
Sonoita, at an elevation of just under 5000 feet had 5 inches of snow. Meanwhile, the higher elevations of the Santa Rita mountains had in excess of one foot of snow.
Most of the lower elevations in Cochise county including Benson and Willcox had anywhere from 2 to 4 inches of snowfall.
The Geronimo wildfire burned nearly 2500 acres of mainly grass near Sunizona in Cochise County. There were about 8 small structures burned including two vehicles.
A suspected illegal immigrant in the Altar valley was struck by lightning and suffered minor injuries.
The Douglas-Bisbee airport ASOS recorded sustained winds of 43 mph for two consecutive hours.
A residence on the Northwest side of Tucson was struck by lightning. A cinder block retaining wall suffered the brunt of the damage.
Dry Lake RAWS measured a wind gust of 50 knots at 2-3 PM LST.
A trained spotter in Rio Rico measured a wind gust of 61 mph.

Wildfire burned near 5,000 acres near Fort Huachuca in Santa Cruz County. The fire burned at least four homes and six private vehicles near the west gate entrance. One injury was reported due to burns from the fire.
ASOS measured a wind gust of 62 mph at the Safford Airport.

A strong microburst wind gust of 70 mph snapped a 125-foot flag pole in half. The wind gust was recorded via a local television station's weather station at the RV park where the flag pole was located. No other damage was noted nearby.

Severe thunderstorm outflow winds tore a portion of the roofing material off a strip mall store near the intersection of Grant and Campbell. The debris from the roof blew into the parking lot, but resulted in no injuries. Winds from the same thunderstorm uprooted trees at the intersection of Pantano and 22nd Street, and damaged an awning on a mobile home. One woman and one child received minor injuries after a tree limb fell on them on the 1800 block of Mission Road. A large tree also fell onto two vehicles.
Severe thunderstorm outflow winds caused 1/4 mile visibility near the Willcox Playa due to blowing dust. The trained spotter measured a wind gust of 72 mph.
Streets were flooded in Willcox after an estimated 1-2 inches of rain.
Severe thunderstorm outflow winds estimated at 60 mph blew down a large tree near downtown Nogales.
Thunderstorm outflow winds blew down a power line at the intersection of Blacklidge and Campbell, and then also at the intersection of Speedway and 6th Avenue.

A thunderstorm outflow wind gust estimated at 60 mph destroyed a horse barn on the Diamond P Ranch on Brookerson Road, 17 miles north of Willcox. The 10-stall horse barn was completely destroyed by the wind gust. Two racehorses that were not in the barn were killed, when debris from the barn landed on them.

Severe thunderstorm downburst winds caused significant damage at Three Points. Several mobile homes and nearby sheds were either heavily damaged or destroyed.  A more substantial brick veneer building was also damaged, with varying degrees of roof damage reported to several homes in Three Points. Several large trees were uprooted completely. Winds from this severe thunderstorm were estimated to be near 85 mph. Three Points Fire reported one injury was received by flying glass, after winds blew out a house window.

Heavy thunderstorm rainfall of 1 to 2 inches fell in only a 30 minute period near State Highway 86 and Three Points. Significant flooding of washes and low water crossings occurred. The Three Points fire department reported several roads were washed out and impassable in the Three Points area. The local law enforcement reported a swift water rescue was performed near the intersection of California and Worden Roads at approximately 9 PM MST.
AWOS measured a wind gust of 59 mph at Ryan Field at 5:55 PM MST.
Severe thunderstorm outflow winds downed power lines near the intersection of Valencia and Mark Rds.
Thunderstorm winds estimated at 60 mph downed several power poles just north of Ajo.
Swift water rescue reported by broadcast media near the intersection of Bonanza and Tanque Verde.

Thunderstorm winds estimated at 60 mph downed several power lines near the intersection of La Canada and Duval Mine Roads in Green Valley. The Green Valley newspaper reported that approximately one dozen power poles were damaged or destroyed. This resulted in a power loss to over 6000 people in the area.
Sheriff closed La Canada Road just south of Duval Mine Road due to flash flooding and flowing debris on the roadway.

Thunderstorm downdraft winds downed power poles near the intersection of Grande and St. Marys Roads, and 10 power poles were downed or damaged near the intersection of Irvington Road and Harrison Road.
Swift water rescue was performed at Stone Avenue underpass near 6th Street.
Thunderstorm winds downed several power poles near the Bonita school.
A trained spotter reported 0.75 inch hail at San Manuel.

Severe thunderstorm winds downed several trees, including one tree that was 60 feet tall in San Manuel. Thunderstorm winds also blew down some fencing in the area. Large tree branches were downed by the same thunderstorm in Mammoth.
Heavy rainfall flooded several roadways between Bonita and Klondyke.
Law enforcement reported a ramada was blown down at the Mammoth swimming pool.
Law enforcement reported numerous tree fires started by lightning, centered near the intersection of Golf Links Road and Kolb Road.
Lightning struck a tree near a restaurant parking lot, near the intersection of Wilmot Road and Tanque Verde Road. The tree caught fire and was destroyed.

Severe thunderstorm winds downed many power poles near the intersection of Tangerine Road and Thornydale Road. A NWS employee reported a large downed tree near the intersection of First Avenue and Orange Grove Road.
Strong thunderstorm winds created a dust storm, with the public reporting visibility of 40 feet in the blowing dust at Eloy.
Strong thunderstorm winds created widespread blowing dust in Safford, with a trained spotter reporting less than 1/4 mile visibility in the downtown area.

Lightning struck a porch of a mobile home in Picture Rocks, creating a fire. The fire spread into the home, causing damage.  One person suffered minor burn injuries to his hands and wrists while attempting to extinguish the fire.
Severe thunderstorm winds downed 20 power poles near the intersection of Valencia Road and Ajo Way.
A trained spotter reported near zero visibility in blowing dust at mile marker 214 along Interstate 10.
Strong thunderstorm downburst winds downed 4 small trees.  Minor roofing damage was reported with missing roof tiles, and one street sign was blown down.
Severe thunderstorm downburst winds downed several power poles and 10 power lines west of Sells. This caused a power disruption to the Papago Farms, Pisinimo, and Hickiwan areas.
Strong thunderstorm downburst winds downed or snapped off 18 power poles in Green Valley. One of the power poles landed on a house.
A trained spotter reported blowing dust, with visibility less than 1/8 mile between Eloy and Picacho. Winds were estimated to be near 50 mph.

A trained spotter reported many trees were downed in the central part of Safford. ASOS measured a 63 mph thunderstorm wind gust at the Safford Regional Airport.|Amateur radio operators reported numerous power poles down near Safford.

Severe thunderstorm downburst winds blew off approximately one half of the roof of a tire shop at Golf Links Road and Kolb Road. The ceiling collapsed causing extensive damage. Downed power lines were reported near 20th and Craycroft Streets. Roof damage to a house was reported near Scarlett Street and Koralee Street. Several trees fell on cars parked at the Tucson Convention Center.

Law enforcement reported 1/4 mile visibility in blowing dust at Guthrie, with strong winds in progress. A trained spotter reported a visibility of 50 feet in blowing dust, along Highway 75, 4 miles southeast of Guthrie. Law enforcement reported 50 feet visibility in blowing dust at the Graham County sheriff office.

Law enforcement reported visibility less than 1/2 mile due to blowing dust at San Simon. Visibility of 1/4 mile in blowing dust was observed on the Arizona Department of Transportation webcam along Interstate 10 near Bowie. The peak gust at the webcam site was 46 mph.

A trained spotter reported visibility less than 50 feet in blowing dust along U.S. Highway 191 south of Safford. Wind gusts of 50-55 mph were reported by ASOS and trained spotters in the Safford area.
ASOS measured a 62 mph thunderstorm wind gust at Fort Huachuca.

Severe thunderstorm winds estimated at 60 mph downed two large trees near the |intersection of La Cholla Boulevard and River Road.  These trees were tall enough to pull down a power line on the opposite end of the street. Another large tree near the intersection of Cortaro Farms Road and Camino de Oeste was downed by the thunderstorm winds, falling through a fence and into a swimming pool.

Severe thunderstorm microburst winds caused significant damage to mobile homes at Mescal.  At least two mobile homes suffered roof damage or roof collapse. Several awnings on the mobile homes were destroyed. Thunderstorm winds were estimated to be near 70 mph.
Broadcast media reported that a swift water rescue was performed in Corona de Tucson.
A trained spotter measured a thunderstorm wind gust of 62 mph.

Thunderstorm microburst winds estimated at 60 mph downed several trees near the intersection of Lambert Lane and La Canada Drive in Oro Valley. The trees ranged in diameter from 5 to 10 inches. Some minor roof tile damage was also reported.

Scattered thunderstorms produced locally heavy rainfall near the intersection of State Highway 80 and Old Divide Road, approximately 2 miles northwest of Bisbee.  Rainfall was not excessively heavy, with radar estimates of near 1.25 inch. However, an earlier fire burned hillsides in the area in May 2009, leaving the landscape prone to flash flooding.  Flooding and debris flows destroyed portions of the road and surrounding culverts, and forced the closure of Old Divide Road.
Strong southwest winds ahead of an approaching cold front produced blowing dust across southeast Pinal county. Blowing dust produced zero visibility on Interstate 10 near Red Rock.
Strong southwest winds ahead of an approaching cold front produced blowing dust across Pinal and Pima counties. Blowing dust produced zero visibility on Interstate 10 at the Pima/Pinal county line.

Strong winds associated with a passing cold front created blowing dust across Cochise county into the overnight hours. Blowing dust created limited visibility on Interstate 10, which led to a three vehicle collision about 20 miles east of Willcox. A commercial truck entered the dust storm and slowed down due to the low visibility. A freight truck collided with the commercial truck from behind, before the freight truck was struck by a bus from behind as well. Three people from the three vehicles suffered injuries.

Strong west and southwest winds continued well into the evening hours as a strong cold front passed through southeast Arizona. A trained spotter measured a wind gust of 60 mph at Bisbee in Cochise county. The spotter noted moderate broken tree branches at the time, along with flying debris and some minor roof damage. ASOS at Fort Huachuca measured a wind gust of 62 mph.

Local areas of blowing dust along Interstate 10 resulted in several vehicle collisions near the Casa Grande and Eloy areas during the morning hours. A fatal collision occurred at approximately 10:30 AM near mile marker 213, between a mini-van and tractor/trailer.  Locally dense blowing dust reduced visibility, causing the mini-van to collide with the tractor/trailer from behind. This collision resulted in two fatalities and one serious injury, all of them occupants of the mini-van. The two occupants of the tractor/trailer were not injured. A total of four other accidents occurred as a result of the locally dense blowing dust, all of them near mile markers 214 and 215 on Interstate 10. One of these collisions involved six vehicles, and three of them resulted in an unknown number of injuries.

A trained spotter reported a funnel cloud from a thunderstorm between Douglas and McNeal in Cochise County.  After obtaining pictures of this funnel cloud from the broadcast media, it was determined that this funnel was briefly in contact with the ground.  Therefore, the funnel was classified as a brief tornado touchdown.  There was no apparent damage from this EF-0 tornado.
Blizzard conditions occurred at the highest elevations in Northern Greenlee County with very strong winds and limited visibility. Over 20 inches of snow fell.
Blizzard conditions occurred on Mt. Graham with strong winds gusting over 85 mph, near zero visibility and about 18 inches of snow.
About a foot of snow fell on Mt. Lemmon in the Santa Catalina Mountains.
Heavy snow occurred at Hannagan Meadow with over 20 inches during this storm.
About 18 inches of snow occurred on Mt. Graham above 9000 feet.
About 20 inches of snow occurred at the top of Mt. Graham at an elevation above 10,000 feet.

Widespread damaging winds occurred across Cochise County during the overnight hours.  Law enforcement reported winds blew out windows of some businesses in Sierra Vista.  Wind gusts near 70 mph blew portions of a roof off a warehouse in Sierra Vista, with the debris striking nearby power lines and causing power disruptions.  Roof damage was also reported at a motel in Sierra Vista, with about half of the roof removed.  Debris from the roof landed in a nearby parking lot, damaging several cars.  High winds damaged a large sign at a restaurant, with numerous traffic signs receiving damage throughout the Sierra Vista area.  Several reports of fallen trees and broken limbs were received, and at least four people in Sierra Vista reported falling trees causing damage to their vehicles. Strong winds caused damage to numerous power poles and power lines in Sierra Vista and surrounding Cochise County, resulting in power outages for thousands of homes and businesses. Many other power poles were damaged by the strong winds near Bowie, San Simon, and Willcox. The ASOS at Fort Huachuca measured a wind gust of 71 mph at 12:38 AM MST.

A trained spotter measured a wind gust of 70 mph three miles northeast of Canelo at 3:10 AM MST. Strong winds caused damage to numerous power poles and lines in Santa Cruz County, causing power outages to thousands of residents in the Sonoita, Elgin and Patagonia areas. A rancher near Sonoita reported 2 barn roofs were blown off by the high winds.

Strong winds gusted to near 70 mph across portions of eastern Pima County during the overnight hours, causing damage in several areas.  Portions of a roof blew off a residence on West Rama Drive in Green Valley, with the debris hitting several nearby mobile homes.  Winds downed several trees in the Green Valley and Sahuarita areas. |High winds also removed a roof from another residence in southwest Tucson, near the intersection of Cardinal Avenue and Valencia Road.  Strong winds also downed hundreds of trees on Mt. Lemmon, near Summerhaven.   Many of these trees damaged power lines as they fell, with dozens of homes and businesses spending several days without power.

High winds caused extensive damage to a manufactured home in Lower Covered Wells.  The roof was completely torn off the home, with damage to the walls as well.  Insulation was left in nearby tree branches.  Another roof was blown off a single wide manufactured home 2 miles northwest of Topawa.  No injuries were reported from either home.
The SNOTEL at Hannagan Meadow recorded 11 inches of snow in less than 12 hours from a fast moving storm.
The ASOS at the Bisbee-Douglas Airport measured a wind gust of 59 mph at 340 pm MST.
Strong winds caused damage to power lines at the intersection of Irvington Road and 12th Avenue in south Tucson.  The winds resulted in low hanging power lines which created a traffic hazard.

Strong winds uprooted a large dead tree near the intersection of First Avenue and Highway 191 in Safford during the early morning hours.  The tree toppled onto an unoccupied residence, causing some roof damage to the home.
ASOS at Fort Huachuca measured a wind of gust of 69 mph at 11:15 PM MST.
A trained spotter reported near zero visibility in blowing dust at mile marker 210 on Interstate 10.

A trained spotter reported near zero visibility due to blowing dust in Avra Valley, along Pump Station Road.  The air traffic control tower at Davis-Monthan Air Force Base reported 1/4 mile visibility in blowing dust.
About 10 inches of snow occurred in Northern Greenlee County around Rose Peak and Hannagan Meadow.
A foot of snow occurred at the top of Mt. Graham.
About 9 inches of snow fell at Summerhaven on Mt. Lemmon.
Three and one half inches of snow fell at the base of the Chiricahua Mountains at 5300 feet with considerably more snow at the top of the mountains.
Heavy snowfall of 12 to 20 inches combined with low visibility and strong winds to result in blizzard conditions across Northern Greenlee County.
Storm total snow accumulations up to 36 deep occurred at the top of Mt. Graham with wind gusts of 60 to 80 mph, which led to near zero visibilities in blowing snow.
The telescopes on Mt. Lemmon at 9100 feet had at least 12 inches of snow. This combined with strong wind resulted in low visibility and blowing snow producing blizzard conditions.
Blizzard conditions occurred on the mountains above 7000 feet in Santa Cruz County.
Blizzard conditions occurred on the Chiricahua Mountains above 7000 feet in Cochise County.
Heavy snow occurred across Northern Greenlee County.
Heavy snow accumulated to a depth of 3.5 in the town of Oracle.
Heavy snow occurred at elevations above 5000 feet in Graham County.
Six inches of snow accumulated on top of Kitt Peak.
Heavy snow accumulated at the lower elevations of the Santa Catalina Mountains.
Five inches of snow occurred near Sonoita.
Heavy snow occurred in numerous low elevation areas of Cochise County including Tombstone where 2 inches accumulated.
The Blue River upstream from Clifton rose out of its banks. The river was still above bankfull at 8 AM MST.

Sixteen hikers were trapped on Sabino Canyon Trail at approximately 11 AM on January 21st after the stream rose above its banks, covering low water crossings.  The San Simon and Vamori Washes in the Tohono Oodham Nation rose 1-2 feet out of their banks during the evening of January 21st.  Several other washes flowed out of their banks, resulting in barricaded roadways near Saguaro National Park East and West, including East Tucson and Avra Valley. A motorist was trapped in the Canada del Oro Wash near Rancho del Lago at approximately 7 AM on January 22nd.  A swift water rescue was performed to rescue the stranded motorist.

Several reports of high winds and wind damage were received from Cochise County during the afternoon and evening hours. The ASOS at Fort Huachuca measured a wind gust of 63 mph at 1:55 PM MST.  At approximately 6 PM, a 70-foot transmission power pole was downed by the high winds along Buffalo Soldier Trail near Sierra Vista, resulting in a loss of power to approximately half of Sierra Vista.  Seven additional power poles were downed near the intersection of Ramsey Road and Highway 92, resulting in power losses to another 500 residences.  A trained spotter measured a wind gust of 67 mph at Bisbee at 10:39 PM MST, while another trained spotter measured a wind gust of 78 mph, 6 miles northwest of Pearce-Sunsites, at 11:30 PM MST.  Damaging winds downed several trees across Monument Roadway near Chiricahua National Monument.
High winds overturned an empty tractor trailer on Interstate 10 near Picacho.

Damaging thunderstorm winds downed the main transmission power line on the Tohono Oodham Nation, at approximately 9 PM.  A major power failure resulted, affecting over 15,000 people.  Mesonet at Sasabe measured a thunderstorm wind gust of 58 mph at 9:33 PM MST.

High winds caused significant roof damage to several structures in the Tohono Oodham Nation.  One residence roof was damaged in Sells, one in Gu Vo, and three more in Hickiwan.  The residents of the damaged homes were displaced into shelters.  In addition, hundreds of saguaro cacti across the Tohono Oodham Nation were blown over by the damaging winds.
Eleven inches of snow occurred at the Hannagan Meadow snotel.
Eight to twelve inches of snow fell on Mt. Graham above 6000 feet.
Eight to ten inches of snow fell on Mt. Lemmon at an elevation of about 8000 feet.
A trained spotter estimated a wind gust of 94 mph near Ajo at 5:20 PM MST.
Mount Hopkins RAWS, which is 3 miles south of Madera Canyon, measured a wind gust of 63 mph at 1:19 AM MST.
The RAWS at Guthrie measured a 69 mph wind gust at 12:04 AM MST.

Damaging thunderstorm winds downed power lines which fell on top of several mobile homes on North Shannon Road in northwest Tucson.  A total of six houses were evacuated.  A small fire started in one mobile home, burning the attic and causing smoke damage to the interior of the house.  A tree approximately one foot in diameter was downed by thunderstorm winds near the intersection of Oracle Road and Wilds Road.

High winds resulted in many reports of damage across eastern Pima County.  Mesonet at Summerhaven on Mount Lemmon measured a wind gust of 75 mph at 1:37 PM.  A power pole was downed near the intersection of Wetmore Road and La Cholla Road in Tucson.  Damaging winds tore the roof off a house at Three Points around 3 PM, with the roof landing on a nearby truck. Near Green Valley, several traffic signals were damaged at Duval Mine and La Canada Roads, and at Calle Verde and Nogales Highway.  More traffic signals were damaged by the high winds in Sahuarita, on Sahuarita Boulevard.  High winds downed several power lines in Oro Valley, and several trees in Sahuarita during the late afternoon hours.  Just southeast of Sahuarita, the winds caused partial roof damage to a pecan processing plant.   |A large tree was downed, falling into a house near 9500 East Harrison Circle in east Tucson at approximately 5 PM.  High winds damaged a parking awning at an apartment complex at Ina and Mona Lisa in Tucson.  Another tree was downed by the winds near Congress and Grande.  Throughout the evening hours, numerous trees and power lines were downed on Mount Lemmon near Summerhaven.  Frequent wind gusts near 70 mph on Mount Lemmon resulted in a complete power outage on the mountain.

Graham County law enforcement performed two swift water rescues just south of Safford during the late evening hours of January 21st.  Deputies responded at 10:15 PM to a truck caught in a wash on Chastain Lane, just north of Highway 366.  Law enforcement rescued the motorist of the truck.  There were no injuries, but the truck was fully engulfed by the water.  At approximately the same time, law enforcement spotted a van stuck in Stockton Wash, along Stockton Road south of Roper Lake.  The occupants of the van exited the vehicle and waded to safety, before the van was washed further down Stockton Wash.
Several inches of snow occurred in the lower elevations of the Santa Catalina Mountains above 4500 feet.
The town of Oracle had two inches of snow.
There was about 14 of snow on top of Mt. Graham.
There was heavy snow accumulation at the top of Mt. Lemmon in the Catalina Mountains.

The ASOS at the Bisbee-Douglas Airport measured a wind gust of 60 mph at 12:31 PM MST.  The ADOT weather station at San Simon on Interstate 10 measured a wind gust of 60 mph. Several trained spotters in Cochise County reported wind gusts near  60 mph during the late morning and afternoon hours, with one trained spotter in Hereford reporting minor shingle roof damage at about 1:30 PM.

A fatal three car collision occurred on Interstate 10 in Pinal County near mile marker 214 and Picacho State Park.  At approximately 12:45 PM MST, a semi-truck slowed down on the interstate due to limited visibility in blowing dust.  A car following the semi-truck failed to slow down, and lost control as it attempted to avoid a collision with the semi.  The car collided with a wall and the semi, before being struck by a third car.  The driver of the second car died on scene.
Fort Huachuca ASOS measured a wind gust of 59 mph.

Two men were injured due to a lightning strike on a golf course.  One man suffered life threatening injuries, which he later died from.  Another man was about 50 feet away, and received a milder shock from the lightning strike.

Thunderstorm winds caused roof damage to six homes in Pisinimo, with two complete roof failures reported, and four roofs partially damaged.  Several power poles were damaged by the thunderstorm winds as well, with five communities reporting power outages.

Thunderstorm downburst winds caused wind damage across portions of the Tucson metro area. Several trees and power lines were downed near the intersection of Ina and Oracle Roads, and the winds caused some minor roof damage in this area as well.  Another power pole was downed near Ajo Way and 6th Avenue, and also near Glenn and Alvernon Way. Small trees were reported in the road near the intersection of Grant and Wilmot.

Thunderstorms produced heavy rainfall that resulted in flash flooding across portions of Cochise County. An automated rain gauge 3 miles southeast of Dragoon reported 2.6 inches of rain in less than 50 minutes.  A vehicle stranded in Terry's Wash was pulled out of the wash by a trained spotter.  Two people stranded in Prude Wash from their vehicle were assisted by the Cochise County sheriff.  Prude Wash, which is normally dry, was running about 3 feet deep.

The ASOS at the Bisbee-Douglas Airport measured a wind gust of 68 mph at 556 pm MST. Law enforcement reported that thunderstorm winds blew a roof off a residence on Double Adobe Road, approximately 7 miles west of the Bisbee-Douglas Airport.  The Bisbee sheriff reported thunderstorm winds blew a roof completely off a large barn along Burnt Adobe Road, and snapped four power poles. A tree was uprooted and fell on a building at the Douglas Municipal Airport.
ASOS at the Bisbee-Douglas Airport measured a thunderstorm wind gust of 58 mph at 731 PM MST.
Law enforcement reported Ward Canyon Road was closed due to flooding.

Severe thunderstorm winds impacted much of Santa Cruz County.  Law enforcement reported a tree was downed by the winds near the intersection of State Highway 82 and Duquesne Road.  A trained spotter measured a wind gust of 60 mph near Rio Rico, and another trained spotter measured a wind gust of 58 mph at Nogales.

Severe thunderstorm winds caused damage near the village of Sheldon in Greenlee County. Several trees were uprooted, and a backyard trampoline was blown 100 yards by the thunderstorm winds.  Doors of mobile homes were blown inward.
AWOS at Pioneer Airfield measured a thunderstorm wind gust of 66 mph at 220 PM MST.

Severe thunderstorm winds caused damage across southern portions of Tucson.  A trained spotter reported several trees downed near Rita Ranch at 5 PM MST.  Power lines were reported down by the winds at two different locations near the Tucson International Airport.  Thunderstorm winds ripped the roof off a mobile home near the intersection of Interstate 19 and Valencia Road.  In addition, several other trees and power lines were downed by the thunderstorm winds across southwest portions of Tucson.  One of these trees was downed on a residence.
A trained spotter reported two chain link fence support poles were downed by thunderstorm winds.
Severe thunderstorm winds downed three power poles on Manville Road, with one of them falling on a police vehicle.  The police officer was safely extracted from the vehicle with no injuries.

Torrential rainfall in the Huachuca Mountains led to flash flooding at the Ramsey Canyon Preserve.  USGS rain gauges measured 3.82 inches of rainfall, leading to rapid rises in Ramsey Creek.  Ramsey Canyon Road was closed at Calle Metate due to flooding and debris.

Thunderstorms produced torrential rainfall on the north side of the Catalina Mountains, producing flash flooding.  Rainfall estimates were locally as high as six inches in portions of southeast Pinal County, specifically near Camp Bonito. Law enforcement barricaded Mt. Lemmon and Peppersauce Roads due to flash flooding.  A trained spotter measured 2.40 inches of rain 4 miles southeast of Oracle.
Law enforcement reported U.S. Highway 191 flooded near Wards Canyon and Clifton.
Lightning struck a home in Sierra Vista, and caused a fire near the kitchen stove.
Lightning struck a home, causing a fire in the attic.  The home was unoccupied at the time, and there were no injuries.

A pecan grove worker was struck by lightning while working near Green Valley. The man received non-life threatening injuries. A palm tree was also set ablaze by a lightning strike in the 700 block of West Rio San Pedro in Green Valley.
The Willcox sheriff reported that thunderstorm winds blew down an outbuilding in Bowie.

A lightning strike caused a house fire during the early morning hours of July 20th.  The lightning strike likely occurred around 1 AM as storms impacted north Tucson, with the sparks smoldering in the roof's insulation until a neighbor noticed the fire spreading around 5 AM. The fire resulted in extension damage to the home before the fire was extinguished.

A severe thunderstorm microburst produced damaging winds in Rio Rico.  A portion of a home's roof was blown off, and brought down a power line as it landed in Rio Rico Drive.  Thunderstorm winds also blew down several dying trees between the Santa Cruz River bridge and the railroad tracks, and blew down a cyprus tree onto the roof of a home on East Rio Rico Drive.  Winds were measured on a neighbor's anemometer at 75 mph.

A strong thunderstorm produced a well-developed funnel cloud near Sonoita.  Video of the funnel cloud was obtained through the broadcast media.  There was no direct evidence from the video that the funnel made contact with the ground.
Thunderstorm winds downed several power poles and power lines near the intersection of Pima Mine Road and Nogales Highway.
Several roads, including Sahuarita Road and Old Nogales Highway, were closed due to flooding caused by heavy rain. Franco Wash flowed across Summit Road in two spots, also resulting in its closure.

Torrential rainfall across portions of eastern Pima county resulted in numerous reports of flash flooding in the Tucson metro area.  Flash flooding was observed on Tanque Verde Creek.  The flow of the creek peeked at 11.69 feet at Tanque Verde Guest Ranch, resulting in the flooding of approximately 30 homes on Barbary Coast Road, Gold Dust Road, and Kitt Carson.  Additionally, numerous swift water rescues were performed in the Tucson metro area, near the county fairgrounds, in the Recon Valley area, and on the Old Spanish Trail in the Hilton Head Ranch area.
The Santa Cruz River near Trico Road was reported to be topping its banks.

Flash flooding from rainfall south of the International Border resulting in the Nogales Wash rising 7 feet in 15 minutes. This caused some damage to the bank protection including three concrete panels in the wash.  Part of Old Tucson Road, which parallels the wash, was partially eroded.
The Santa Cruz river at Cortaro Rd rose to about 3 feet above its flood stage.
There was a 6 foot rise on Nogales Wash in 30 minutes with flooding downstream from the gauge.
Sweetwater wash flooded which covered Camino Del Cerro Rd. Silverbell Road also flooded.
Banning Creek flooded along Highway 82. Several homes were temporarily cutoff from the main road.

Flooding started at about 1035 PM in Cienega Creek southeast of Tucson. Thereafter, heavy rains in the Tucson metro area led to flash flooding in numerous streets in Tucson including at least one swift water rescue.
There was flash flooding on Black Rock and Sanders Road in Fort Thomas.

The lightning-caused Paradise fire burned over 6300 acres of the Apache-Sitgreaves National Forest east of Hannagan Meadow. While no structures were threatened, a 10 mile stretch of highway 191 was closed for several days due to smoke.  An incident meteorologist from NWS Tucson was assigned to the fire for nearly 2 weeks. The fire was turned over to a local Type 3 team on the morning of June 29th.
A 6 inch diameter tree was uprooted by microburst winds.
Several sections of Moson Road were covered in flood waters and debris. Spotter reported a rainfall total of 2.30 inches.
Nickel size hail began at 520 pm, eventually growing as large as 1.25 inches in diameter.
Flood waters flowed across the right lane of Highway 90 north of Huachuca City.
Numerous streets southeast of Sierra Vista were flooded.  A spotter report of 2.45 inches of rain was received.
Lightning struck palm tree in the front yard of a home on Abrego Road, which spread to other nearby trees.
Thunderstorm winds snapped three power poles in half near Catalina Highway and Melpomene Way.
Law enforcement reported windows blown out of a house in Sells.

Law Enforcement reported Brewery Gulch and several streets flooded in Old Town Bisbee and Banning Creek northwest of Bisbee also flooded.  In addition, flooding damaged fiber-optic lines near Tombstone.
Law enforcement reported penny size hail covering the ground at mule tunnel northwest of Bisbee.
Severe thunderstorms resulted in tree limbs eight inches in diameter downed near Elgin.

Local broadcast media reported up to 3 dozen trees damaged or uprooted in Rancho Vistoso neighborhood.  A few ceramic roof tiles were also blown off homes.  In addition, a NWS Employee reported several trees down in Dove Mountain with one tree leaning up against a home.  There was only slight tile damage to the home.  Also, local broadcast media reported trees and power lines down in Marana at Interstate 10 and Marana/Trico Road as well as a roof ripped off a mobile home. The Marana Airport also sustained damage.  Two small airplanes were ripped from their tie down chains and were flipped over while another plane was blown into a field. A large hangar door was blown off its tracks and a few other hangars also sustained light damage.  In the same area, several power poles and lines were downed on Twin Peaks Road east of N. Sandario Road.

A storm spotter reported that several streets in Ajo were beginning to flood as of 1:45 pm.  Thereafter, at 2:47 pm a report from law enforcement stated that all roads along the Gibson Wash were barricaded due to water over the road crossings.  The affected road crossings included Rasmussen Road, 22nd Avenue, and Highway 85.
A trained weather spotter measured a thunderstorm wind gust of 91 mph and law enforcement estimated wind gusts of 70 mph in town, but no damage was reported in Ajo.

Thunderstorms developed and moved across southern portions of Tucson producing 50 mph winds at the Tucson International Airport, but no damage was reported.  Storms moved to the northwest through western portions of Tucson with an outflow racing out in advance.  Damage occurred to six saguaro cacti, one which was over 35 feet tall, at El Camino De Cerro and the Tucson Mountains.  Tucson weather observation site CW8334, which is 5 miles southeast of the damage, recorded a wind gust of 42 mph at 5:09 pm.  Based on damage and stronger velocities where the damage was reported, winds were estimated to be about 50 mph.
An isolated severe thunderstorm produced a downburst in the vicinity of Snyder Road and Houghton Road downing several power poles and lines.

An owner of a grape vineyard in Elgin reported hail for 15 minutes with the largest being golf ball size (1.75).  Damage to the vineyard was extensive, with nearly all the 2010 grape crop lost.  Crop losses at this one vineyard were estimated at six tons which translated to between 10 and 15 thousand dollars, ultimately resulting in a loss of wine valued at 100 to 150 thousand dollars.  Extensive damage was also sustained at other vineyards in area.  Hail also dented vehicles and broke their windows.

This report goes along with thunderstorm which produced 1.75 inch diameter hail in Elgin.  Just before and during the storm, the vineyard owner reported an estimate of at least 60 mph winds.  Damage was limited to farm structures and not dwellings.
A trained spotter reported wind damage to awnings of a residence near Dragoon. The Willcox sheriff reported a horse was killed near Cochise, after a downed power line electrocuted the animal.

Heavy rain caused poor visibility and ponding of water on Interstate 10.  The driver of an automobile lost control of vehicle in the rain and crashed into a semi-tractor trailer which had slowed to under 15 mph because of the rain. The driver of the automobile died at the scene.  In addition, heavy rain caused a berm to breach, which flooded an equestrian center. Hay and feed used for horses at the facility was ruined.
Several 75 to 100-year-old trees were uprooted in Bisbee and Naco.
San Simon Wash west of Pisinimo overflowed its banks, cresting at 8.3 feet, just above its 7 foot flood stage. A tributary, Gu Vo Wash, flooded Indian Road 28.
Very heavy rain in Nogales, Sonora caused the Nogales Wash to rise 7 feet in less than one hour. The wash rose above flood stage, causing erosion to one roadway in Nogales, Arizona.
Thunderstorm winds downed tree limbs.
Lightning struck a palm tree at the Randolph Community Center. A fire was ignited, which spread to surrounding brush, prompting the evacuation of the center.

Thunderstorms produced heavy rain of up to 2 inches across portions of the Tucson metro area. Heavy rains resulted in a vehicle stalling in rising water at the intersection of Tucson Blvd. and Elm Street at 3:20 pm. By 4:00 pm, numerous streets were flooding near the University of Arizona campus in Tucson. Heavy rains falling near Ryan Field Airport resulted numerous washes flooding into residential neighborhoods.  At 6:00 pm, firefighters pulled an 11 year old boy out of Alamo Wash near Tucson Medical Center.

Local law enforcement reported that Highway 191 between Safford and Interstate 10 had been closed due to flooding.  At 7:00 pm, a spotter located in southern portions of Safford reported that he had received just over 3 inches of rainfall and that a majority of surrounding roads were impassable due to street flooding.  According to Thatcher Police, a few homes near the Eastern Arizona College had water seep into their garages, one apartment suffered water damage, and the back room of a home on Fourth Avenue had water running into it.  Also, a home south of Safford reported flood damage, and the Highway Department closed Safford/Bryce Road from Eighth Ave. to Bryce Eden Road due to flooding and debris.  A vehicle also stalled in running water on Quattro Cerros Road near the Artesia area south of Safford.  Water was running through the vehicle, but two passengers were able to get out.  There were also several other reports of washed out roads and drainage problems.

Thunderstorms dropped heavy rain with amounts ranging from 1 inch up to 3.5 inches, causing numerous streets to flood in Sierra Vista. In addition, the Hereford Road Bridge at the San Pedro River was closed due to flooding.

Thunderstorms developed over eastern portions of the Tucson area around 2:30 pm MST.  Storms slowly moved to the east at around 5 to 10 mph dropping heavy rainfall and putting out thunderstorm winds in excess of 60 mph.  The first reports of damage were received at 3 pm on the east side of Tucson.  Several tree limbs were downed on Columbus Blvd, with a few power poles down on 6th street.  At 3:09 pm, reports were received of several street signs down in the La Paloma Estates.  By 3:15 pm, reports were coming in from the media about several roofs damaged in eastern sections of Tucson. Also around 3:15 pm, spotters reported several large trees downed in east Tucson, including trees down on 22nd St and Broadway Blvd. A large was blown into an election polling station building near S. Alvernon and E. Benson Highways in southern Tucson.
Thunderstorms moving into Oracle resulted in trees and power lines downed across a roadway.  The most extensive damage was a roof blown off of a home located on Bonito Drive in Oracle.
Local Law Enforcement reported several trees and power lines down after thunderstorms moved through Whetstone.
After a majority of the thunderstorm activity had started to wind down, lightning struck a house in Oro Valley.  The house then caught fire causing extensive damage.

The Benson News-Sun reported that a man was pulled from a running wash after he attempted to drive through 2 feet of running water on an adjacent street.  The force of the water on the street carried his car into the wash and up against a concrete wall.  The driver then attempted to get out of the vehicle, but fell 10-15 feet down into the wash underneath his car.  Fire crews were able to quickly rescue the driver.  He was escorted to the local hospital.  City officials also reported numerous washes flooding neighborhood streets.

The Benson News-Sun and a local city official reported extensive damage to much of the city of Benson from thunderstorm activity. The city official reported numerous mature and young trees uprooted, street signs bent or pulled completely out of the ground, damage to dwellings from uprooted trees, small sheds and car ports were lifted and thrown 50-75 feet, and shingle damage to numerous homes. Also, property fences were knocked over, camper trailers were turned over, and numerous power outages.  The newspaper added that one particular insurance provider received 40 claims from residents, mostly related to roof damage. Additional information from the newspaper stated that at least 80 street signs had to be replaced.  Extensive damage was also done to the Turquoise Hills Golf Course where numerous large trees were downed and buildings damaged.

The Benson News-Sun reported several lightning strikes causing damage and fires in and around Benson.  The most extensive lightning damage was done to two motors at the waste water treatment facility.  Lightning also damaged numerous transformers.

Very heavy rainfall fell across portions of southwest Cochise county, especially around the Sierra Vista and Hereford areas.  The Department of Highways reported that several roads in Sierra Vista and Hereford had to be closed due to street flooding.  In addition, several washes were flooding in the area.

Nearly stationary thunderstorms developed over southern portions of the Tucson metro causing very heavy rainfall.  This heavy rainfall lead to road closures in South Tucson including the closure of Hughes Access Road at South County Club Road.
Very heavy rainfall across portions of eastern Tucson brought flash flooding that resulted in a swift water rescue on the Alamo Wash at Lee St and Alamo Ave.
Thunderstorms developed over the Tucson metro area resulting in small hail and damaging winds up to 60 mph.  Spotters reported trees down at Campbell Ave and Skyline Road.

Spotters reported about five trees uprooted at Golf Links and Swan Road at the entrance to Davis-Monthan Air Force Base.  City officials also reported numerous arching power line wires and tree fires throughout the east side of the city.

Severe thunderstorm winds downed at least 15 one foot diameter trees, most up to 30 feet tall, in eastern and central Tucson. One tree was blocking the entrance to an apartment complex with another tree blocking Prudence Road just north of Speedway Blvd. Another tree was downed on Sarnoff Road at the intersection with Broadway Blvd. Power poles were also downed on Alvernon Way between Broadway and Speedway Blvd. Another tree was reported downed at Tucson Blvd and 6th St.

Severe thunderstorm wind gusts downed 7 power poles along Interstate 10 near Houghton Road. Thunderstorm winds quickly spread toward Tucson International Airport where the airport ASOS reported a peak wind gust of 60 knots (69 mph). A storm spotter also recorded a peak gust of 62 mph at Valencia and Kolb Roads. High winds resulted in 14 downed power poles along Hughes Access Road just south of the airport.  A downed tree fell on a home in the 100 block of W. Los Reales Road in South Tucson.

Thunderstorms produced very heavy rainfall across portions of east Tucson. Heavy rains resulted in storm drains being overwhelmed near Morris K. Udall Park at the intersection of Tanque Verde and Sabino Canyon Road. Up to four feet of water covered the park and intersection resulting in several vehicles stalling in the intersection.
Severe thunderstorms redeveloped over central Tucson, moved westward and generated high winds causing a car port to collapse in midtown Tucson and a 63 mph wind gust to be recorded at Ryan Air Field.

Thunderstorms developed over Clifton around 4:30 pm and intense rainfall resulted.  According to Clifton officials, 2.25 inches fell in about 45 minutes, on already saturated soil.  The storm resulted in tons of mud and rock piled on city streets.  Two unoccupied vehicles parked on Turner Avenue were washed down Ward's Canyon and into the San Francisco River.  A third vehicle was tossed onto its side in the canyon about 100 yards from the canyon's confluence with the river.  Flash flooding also resulted in damage to a main water line feeding Clifton.

Isolated storms formed south of the Tucson Metro area around 6:15 and quickly merged, formed a bowing segment, and raced north through the Tucson area.  As the storm moved through Tucson, a tree limb was downed at the intersection of Speedway and Wilmot.  A sign was also blown off of a shopping center facade near the intersection of Silverbell and Wade Road.  In addition, 70 knot winds were recorded on top of a three story building downtown.

events.cz_name: WHITE MOUNTAINS OF GRAHAM AND GREENLEE COUNTIES
events.event_narrative: Hannagan Meadow received about 2 feet of snowfall from this winter storm.
The Pinaleno mountains including the Mt. Graham area received well in excess of a foot of snow with this major winter storm.
The higher elevations of the Santa Catalina mountains received about 2 feet of snow for this event.
Some parts of the Tucson Metro area including the Vail area had about 2 inches of snowfall.
Several inches of snowfall occurred throughout portions of the Upper San Pedro River Valley.
Several inches of snow occurred mainly in northern Cochise county below 5000 feet.
Heavy snowfall occurred in the higher elevations of the Chiricahua Mountains above 6000 feet.
Heavy snowfall occurred in the higher mountain elevations.
About 4 inches of snowfall occurred in the Oracle area at an elevation about 4500 feet.

events.cz_name: UPPER GILA RIVER AND ARAVAIPA VALLEYS
events.event_narrative: The Fort Grant area of Graham County had about 6 inches of snowfall.
Two inches of snow occurred in elevations above 3000 feet in the Tucson Metro area including Catalina and Vail.

events.cz_name: WHITE MOUNTAINS OF GRAHAM AND GREENLEE COUNTIES
events.event_narrative: Eight inches of snow occurred at Hannagan Meadow at an elevation of about 9000 feet.
About eight inches of snow occurred on Mt. Graham at an elevation above 9000 feet.
Six inches of snow occurred in Oracle at an elevation of about 4500 feet.
Three inches of snow occurred at Redington Pass at an elevation of about 3500 feet.
Eight inches of snow occurred on Mt. Lemmon at an elevation of 8000 feet.
Eight inches of snow occurred at Kitt Peak at an elevation of near 7000 feet.
A trained spotter recorded a wind gust of 63 mph at 12:45 pm. The same spotter later recorded a gust of 73 mph at 119 pm. The high winds downed numerous telephone and cable television lines.

Strong winds threw an inflatable jumping castle into the air, later landing a 9 year old girl on a neighboring rooftop. The castle traveled about 100 feet and landed about 13 feet off the ground. The girl suffered serious head injuries. An 11-year old girl was also injured as she fell out of the castle as it flew through the air. It occurred in Continental Ranch in Marana.

Record cold resulted in two fatalities in the Tucson Metro Area. A woman in her late 30's was found dead in an alley near East Speedway and North Campbell Ave. A second woman was also found dead near East Grant and North Craycroft. An autopsy was performed.  Another person was also found lying out in the cold nearly frozen and was taken to the hospital with non-life threatening injuries.

Temperatures dropped into the mid to upper teens across the Tucson area overnight resulting in numerous burst water pipes. A water pipe at a main Metro Water location froze, leaving almost 30 residences and businesses without water on the northwest side. More than 200 customers in Tucson reported frozen or burst water pipes. In all, at least 2000 residents and businesses were without water at some point during the day. AAA saw a 20% increase in local calls on Thursday, mostly about dead car batteries. Davis-Monthan Air Force Base had several buildings damaged by flooding frozen fire sprinkler pipes, which resulted in the buildings being closed for safety reasons. The intersection of Grant Road and Stone Ave. was also closed due to a burst water main that was causing slick road conditions. The Reid Park Zoo was also closed due to numerous broken water pipes.  ||Southwest Gas Company also could not meet natural gas demand, which resulted in about 14,000 Tucson customers being without heat.||In Green Valley, over $17,000 in damage was sustained at 11 Green Valley recreational centers due to broken sprinkler systems. ||Untold numbers of plants, trees, and shrubs were also killed by the record cold, including the prized southern Arizona Saguaro Cactus.

Temperatures dropped to as low as 0 degrees across eastern Cochise County as several communities experienced frozen or burst water pipes. Most notably, Willcox received over 790 calls for frozen or burst water pipes. Damage was also done to Safeway when a pipe burst in the ceiling causing several ceiling tiles to collapse. The Willcox School District had a broken pipe in the wood shop room and a back flow preventer burst outside the wood shop causing minor water damage.||In Douglas, several businesses were closed due to broken pipes including; Chiricahua Community Health Center, Copper Queen Medical Associates, the Douglas Library and APS Energy. Douglas School District also canceled classes due to burst pipes. The worst damage was done to a home on Fourth Street when the pipes in the attic burst causing the ceiling to collapse and the home to be flooded.

events.cz_name: UPPER SANTA CRUZ RIVER AND ALTAR VALLEYS
events.event_narrative: The Upper Santa Cruz River Vally experienced numerous issues with broken water pipes as temperatures dipped into the upper single digits to mid teens. Robert Bracker Elementary School in Nogales was canceled due to broken pipes. An underground water line ruptured in the Monte Carlo neighborhood, where the road had to be dug up to replace the line. Also, an air release valve on a 16 inch pipeline that feeds the city water system from the Santa Cruz River burst, blasting water into the air. The Nogales Fire Department also responded to a two car collision caused by icy roads on Target Range Road. Four people were involved and two were injured and taken to the Holy Cross Hospital. ||In Patagonia, an elderly resident had to be evacuated to her sister's house after the pipes in the ceiling burst causing drywall to fall.||Also, ranchers near Sonoita reported a water pump bursting causing a cattle tank with thousands of gallons of water to drain out.

Several communities across the Upper San Pedro River Valley suffered from frozen and burst water pipes as temperatures dropped into the single digits to low teens. In addition, 4500 Sierra Vista Southwest Gas customers lost their natural gas flow. Most of the damage was at Fort Huachuca where over 400 homes suffered from broken water pipes with more than 100 homes sustaining damage. About 40 outpost buildings had ceilings collapse due to broken water pipes. Sierra Vista Fire Department also responded to several fire calls related to space heaters and candles.||In Benson, the city received over 100 calls regarding burst water pipes. The San Pedro Terrace Apartments on Pearl Street and the Desert Road Inn suffered damage from burst pipes and had to be evacuated. Residents and guests were transported to Sierra Vista hotels. A water pipe burst in the Benson Middle School Library ceiling causing damage to the ceiling, carpets, and shelves. Books on the shelves sustained light damage. The Benson Visitors and Community Center, Benson Public Library, and Cochise College Benson Center also sustained damage.||The St. David School District reported damage to one boiler, the main fire raiser for the sprinkler system, broken pipes in the weight-room wall and one drinking fountain. School did not have to be canceled.

events.cz_name: UPPER GILA RIVER AND ARAVAIPA VALLEYS
events.event_narrative: Temperatures dropped into the single digits across the Gila River Vally with wind chills dropping as low as -10 degrees. As a result, a water main line broke at Fifth Avenue and Second Street. More than 100 calls were received by Safford Utility in response to frozen pipes that later turned to broken pipes. Safford Fire Department responded to more than a dozen calls for malfunctioning sprinkler systems. Some businesses that received minor water damage were the Arizona Credit Union, the Veterans Administration Office and Thriftee Supermarket. ||In Thatcher, the Fire Department responded to the Thatcher school where sprinkler systems and backflow preventers in several buildings burst. ||Pima also had numerous water lines burst as a result of the cold. One pipe burst at the entrance to the Pima Fire Station. The Graham County Jail also had water damage sustained in the honor pod by a broken pipe.||Fire Departments in Safford, Thatcher and Pima also responded to fires involving space heaters and candles used to keep water pipes from freezing.

Strong winds downed power lines east of Naco, sparking a brush fire that resulted in an hour-long closure of roads in the Bisbee Junction area.
The Cochise County Sheriff's Office reported that a brush fire created dense smoke and the closure of Highway 90 between Camino de Tundra and Camino de Manana on Highway 90 in the Whetstone area.

events.cz_name: UPPER SANTA CRUZ RIVER AND ALTAR VALLEYS
events.event_narrative: Extreme drought conditions coupled with strong winds resulted in a human caused fire getting out of control and spreading into rugged terrain of Santa Cruz county. A total of 4,052 acres of grass, shrub, oak, and mesquite burned during May.

events.cz_name: UPPER SANTA CRUZ RIVER AND ALTAR VALLEYS
events.event_narrative: Extreme drought conditions coupled with strong winds resulted in a human caused fire getting out of control and spreading into rugged terrain of Santa Cruz county. The fire was started on May 30 and continued through mid June. A total of 68,078 acres of grass, shrub, oak, and mesquite burned. Two structures were lost including the historic Atascosa Lookout in the Atascosa Mountains and an outhouse at Pena Blanca Lake. The estimated total cost of resources devoted to fighting the wildfire was $5.5 million.

Strong daytime heating resulting in record high temperatures and dry conditions created a ripe environment for dust devils. One dust devil formed near Speedway Blvd. and N. 11th Ave. where an annual Children's Festival was in progress. The dust devil quickly moved across the yard lifting a jumping castle several feet into the air with two children inside. The jumping castle then traveled several feet before getting caught in telephone wires and landing in the median of Speedway Blvd. A 9-year-old girl was serious injured in the accident, suffering a broken shoulder, leg, and several fractures to her face. A 10-year-old boy also sustained injuries to the back of his head.

Strong daytime heating and unstable conditions caused several dust devils to form across the region. One dust devil formed at Hoffman Park located at the 4800 block of South Cecilia St. in Tucson. Parents were able to pull their children out of a jumping castle just before the stakes were pulled out of the ground as the jumping castle was lifted several feet into the funnel and tossed into a light pole. The dust devil also picked up several other pieces of debris before dissipating over the concrete street. Six children were injured by flying debris. Five were evaluated at the scene, while one 16-year-old boy was transported to a hospital with minor injuries.

Strong afternoon winds resulted in a dust storm along Interstate 10 between Red Rock and Picacho. A three vehicle accident was reported just north of Red Rock. One of the vehicles was a jack-knifed tractor-trailer. Northbound lanes were closed for approximately one hour and the interstate was backed up for several miles.

The Horseshoe 2 fire started on May 8 in Horseshoe Canyon in the Coronado National Forest. Gusty southwest winds caused the fire to grow over 9,000 acres on the first day. This extreme fire behavior was caused by extremely dry fuels caused by a long term drought and a killer winter freeze of oak trees. Residents of the communities of Paradise and Portal were evacuated at times due to thick smoke and from the threat of this rapidly growing wildfire overtaking these locations. By the end of May, 77,933 acres had been burned and 12 firefighters had suffered minor injuries.

The Horseshoe 2 fire continued to burn through much of the month of June as extremely dry conditions and fuels, and strong winds aided in the fire's growth. As the fire continued to grow to the northwest, the communities of Cave Creek Canyon, Paradise, Whitetail Canyon, West Turkey Creek, and West Pinery Canyon were evacuated. Crews were put in place to protect the communities, but some structures were lost. In all, 9 homes and 14 outbuildings burned, including the historic Barfoot fire lookout. Chiricahua National Monument in the northern portion of the fire was closed on June 3 and remained closed through the summer. ||One firefighter was injured when he and another lookout were caught between two burnouts. The firefighter required several stitches in his hand after using it to break a window for access to a rock shelter in order to escape the rapidly approaching flames. The fire passed over and into the shelter, but no injuries directly attributed to the fire occurred. However, this indirect injury, when added to the 12 suffered in May, brought the total to 13 firefighters indirectly injured fighting the Horseshoe 2 Fire.
Strong thunderstorm outflows raced through the Bisbee-Douglas Airport resulting in a measured wind gust of 56 knots. No damage or injuries were reported.
A strong thunderstorm outflow moved through the higher terrain of southern Greenlee and eastern Graham Counties.

Early morning thunderstorms produced brief gusty winds across South Tucson and resulted in one tree being uprooted, and another tree toppling over onto an apartment complex roof at Mission Road and Drexel Road. The Apartment complex suffered minor tile damage.

Strong surface winds occurred in Sierra Vista. Homeland Security's aerostat, an anti-trafficking balloon, broke free from its tether and crashed into the Canyon de Flores neighborhood in Sierra Vista. Equipment from the aerostat was picked up from 39 different sites throughout the neighborhood. Minor damage was reported to a few vehicles and homes, as well as a damage to power lines south of Fort Huachuca. The aerostat, based at the fort since 1986, was a total loss and will be replaced.

Extremely dry conditions continued during the month of May across all of southeast Arizona. Extreme drought conditions (D3) expanded to include all of Greenlee and Graham Counties, as well as extreme southeast Pinal County to start the month after an extremely dry April. May brought no measurable rainfall to a majority of southeast Arizona, including the Tucson Metro area. The White Mountains of northern Graham and Greenlee Counties received only a few hundredths of an inch of rain. The combination of extreme drought conditions, strong winds, hard winter freezes and the resulting dry fuels created extreme fire danger. This fire danger was realized on May 8 when a human caused fire in the Chiricahua Mountains, named Horseshoe 2, quickly grew out of control. Strong winds and prime fuels resulted in the Horseshoe 2 Fire growing over 9,000 acres on the first day alone. The Horseshoe 2 Fire charred 77,933 acres by the end of May. Over 83,000 acres had burned by the end of May in southeast Arizona with little containment.  ||Arizona Drought Watch reported very low soil moisture resulting in plant stress in the Santa Cruz River Basin. Native low water use plants were severely drought stressed with some cacti dying.

events.cz_name: UPPER SANTA CRUZ RIVER AND ALTAR VALLEYS
events.event_narrative: Abnormally dry conditions continued during the month of March. The southeast quarter of the state received less than 25% of average rainfall year-to-date and less than 50% for the water year (October to September). This lack of rainfall resulted in an upgrade from D2 conditions to D3 conditions across much of Cochise County on March 8. Later in the month on March 29, all of Cochise County as well as Santa Cruz County, southern Graham County, southern Greenlee County, and eastern Pima County were upgraded to D3 conditions. Prolonged drought conditions helped worsen critical fire weather conditions which helped contribute to numerous small brush fires. The Arizona Drought Watch report for extreme southeast Cochise County, including the Rio Bavispe watershed, found many ponds that normally have water during March were dry. Also, intermittent streams that normally flow were dry in many or all segments. Little to no green forage existed in the grasses or forbs, and pipelines and troughs have replaced most pond water resulting in significant agriculture impacts. The Arizona Drought Watch report for extreme southeast Pima County, including the Santa Cruz River watershed, found that drought impacts are present and severe. The flow in the Santa Cruz is less than last year and about half the average flow seen within drought years. Rising severity was also observed. Water levels were approximately two feet lower than last year and approxiamately six feet lower than pre-drought levels.

events.cz_name: UPPER SANTA CRUZ RIVER AND ALTAR VALLEYS
events.event_narrative: Dry conditions continued during the month of April across much of Arizona as only one significant winter storm moved through the state. Portions of southeast Cochise County received no measurable rainfall. Portions of south central Arizona received amounts from one tenth to one half inch while other areas, including eastern mountain ranges, received one tenth of an inch or less. More than 27,000 acres in Arizona have been consumed by wildfires through the end of April, mostly in the southern part of the state. Extremely dry conditions continued during the month of May across all of southeast Arizona. Extreme drought conditions (D3) expanded to include all of Greenlee and Graham Counties, as well as extreme southeast Pinal County to start the month after an extremely dry April. May brought no measurable rainfall to a majority of southeast Arizona, including the Tucson Metro area. The White Mountains of northern Graham and Greenlee Counties received only a few hundredths of an inch of rain. The combination of extreme drought conditions, strong winds, hard winter freezes and the resulting dry fuels created extreme fire danger. This fire danger was realized on May 8 when a human caused fire in the Chiricahua Mountains, named Horseshoe 2, quickly grew out of control. Strong winds and prime fuels resulted in the Horseshoe 2 Fire growing over 9,000 acres on the first day alone. The Horseshoe 2 Fire charred 77,933 acres by the end of May. Over 83,000 acres had burned by the end of May in southeast Arizona with little containment. Arizona Drought Watch reported very low soil moisture resulting in plant stress in the Santa Cruz River Basin. Native low water use plants were severely drought stressed with some cacti dying.

events.cz_name: WHITE MOUNTAINS OF GRAHAM AND GREENLEE COUNTIES
events.event_narrative: Strong gusty winds, along with a continued prolonged drought allowed for an unattended campfire to quickly spread out of control. Thanks to strong winds, the fire grew 1,445 acres by the end of the second day. On the 31st, the fire grew another 1,171 acres for a total of 2,616 acres chard in May. Fire activity was located in extreme northern Greenlee County west of Highway 191 along County Road 25. No evacuation orders were issued by the end of May, although portions of the Apache-Sitgreaves National Forest were closed.

Extreme drought conditions, coupled with adequate fuels and strong winds allowed a human caused fire to quickly spread out of control. The fire was first reported on June 12 by Border Patrol west of Hereford near the Mexico Border. Favorable weather conditions, rugged terrain, and extremely dry fuels allowed the fire to quickly spread out of control, growing 3,159 acres on the first day. By the end of the month, nearly 30,000 acres had burned. Strong southwest winds were funneled through the canyons of the Huachuca Mountains on July 14 allowing for a strong fire run into the city limits of Nicksville. Only a few homes and outbuildings were damaged or destroyed. A more significant run occurred of July 16 and 17 as strong winds pushed the fire into southern Sierra Vista resulting in several homes, outbuildings, and business either being damaged or destroyed. Several homes and outbuildings located in the Huachuca Mountains were also damaged or destroyed. A bulldozer sparked a fire on the army base of Ft Huachuca on June 18. That fire was quickly contained, but residents were evacuated. Thousands of residents were also evacuated from southern Sierra Vista during the blaze.

Heavy rain fell across portions of the Tucson Metro on July 4 with rainfall amounts ranging from 1 to 2.5 inches. The heaviest rains were reported in the Catalina Foothills and across eastern Tucson. This resulted in the Pantano Wash flooding several surface streets and low water crossings in southeast Tucson, including the closure of East Irvington at Houghton Road. Additional street closures included the 6500 block of Old Spanish Trail at Rincon Creek on the east side and Camino De La Tierra at the Rillito Wash in midtown.
Thunderstorm winds downed a tree and ripped off a porch roof near Houghton Road and Ridgeside Drive.

Lightning struck a tree causing the tree to fall on to the Zona Rio Apartments building, located near St Mary's Road and Bonita Ave. A family was trapped inside their third story apartment until rescued off the back balcony by Tucson Fire using their ladder truck.

Lightning struck a 35-foot palm tree causing the tree to catch fire. Fiery debris fell onto a home and car, but heavy rains were able to dose the flames on the home. The car sustained minor damage to the fenders.

A strong fast moving storm caused widespread damage across the Tucson area. Power lines and a large tree were downed near Oracle Road and Hardy Road. More power lines were downed near Park Avenue and Broadway Boulevard in midtown Tucson. Several additional trees were downed including two large trees in Vail, a 60-foot tree near Tanque Verde and Wrightstown Road, and a 100-foot tall tree onto a vehicle in northern Tucson. Two additional trees were also downed on vehicles. One fell on a car in the Fairview Manor near Miracle Mile and Fairview and another tree fell on a car near Broadway and Craycroft. The same tree also brought a light pole down on a truck. Strong winds also ripped a roof off a mobile home in southwest Tucson and destroyed several outbuildings throughout the city. In addition, winds peeled the roof off the Literacy of Life office in Mid-town. Over 20,000 Tucson Electric Power customers were without power after the storms passed.

events.cz_name: WHITE MOUNTAINS OF GRAHAM AND GREENLEE COUNTIES
events.event_narrative: The Wallow Fire continued to burn out of control during the entire month of June. While the brunt of the fire was burning in neighboring Apache County, the fire charred nearly 100,000 acres in northern Greenlee County. The Hannagan Meadow Lodge was evacuated and closed, followed by the closure of Highway 191. Most of the outbuildings and homes damaged were in Apache County, with only a few outbuildings destroyed in northern Greenlee County.
A strong thunderstorm outflow moved through the higher terrain of southern Greenlee and eastern Graham Counties.

Well above normal daytime temperatures settled over southern Arizona on June 27 and 28. On June 27th, a record 112 degrees was recorded at the Tucson ASOS. Several valley locations below four thousand feet reached heat criteria levels. Heat criteria was also reached in the higher elevations. The Chiricahua National Monument (5133 ft) recorded a high temperature of 102 degrees.

Extremely dry conditions continued in June with no rainfall to begin the month. The first Drought Monitor issued during June expanded D3 conditions to include all of Graham, Greenlee, and Cochise Counties. It also introduced the first D4 exceptional drought condition into extreme eastern Cochise County and extreme southern Greenlee County. The D4 drought areas had received no significant rainfall since October, 2010. The last measurable rainfall at Bisbee-Douglas International Airport was on February 27, 2011. The airport finally received two hundredths of an inch on June 29 bringing an end to 122 consecutive days without measurable rainfall. The Tucson Airport also went 81 days with no measurable rainfall, making it the fourth longest dry spell on record. ||The large Wallow Fire and Horseshoe 2 Fire prompted the U.S. Forest Service to close Coronado National Forest on June 10. However, a new fire, the Monument Fire, started on June 12 in the Huachuca Mountains that threatened the city of Sierra Vista. By the end of the month, these three massive fires had charred more than three-quarter of a million acres. ||The Arizona Drought Watch continued to report serious watershed conditions all across southern Arizona in June. Unusually low water levels in reservoirs, lakes, and ponds with unusually low flows in streams rivers, and springs. This resulted in unusually low forage and vegetation range productivity, along with poor forage nutrition and increased toxicity of forage. Due to drought-related wildfires, hundreds of thousands of acres of range land forest was lost. Agriculture impacts included limited cattle grazing which in turn caused a leaner herd that needed to be sent to market prematurely because of a lack of food and water sources. Tourism was also impacted from the closure of national and state parks due to wildfire concerns. Native reptile and amphibian species were also harmed as a result of dried up ponds and streams.

Strong thunderstorm winds resulted in significant damage around southern portions of the Tucson Metro area. Davis-Monthan Air Force Base recorded a wind gust of 67 knots (77mph) while the Tucson International Airport recorded a gust of 61 knots (70 mph). The most significant damage was sustained by businesses in South Tucson. Near Ajo Way and County Club, two industrial buildings sustained partial roof collapses with one business losing the entire roof. A Safeway Grocery Store in the Rita Ranch Village suffered a partial roof collapse. Several power poles and power lines were also downed with several blown transformers. Around 27,000 residents were without power at the peak of the storm. Several trees were downed, with trees falling on homes, cars, and into traffic creating road closures. The most significant tree damage was at the McGuire Hills Apartment Complex. Several trees were downed blocking access to many of the apartments.

A strong line of thunderstorms continued to track to the northwest across the Tucson area resulting in more significant wind damage. Several trees were downed along a line from River Road and Interstate 10 to the Gladden Farms neighborhood. In Gladden Farms, aside from trees downed, a twenty foot section of a brick wall was blown down. Additional damage was observed in Oro Valley with several trees down and outbuildings blown apart.

A trained spotter in Saddlebrooke reported significant thunderstorm wind damage. Several large, established trees were downed causing minor roof damage, and brick walls blown down. In Avra Valley, mesquite trees were snapped at the base while large limbs were broke off others.
Trained spotter reported one inch diameter hail covering the ground with hail depths up to 2 inches in spots.
Tohono O'odham Emergency Manager reported structural damage to two homes in Sells with estimated winds near 50 knots (58 mph). The homes both suffered partial roof collapses.

Tohono O'odham Nation Emergency Manager reported thunderstorm winds caused structural damage to two homes in Lukeville. One home suffered minor roof damage while the other home suffered a partial roof collapse. Another home was damaged in the Gu Vo District of the Tohono O'odham. The home had damage to the roof and walls.

Widespread rainfall amounts across the Tucson Metro area ranged from one half to three quarters of an inch with some spots receiving up to two inches. Several washes were running with some spilling over into local streets. This resulted in several streets being closed. There were also a stalled car on East Irvington at the Rodeo Wash near the Tucson International Airport. The driver was able to safely seek higher ground.
The Bisbee-Douglas International Airport ASOS recorded a 53 knot (61 mph) wind gust.

Widespread heavy rain ranging from one half to one and a half inches in Oro Valley and northern Tucson resulted in flash flooding. A woman had to be rescued from a wash as she was swept away downstream. She was taken to a local hospital and treated for hypothermia. Several area roads were closed including a large section of Magee Road between La Cholla Road and Oracle Road.
Spotter reported several one inch diameter hail stones.
Public reported hail as large as quarters covering the ground at La Canada Drive and Orange Grove Road.

Thunderstorm winds downed eight power poles along Oracle Road near Magee Road,  resulting in the closure of some lanes of Oracle Road. Significant tree damage was along Campbell Avenue between Glenn Street and Grant Road. A tree was also downed on a vehicle in a business parking lot near Ina Road and La Cholla Boulevard. A trained spotter measured a wind gust of 60 mph.
A Mesonet site recorded a wind gust of 51 knots (59 mph) at Tangerine Road and Thornydale Road. Several large trees were also downed in the Eagle Crest neighborhood in Saddlebrooke.
Public reported several palo verde trees downed in Sahuarita.

A trained spotter reported an estimated wind gust of 52 knots (60 mph) in northern Sahuarita. Several large trees and a few power poles were downed. The most significant damage was sustained on Pima Mine Road near Interstate 19 where a pole fell onto a moving vehicle. The driver sustained minor injuries and was held overnight for observation.
Willcox Police reported several minutes of one inch diameter hail.
Thunderstorm microburst winds downed 20 power poles in Sahuarita along La Canada Road. Several additional trees and branches were also downed.

Well above normal daytime temperatures settled over southern Arizona on June 27 and 28. On June 27th, a record 112 degrees was recorded at the Tucson ASOS. Several valley locations below four thousand feet reached heat criteria levels. Heat criteria was also reached in the higher elevations. The Chiricahua National Monument (5133 ft) recorded a high temperature of 102 degrees.
