Very heavy rainfall (1.5 to 3 inches) occurred over the Monument Fire Burn area in the Huachuca Mountains resulting in significant flash flooding and damage to areas in Ash, Miller and Carr Canyons, as well as along Highway 92. Heavy rain fell only over the Ash, Miller, and Carr Canyons, but due to the burn scars, water quickly flowed down the mountain to areas that received little or no rain. Boulders, trees, mud, and propane tanks were carried by the flood waters. At least a dozen homes were damaged with most having significant structural damage. A propane tank crashed through one home's wall and into the living room leaking liquid propane. Other homes had all their lawn furniture, fountains, and outbuildings washed away. The most significant damage was sustained by Beatty's Guest Ranch in Carr Canyon. The pond was filled with over 6 feet of mud, the camp restrooms were washed down the mountain, and several units were filled with mud. One of the camp areas has also been reported as being a new channel of Miller Creek. Rail Oaks Ranch had many of the same issues as Beatty's Ranch. Further down the mountains, water and mud roared over Highway 92 and into Nicksville where several homes were damaged and filled with mud. Due to impassable roads, at least 100 people became only accessible via helicopter for nearly 3 hours. Several additional communities were evacuated. Tombstone also lost 80% of its water supply due to pipes being damaged by erosion from the rapid runoff.

Heavy rain fell over portions of the Wallow Fire burned White Mountains resulting in flash flooding near Hannagan Meadow. A mud slide from rapid runoff forced the closure of Highway 191 from mile marker 232 to 239.

Heavy rain occurred over the Horseshoe 2 burn scar area of the Chiricahua Mountains. The Horseshoe 2 BAER team reported three washouts on Pinery Road in the northern portions of the Chiricahua Mountains.
Thunderstorm winds downed several power poles and lines in Douglas. A trained spotter measured a wind gust of 60 mph.

Well above normal daytime temperatures settled over southern Arizona on June 27 and 28. On June 27th, a record 112 degrees was recorded at the Tucson ASOS. Several valley locations below four thousand feet reached heat criteria levels. Heat criteria was also reached in the higher elevations. The Chiricahua National Monument (5133 ft) recorded a high temperature of 102 degrees.
A microburst caused localized damage near 22nd and Wilmot in Tucson. A roof was peeled off a house, with part of it landing 22nd Street.

A microburst over downtown Willcox caused damage along Haskell Street. A tin roof was blown off one building while part of a roof was peeled off another. Several trees were downed including a large tree in Railroad Park.

Thunderstorm winds blew off the roof of an industrial building in Sierra Vista. Part of the roof knocked over a brick wall. Part of one wall of the building also collapsed. Several trees and branches were also downed in the same area.
Thunderstorm winds flipped over a trailer home and downed several trees west of Santa Rosa.

Heavy rainfall fell across South Tucson with rainfall amounts ranging from one and a half inches to two inches. Significant street and neighborhood flooding occurred along Old Vail Connection from Wilmot Road to Interstate 19.

Heavy rainfall occurred over eastern Tucson with rainfall amounts in excess of one inch in less than one hour. A swift water rescue was performed near Tanque Verde Road and Houghton Road. A motorist drove into four feet of water before the vehicle stalled, turned 180 degrees, then floated into a group of trees. Firefighters were able to pull him out safely.
Thunderstorms produced an inch of rain in less than 30 minutes over the Horseshoe 2 burn area of the Chiricahua Mountains. This caused a flash flood and significant debris flow near Portal.
Thunderstorm winds flipped over a truck over near Interstate 19.
Heavy rains produced rainfall amounts greater than one inch in mid town Tucson. This resulted in several intersections being closed along First Street between Speedway Blvd. and Grant Rd.

Between one and three inches of heavy rain occurred over the Horseshoe 2 burn scar in the eastern Chiricahua Mountains. The result was flash flooding and a debris flow across Cave Creek Road and 42A Forest Road. The Research Center also noted the normally dry creek near their building was roaring with large amounts of debris in the water.

Thunderstorm winds blew through northwest portions of the Tucson area uprooting several trees from Ina Road and Interstate 10 to the Continental Ranch subdivision at Cortaro Road and Silverbell Road. Tree limbs were downed onto Interstate 10 creating traffic delays. Several trees were also downed in Arizona Pavilion Shopping Center. One tree in the Continental Ranch neighborhood knocked a brick wall down. Also, a trampoline was blown into a house causing minor damage to the home.

events.cz_name: WHITE MOUNTAINS OF GRAHAM AND GREENLEE COUNTIES
events.event_narrative: The Wallow Fire saw very little spread during the beginning of July thanks to very beneficial moisture. The fire was officially contained on July 8, 2011 at 1800 MST. A total of  538,049 acres were charred with around 100,000 acres charred in northern Greenlee County. Most of the structure damage and injuries were sustained north of Tucson's warning area, however, a few outbuildings were destroyed in Greenlee County. Crews stayed on scene throughout the much to monitor hot spots and work to mitigate the flash flood concerns due to the burn scar.

The Monument Fire was contained on July 7, after charring 30,526 acres (nearly 47 square miles). The fire destroyed 62 homes, four businesses, 18 outbuildings, and damaged seven homes. Nearly 10,000 people were evacuated from areas south of Sierra Vista at the peak of the fire.
After strong winds peeled the roof off a volunteer organization, heavy rain caused ceiling tiles to collapse in the computer lab and over an office. Several computer units sustained water damage.

events.cz_name: UPPER SANTA CRUZ RIVER AND ALTAR VALLEYS
events.event_narrative: July brought much needed monsoon moisture to southern Arizona, but rainfall amounts were not sufficient to drastically reduce the severity of the drought conditions. Drought conditions were unchanged to start the month with some reduction of D3 and D4 conditions by the end of the month. The Tucson area was downgraded from D3 to D2 conditions as well as portions of western Pima County, southeast Pinal County, and northwest Graham County. Extreme southwest Cochise County was downgraded from D4 conditions to D3 conditions. Most areas ended the month with below normal rainfall, with only portions of western Cochise County and northern Greenlee County experiencing above normal rainfall. Above normal rainfall over the Monument Fire area resulted in significant flash flooding and additional damage to the area. According to state officials, range conditions continued to be extremely poor with dry stock tanks. Water was being hauled to fill stock ponds and tanks, and feed had to be brought in to supplement poor forage conditions. Wildlife was also being impacted due to lack of water and available forage. The Arizona Drought Watch reported severe impacts in the Upper Gila River Valley in southern Greenlee County. Unusually low water levels were observed in reservoirs, lakes, and ponds. Poor water quality due to low levels and low flows were also reported. Cattle were being supplemented, but herds were still losing fat levels.

Most areas ended the month with below normal rainfall, with only portions of western Cochise County and northern Greenlee County experiencing above normal rainfall. Above normal rainfall over the Monument Fire area resulted in significant flash flooding and additional damage to the area. According to state officials, range conditions continued to be extremely poor with dry stock tanks. Water was being hauled to fill stock ponds and tanks, and feed had to be brought in to supplement poor forage conditions. Wildlife was also being impacted due to lack of water and available forage. The Arizona Drought Watch reported severe impacts in the Upper Gila River Valley in southern Greenlee County. Unusually low water levels were observed in reservoirs, lakes, and ponds. Poor water quality due to low levels and low flows were also reported. Cattle were being supplemented, but herds were still losing fat levels.

Well above normal temperatures were recorded in the Tucson area during the afternoon of July 2 with a high temperature reading of 111 degrees. This tied the record high for the day. As a result, a teenage boy was treated for dehydration while hiking during the late morning. Other locations across the western deserts of southern Arizona also reached heat advisory thresholds with daytime high temperatures up to 112 degrees.

Tohono O'odham Nation Emergency Managers reported damaging winds in the Vaya Chin and Hickiwan villages. Several trailers and a home was damaged. One trailer received major structural damage and another trailer was completely destroyed. The homeowners were not home at the time. A vacant trailer was also destroyed. In addition, a traditional style home received significant roof damage and a HUD (Housing and Urban Development) home also received roof damage.
Thunderstorm winds caused significant structural damage to a home and damaged an outhouse in South Komelik.
A trained weather spotter near Tubac estimated a thunderstorm wind gust of 60 mph at her home.

A trained weather spotter recorded wind gusts of up to 76 mph in the Catalina Foothills area which resulted in considerable damage. Several homes received minor roof damage and broken windows and one home had its air conditioning unit blown off. Several mesquite trees were also uprooted and a brick wall was blown over near Harrison Road and Snyder Road. Some of the larger trees fell onto homes but caused only minor damage.
Thunderstorm wind gusts uprooted up to two dozen trees at the Oro Valley Marketplace shopping center.

Lightning struck a gas station in Catalina while a tanker was off-loading diesel into a 10,000 gallon tank. The strike blew open two manhole covers causing fuel vapors to ignite. The area was evacuated while the vapors quickly burned out.

Thunderstorm winds downed several downed power poles near the Tucson International Airport. This caused the closure of East Los Reales Road between South Sixth Avenue and South Nogales Highway and 3,200 customers to lose power.
Tohono O'odham Nation Emergency Managers reported a car being struck by lightning on Highway 86 near Indian Route 34.
Heavy rainfall fell along Highway 286 in southern Pima County with rainfall amounts up to 2.5 inches. This resulted in the flooding and closure of Highway 286 for about an hour.
Thunderstorm winds caused minor damage to homes and trailers in Vaya Chin. One home's roof was blown off, allowing heavy rainfall to damage the interior of the home.
Tohono O'odham Nation dispatch reported thunderstorm winds downed several power poles down along Highway 85 between Why and Ajo.

Rainfall amounts between 1.5 inches and 2.5 inches resulted flooding and the closure of  several roads at Organ Pipe National Monument. In addition, a 40 foot section of the international border fence between the United States and Mexico was destroyed.

Thunderstorm wind gusts over 60 mph resulted in minor damage in Fort Thomas. Several truck trailers were blown through yards resulting in a few outbuildings being destroyed. A tool shed was also severely damaged and a few small trees were downed.
Rainfall amounts up to 2.5 inches resulted in flash flooding in the Kino Springs area. Several washes and the Santa Cruz River flooded resulting in the closure of several local roads.

Rainfall in excess of one inch under one hour on the Monument Fire burn area resulted in flooding along Montezuma Canyon Road. Heavy rainfall also resulted in water rushing across and down Hereford Road making the road impassable.

Thunderstorms winds in Marana downed numerous trees from the Dove Mountain Community to Continental Reserve. A few trees were downed on homes with only minor damage sustained to roofs. The most significant damage occurred along Ina Road where 18 power poles were downed. Some poles fell on businesses and fences, and one fell on a moving commercial vehicle. Ina Road was closed for several hours, effectively isolating people in area businesses, parking lots and homes from the rest of the community.

Heavy rainfall amounts of 1 to 2 inches in less than 20 minutes resulted in widespread flash flooding near the Dove Mountain Community and Marana. Several streets were impassable for nearly an hour as water rushed through flooded washes and ditches. Notable road closures included Tangerine Road and Camino de Manana.

Heavy rainfall amounts of 1 to 2 inches resulted in flash flooding and several road closures across the Marana area. Flooding washes and ditches resulted in the closure of Cortaro Road from Thornydale Road to Interstate 10. Several additional neighborhood roads were flooded.
Heavy rainfall in the Benson area resulted in several overflowing washes and closed neighborhood streets.
Cochise County Emergency Manager reported water across Highway 90 at several locations from Sierra Vista to Bisbee.
Trained spotter recorded a wind gust of 62 mph at his home near Patagonia Lake.
Thunderstorm winds downed eleven power poles along Highway 86 between Three Points and Sells. The city of Sells and other portions of the Tohono O'odham Nation were without power for several hours.

Rainfall amounts in excess of 2 inches resulted in flash flooding across portions of the northeast Tucson metro area including the foothills of the Santa Catalina Mountains. One motorist had to be rescued at the intersection near Fort Lowell Road and Melpomene Way. Water reached the top of the car, trapping him inside. In addition, several rock slides were reported along Mount Lemmon Highway due to runoff from the heavy rainfall.

Thunderstorm winds up to 75 mph impacted Eloy, Arizona when a microburst descended near the Volvo equipment rental facility. These strong winds resulted in significant damage in a divergent pattern across southeast portions of Eloy. A total of 20 homes sustained significant damage. Some had roof structures blown off, while some suffered total roof collapses and one had a tree fell on it and a nearby vehicle. Of the 20 homes, 14 were condemned. Several other homes sustained damage due to flying debris while still others only had shingle damage. In addition, eight businesses were damaged beyond repair including one that also collapsed onto cars and equipment. Several power poles were also downed resulting in widespread power outages in the August heat forcing Eloy to set up a cooling center in a local high school. A number of semi-tractor trailers were also blown over in a parking lot. One person sustained minor injuries when winds ripped the roof off a mobile home.
Heavy rainfall over the Monument Fire burn area resulted in flooding in Miller Canyon and the closure of Miller Canyon Road.
Heavy rainfall lead to a quick five foot rise in the Nogales Wash and subsequent flooding along its banks.
Thunderstorm winds downed power poles on Central Highway between Latimer Road and Hopkins Road in Elfrida.

Heavy rainfall resulted in flash flooding along Central Highway in McNeal. Law Enforcment reported three cars stranded in rushing water at the intersection of Davis Road and Central Highway with two additional cars swept down Davis Road. No injuries were reported.
The highest of several measured thunderstorm gusts in excess of 60 mph ripped a roof off a barn in Canelo.

Heavy rainfall resulted in flash flooding along the San Francisco River in southern Clifton. The flooding was confined to Ward Canyon where a few homes sustained minor water damage along Ward Canyon Road.

A fiery ten vehicle accident killed an infant and closed westbound lanes of Interstate 10 near Red Rock. The cause of the accident was zero visibility due to a dust storm. The infant was in a car seat in the backseat of a car that apparently slowed down when it entered the dust and was struck in the rear by a semi-tractor trailer. The driver also received serious injuries and an older child who was a passenger received minor injuries. Both were transported to the hospital. Westbound lanes remained closed for several hours following the accident.

Thunderstorm winds damaged homes and downed power lines from Big Fields to Covered Wells on the Tohono O'odham Nation. Four homes incurred roof damage and one power pole was downed in Big Field. Three power poles were also downed in Covered Wells along Highway 86 which resulted in power outages.
Thunderstorms winds downed trees and power poles in Rio Rico along Interstate 19.

Two illegal immigrants were struck by lightning near Sierra Vista and transported to a hospital. The Border Patrol reported that the injuries sustained by the two illegal immigrants was consistent with a lightning strike.
Heavy rainfall over the Horseshoe 2 Burn area resulted in rapid runoff into washes and down roadways near the Chiricahua National Monument resulting in the closure of several park roads and trails.

Heavy rainfall resulted in zero visibility along Interstate 10 near Ina Road resulting in an accident. A tractor trailer drove into the median and flipped as a result on the heavy rainfall. The driver sustained minor injuries and was treated on scene.
Thunderstorm winds downed several power poles along Sunland Gin Road between Harmon Road and Pretzer Road.
Thunderstorm wind gusts of 52 knots (60 mph) resulted in three power poles downed along Route 15 between Santa Rose and the Pinal County line.

After beneficial rainfall in July and early August, the entire month of August ended with below normal rainfall except across parts of western Cochise County. The result was that D3 extreme drought conditions retreated eastward, completely exiting Santa Cruz County, by the middle of the month, but expanded even farther westward across Pima and Pinal Counties by the end of August. D4 exceptional drought conditions did show an overall decrease in state coverage from 4.83% to 1.35%, with only extreme eastern Cochise County, southern Greenlee County, and extreme southeast Graham County remaining in exceptional drought conditions in southeast Arizona. The most impacted watersheds during August were the San Simon watershed (2nd percentile for rainfall) and the Santa Cruz watershed (2nd percentile for rainfall), which received very little rainfall. July's rainfall brought an end to the fire season so many recreational areas were reopened in August. The state and federal forest services conducted large scale seeding operations across the burn scar areas attempting to mitigate the flash flooding concerns. Very few ranchers were still holding onto cattle, so agriculture impacts were somewhat lessened during the month. Cotton and vegetable crops were reported as being fair to excellent as irrigation was being maximized.

Sustained winds reached up to 40 mph for several hours across southeast Arizona as a large low pressure system tracked through the region. Several wind gusts in excess of 58 mph were also observed. A few gusts even approached 70 mph. No damage was reported.

Sustained winds reached up to 40 mph for several hours across southeast Arizona as a large low pressure system tracked through the region. Several wind gusts in excess of 58 mph were also observed. A few gusts even approached 70 mph. No damage was reported.

Strong thunderstorm winds resulted in several downed trees along Fry Blvd. in Sierra Vista. Some of the trees were blocking the driving lanes on Fry Blvd.

An intense thunderstorm produced torrential rainfall along Interstate 10 between mile markers 285 and 292 near the Pima County and Cochise County line. The Arizona Department of Transportation worked six accidents involving a total of nine vehicles resulting in seven non-life-threatening injuries. Arizona DOT reported that heavy rainfall, zero visibility, and hydroplaning were to blame. Interstate 10 was partially closed for about 30 minutes.

Heavy rainfall resulted in flooded streets and washes near Red Rock. Two elderly women attempted to drive through the flooded intersection at Park Link Dr. and Pecan Rd. when their vehicle stalled. Avra Valley Fire Dept. responded and rescued the women and a dog with water up to the windows.

Heavy rainfall of 2 and 3 inches near and east of Sahuarita caused the closure of  several roads including Alvernon, Comsoft, Wilmot and Kolb. Swift water rescues from vehicles were performed near the intersections of Delgado and Davis Roads and Wilmot and Sahuarita Roads.
A severe thunderstorm produced a swath of large hail from Green Valley northeastward several miles out of town.
Severe thunderstorms produced large hail in Sierra Vista and Hereford.

Thunderstorm winds downed several trees on Tucson's south side. One tree fell on a truck and another onto an apartment building. The truck was totaled but the building only received minor damage. In addition, strong winds ripped the air conditioning unit and tiles off the roof of the Southgate Academy Charter School.
Lightning struck a home in the 36000 block of Stoney Flower causing significant damage. Twenty-five firefighters responded and were on scene for two hours.

Strong thunderstorm winds occurred on Tucson's south side for the second day in a row, downing numerous power poles, electric lines, street signs, and trees. As many as 25,000 were left without power. One power pole was downed on a trailer leading to the evacuation of the trailer park near East Drexel and South Country Club Roads. Another Tucson resident woke up to a power pole entering the dwelling. Part of a roof was also blown off a residence on Valencia Road, blowing across the road into another home damaging the roof.
Thunderstorm winds downed several trees in the Catalina Foothills. A large mesquite tree blocked the road at Rudasil and Tiburon Roads.

Heavy rainfall with amounts between one and two inches resulted in flash flooding across a wide swath of the Tucson area. Several swift water rescues were conducted with two near the 3800 block of West Goret Road in the Tucson Mountains. Another swift water rescue was conducted in the 9400 block of Hartman Lane, where a motorcyclist had to be rescued with a rope and flotation device.
Heavy rainfall resulted in two, single car accidents on Interstate 10 between Ina Road and Orange Grove Road due to hydroplaning. One person was taken to the hospital with minor injuries.

Heavy rainfall resulted in rapid runoff and flash flooding on Tucson's south side. Several streets were flooded around the Tucson International Airport and a swift water rescue was conducted at Old Nogales and Old Vail Roads. The most significant damage was sustained by the Marshall Home for Men near Interstate 10 and Interstate 19 where a small wash overflowed into the business, resulting in significant water damage to the interior. The force of the water also broke through the front door.
Thunderstorm winds downed several trees, including one with a three foot diameter trunk, near the community of Pima.

Heavy rainfall resulted in several flooded washes and ditches which closed streets.  A swift water rescue was performed on Wilmot north of Sahuarita Road. Firefighters worked to rescue a stranded women from her car but were forced to walk to her as high water was blocking the roadway. Additionally, a wall of water rushed down the Pantano Wash catching two kids off guard. Firefighters had to rescue the kids from waist high water. No injuries were reported.

The fifth highest daily rainfall total in recorded history occurred at the Tucson International Airport. A total of 2.84 inches of rain fell at the airport with other amounts up to 3 inches in the area. Significant flash flooding with major damage, several swift water rescues, rivers flooding their banks, and several flooded structures were a result of this heavy rainfall. A total of 6 swift water rescues were conducted and at least six people were rescued from flooded homes on Calle Medina. At the peak of the storm, nearly 3 feet of water covered most of the roads in and around Tucson International Airport with over 30 roads being closed and several more impassible. Two flights were also detoured to Phoenix Sky Harbor Airport. Several homes and businesses were flooded as well. A Jiffy Lube had water get into the oil pit causing the oil pit to overflow into the streets and washes around the business creating a HAZMAT situation. Several businesses were closed for the remainder of the day while repairs and cleanup occurred.

Extremely heavy rainfall across southern Tucson resulted in significant wash and stream flooding downstream from Tucson. Overflowing washes toppled a wall in the Rancho Sahuarita subdivision in Sahuarita resulting in damage to 15 homes and a muddy mess. Water up to one foot was observed in some of the homes.  The raging Santa Cruz River also claimed the life of a homeless man that was living under the Grant Road Bridge. Rescuers spotted the man holding onto the bridge pillar, but before they were able to reach him he lost his grip and was swept down the river. His body was found the next day near the Ina Road bridge.

Strong thunderstorm winds kicked up an area of dust along Interstate 10 near Picacho Peak, dropping visibility to near zero. One driver slowed enough to cause a tractor trailer to rear end the vehicle setting off a 13 vehicle accident. In all there were 12 injuries with 5 people being transported to local hospitals.

Lightning struck a palm tree in the 3400 block of South Camino Seco in Tucson igniting the tree. Debris then fell onto a mobile home, setting the home on fire. The occupants were able to safely escape. Only minor damage was reported to the roof of the home.

The month of September started off with above average rainfall across eastern Pima County and well as western Cochise County. However, the rest of the area continued to receive below normal rainfall and above normal temperatures. Tucson International Airport received the fifth highest rainfall amount in recorded history on September 15 of 2.84 inches. However, locations nearby received a tenth of an inch or less. This allowed the Tucson area, and northeast Pima County to be dropped from extreme drought conditions (D3) to severe drought conditions (D2). Extreme drought condition areas were lowered by almost 4 percent by the end of the month. However, due to the lack of rainfall across eastern Cochise, Graham, and Greenlee Counties, exceptional drought conditions (D4) expanded across southern Greenlee County. Most areas received less than 50 percent of the average rainfall, while areas in eastern Pima County and western Cochise County received greater than 300 percent of normal. Drought impacts across the state actually lessened in September as dry conditions have continued for several months with little change from month to month.
A funnel cloud was observed near Vail. It extended about a quarter of the way from the cloud base to the ground.

events.cz_name: WHITE MOUNTAINS OF GRAHAM AND GREENLEE COUNTIES
events.event_narrative: About 20 inches of snow occurred at Hannagan Meadow.
Mt. Graham had between 32 and 36 inches of snow.
The higher elevations of the Chiricahua Mountains had 10 to 20 inches of snow.
Mt. Lemmon had about 24 to 30 inches of snowfall.
The higher elevations of the Santa Rita and Huachuca Mountains had 20 to 30 inches of snowfall.
Kitt Peak had between 10 and 12 inches of snowfall.

Extremely dry soils and strong southwest winds caused localized dust storms along Interstate 10 in southern Pinal County. One dust storm reduced visibility to less than one quarter of a mile causing a fatal 16-vehicle accident that closed the westbound lanes of Interstate 10 for several hours. A Texas man was killed in the accident and a total of 15 people were injured, two seriously. The dust storm prohibited air traffic, so the critically wounded were escorted by ambulance to the nearest hospital.

Following near normal Monsoon rainfall, dry and warm conditions returned to southern Arizona in October. Most areas received less than 50 percent of October's normal rainfall with a large swath receiving less than 10 percent of normal rainfall. Tucson International Airport received six hundredths of an inch for the month, while the worse drought areas of southeast Cochise County received up to fifteen hundredths of an inch. As a result, only enough precipitation fell to prevent conditions from getting much worse during the month. The lone positive was slight improvement in Greenlee County where D4 (exceptional) drought conditions dropped from 1.67 percent of the state in September to 1.24 percent in October. Local drought impacts were somewhat mitigated as the drought has persisted for several months. However, with the help of irrigation and normal Monsoon rainfall, the fall cotton crop has been reported to be fair to excellent.

After a dry October, D3 (extreme) drought conditions spread across much of southern Arizona to begin November. That marked an increase from 13.88% of the state to 28.59% under D3 conditions. That's the largest total area for D3 conditions since the drought began last winter. There was some relief the first half of the month with a couple of storm systems bringing very beneficial rainfall. Tucson and Douglas ended the month with above normal rainfall, but a majority of southern Arizona ended below normal, including the White Mountain region. Though shower activity in November brought temporary relief, the Arizona State Climatology Office reported that it was too late in the season to help range conditions impacted by the spotty rainfall and hot conditions from the past summer. The light nature of the rainfall also did very little to help rangeland water resources, including ponds and streams. However, rainfall will help winter annuals and crops.

Drastic improvements were made to drought conditions during the first half of December as widespread beneficial rain fell across the entire region. The early December rainfall coupled with above normal rainfall in November was sufficient to remove D3 (extreme) and D4 (exceptional) drought conditions from all of southern Arizona by December 20th for the first time since March.  While rainfall will be beneficial to winter annuals and crops, little improvement was seen in streams, ponds, and stock tanks. The last half of the month ended with no additional rainfall, so the concern for a dry winter remains.

The light nature of the rainfall also did very little to help rangeland water resources, including ponds and streams. However, rainfall will help winter annuals and crops.

events.cz_name: UPPER SANTA CRUZ RIVER AND ALTAR VALLEYS
events.event_narrative: Drastic improvements were made to drought conditions during the first half of December as widespread beneficial rain fell across the entire region. The early December rainfall coupled with above normal rainfall in November was sufficient to remove D3 (extreme) and D4 (exceptional) drought conditions from all of southern Arizona by December 20th for the first time since March.  While rainfall will be beneficial to winter annuals and crops, little improvement was seen in streams, ponds, and stock tanks. The last half of the month ended with no additional rainfall, so the concern for a dry winter remains.

About 6 inches of snow occurred on Kitt Peak on the Baboquivari Mountains.

events.cz_name: WHITE MOUNTAINS OF GRAHAM AND GREENLEE COUNTIES
events.event_narrative: About 1 foot of snow occurred at Hannagan Meadow in Northern Greenlee County.
About 3 to 4 inches of snow occurred at Oracle in Southeast Pinal County.
Sustained winds of 40 MPH with gusts to 55 MPH occurred at Douglas-Bisbee airport.

events.cz_name: UPPER GILA RIVER AND ARAVAIPA VALLEYS
events.event_narrative: Two to four inches of snow occurred in elevations from about 3500 to 4000 feet in Graham County.

Sustained southwest winds of 25 to 35 miles per hour resulted in minor damage in Sierra Vista. Just after midnight, a wind gust near 50 mph lifted a tent that housed the Sierra Vista Cowboy Church, carrying it over 100 yards, before landing on horse pens. The pens sustained minor damage while the tent received several tears and bent rods, but was able to be repaired. A stop sign was also blown over at the intersection of South 1st St and Witt Drive. A tree was also reported downed on Avenida Tienda.

November and early December precipitation resulted in widespread improvements in drought conditions across all of southern Arizona. During the first half of December, portions of Pinal County received over 150% of normal rainfall. However, an extremely dry January through March period caused drought conditions to worsen once again. Extreme drought conditions (D3) returned to roughly the northwest half of Pinal County, including far northern sections of the Tohono O'odham Nation by mid March.

A 23-year-old female tourist died from heat exhaustion/heat stroke while hiking in the Tortolita Mountains with family. The high temperature at Tucson was 93 degrees. She was pronounced dead at 130 pm.
A 35-year-old female tourist from Germany died rom heat exhaustion/heat stroke at 200 pm while hiking in Saguaro National Park West. The high temperature in Tucson was 105 degrees.

Extreme drought (D3) conditions persisted in April across portions of Pinal County. April is normally when the driest three month period across southern Arizona begins. While on the only day of the month with measurable precipitation, April 14th, Pinal County actually received precipitation amounts that were near or slightly above the monthly normal amount for April, this was only enough to keep drought conditions from worsening. The rest of southern Arizona received less than 50 percent of normal monthly rainfall, and in some cases, none at all. While the long term impacts of the drought stretch back to Winter 2010-2011, the impacts continue to be mitigated by being previously dealt with by ranchers, farmers, Forest Service, and other industries and agencies affected. For example, cattle have been sold off and what little herds remain continue to be subsidized by trucking in water and feed. Dry thunderstorms developed on April 23, sparking small wildfires across portions of Cochise and Graham Counties, the largest being the Cedar Fire near Klondyke. Other human caused fires were also reported during the month, including the Apache Pass fire near Ft. Bowie which grew to over 1600 acres before containment was reached.

Several four inch diameter tree limbs were broken in eastern sections of Tucson.  The Tucson ASOS measured a peak gust of 52 mph.

Extreme drought (D3) continued in portions Pinal County throughout May. The overall D3 area remained unchanged from April.  While portions of southeast Arizona near the New Mexico and International Borders received near normal precipitation for May, which is about two to six tenths of an inch depending on elevation, Pinal County received little or no rainfall.  Since the impacts of this drought began with the winter of 2010-2011, most have already been mitigated.  One notable event that occurred on May 9th saw convective outflow initiate substantial blowing dust that propagated northwest across Tucson as well as Pinal County.

A dust devil briefly spun up into a landspout tornado just south of Rio Rico.
Hail up to the size of pennies covered the ground in Rio Rico.
Hail up to the size of pennies covered the ground in Douglas.  Heavy rain and minor street flooding accompanied the hail.
A dust devil formed in a church parking lot near Pima and Swan in Tucson.  The dust devil grew and moved over the church, displacing and damaging a number of roof tiles.
Thunderstorm winds broke off tree limbs as large as 4 inches in diameter and peeled bark off a tree near Pima Street and Sahuara Avenue.
Thunderstorm winds downed tree limbs about a mile west of the Twin Peaks exit of Interstate 10.

Lightning struck a two-story house at 11th Street and C Avenue in Douglas causing the house to catch fire. Firefighters extinguished the fire in 20 minutes.  Smoke damage was confined to the second story.

Hot temperatures of 100 to 106 degrees resulted in the death of a construction worker from Indiana.  Paramedics were called to treat a man suffering from cardiac arrest who had been suffering from heat-related illness for two hours before his collapse. He was pronounced dead at 455 pm at the construction site.

Strong thunderstorms moved across the Three Points, Picture Rocks and Avra Valley areas, generating strong outflow winds that resulted in a reduced visibility in blowing dust. A haboob was photographed moving through these areas and across south central Pinal County.  Four separate accidents occurred on Interstate 10 between mile markers 214 and 226, but the interstate remained open. One accident near Red Rock resulted in seven injuries when a sport utility vehicle rear ended a cement truck. Two adults in the front seat of the SUV were taken to the hospital with serious although not life-threatening injuries. Another two-vehicle accident in the same area left two people with minor injuries.

Extreme drought (D3) continued in portions of Pinal County throughout June. The overall D3 area remained unchanged from May. While some areas actually received more rain than normal, those spotty rains amounts only totaled between a tenth and a half of an inch and therefore did little to improve drought conditions, especially since temperatures were above normal.  In fact, the Tucson airport experienced its 5th warmest June on record and had 28 days of 100 degrees or warmer. Since the impacts of this drought began with the winter of 2010-2011, most have already been mitigated. The extent of the dry weather was manifested in dust storm events that occurred on several dates in June.  Thunderstorms that brought the little rain that did fall, also created gusty outflow winds that kicked up dust, ultimately developing into haboobs.  These large areas of blowing dust rolled northward across portions of Pima and Pinal Counties toward Phoenix on three occasions in June.  Two of these dust storms reduced visibilities to less than one quarter of a mile on Interstate 10.

Gusty winds blew the awning off the front of a mobile home near Ajo and Interstate 19.

Flash flooding was first reported along Davis Road east of Tombstone where 5 vehicles were stuck in flood waters. Another motorist was stuck on Frontier Road. Two homes were also flooded within the city of Tombstone.

Rainfall reports between 2 and 4.5 inches caused extensive wash and street flooding in Oro Valley which resulted in numerous road closures. Where washes crossed roadways, damage occurred to roadside ditches and flood control embankments. A motorist was rescued from flood waters at Tangerine and La Canada.

Several roads, including Manville Road, Pump Station Road and El Tiro Road were flooded on the far west side of Tucson.  Blanco Wash also flooded, stranding a teenager who was horseback riding in the area Derringer Road and Lambert Lane.

Heavy rain caused washes and roads to flood on the southwest side of Tucson. A motorist was rescued near South Gila Avenue and Calle Torim. Three others were rescued from their Jeep where the Black Wash crosses Mardick Avenue.
Heavy rain caused several roads to be closed in the Mammoth area including Copper Creek Road and River Road.
A funnel cloud briefly descended from a thunderstorm west of Tucson.  The funnel cloud quickly dissipated.
Heavy rain fell on part of the 2011 Monument Fire burn scar area. In particular, the Ash Canyon watershed was affected which caused flooding along Prince Placer Road and Stone Ridge Road.

Thunderstorm winds caused damage in Green Valley.  Several trees were downed along Abrego and La Canada Drives and power outages resulted. Winds peeled a carport and tin roof off a residence in Pueblo Estates. Railroad crossing arms were also damaged by the strong winds.
Thunderstorm winds damaged eight homes in the Cowlic area. Three homes sustained major roof damage. One of those also had a wall collapse.
Thunderstorm winds damaged two homes in Ali Chukson.  One home had major roof and wall damage.
Thunderstorm winds caused minor roof damage to seven homes in Santa Rosa.
Heavy rain caused flooding in Gunsight and along Gunsight Wash, which washed out Indian Road 3.
A Department of Defense weather sensor recorded a wind gust to 59 mph which confirmed estimated wind gusts near Stoa Pith.  No damage was reported.

Brief but heavy rain over the Monument Fire burn scar caused flash flooding in many of the canyons on the southeast side of the Huachuca Mountains. In Miller Canyon, the road was washed out. Additionally, dozens of feet of Tombstone pipeline which provides water to that community were exposed as flood waters removed the soil which normally covers the pipeline. The water supply line itself was not impacted. Stone Ridge Road and Coronado Memorial Road were flooded and covered with boulders and mud.
Heavy rain caused urban flooding in northeast Tucson. A motorist was rescued when a minivan became stuck in two feet of water in an intersection at Tanque Verde Road and Conestoga Avenue.

Thunderstorm winds downed numerous trees and power lines in Douglas. Power was out in parts of the city for over 2 hours.  Winds also removed a portion of a roof from a business at 21st Street and I Avenue. Wind damage was more extensive across the border in Agua Prieta.

Over 2 inches of rain caused urban flooding in Douglas. Many streets, including G Avenue were flowing with up to 2 feet of water. Some businesses also experienced minor flooding. Flash flooding was even more severe across the border in Agua Prieta.
Thunderstorm winds blew down 12 power poles along Tangerine Road near Gladden Farms. Around 2000 customers lost power in Marana.

Thunderstorm winds blew a trailer over in Drexel Heights. That same thunderstorm earlier produced a gust to 60 mph at the Tucson International Airport.  Downed power lines left about 2000 customers without power on the southwest side of Tucson. Twelve power poles were knocked down on the west side of Davis-Monthan Air Force Base.
Quarter size hail was reported near Grant and Alvernon as well as near Prince and Campbell.

Thunderstorm winds uprooted trees near Prince and Campbell and near Fort Lowell and First Avenue.  One tree fell through the roof of a residence. A storm spotter in this area measured a gust to 61 mph. Wind damage became extensive near the Tucson Mall. Numerous large wooden power poles were snapped or toppled along Oracle from Limberlost to River Road. Other poles were knocked down along Roger Road from First Avenue to Oracle Road.  About 15,000 customers were left without power. These road was closed for much of the following day. In addition, thunderstorm winds blew in a door at the Tucson Mall, knocking down an interior construction wall which damaged part of JC Penney and Forever 21 stores. About 50 trees were blown over near the mall, damaging a few parked vehicles.

Between 2 and 3 inches of rain fell in a little over an hour in parts of Tucson.  Heavy rain caused the roof of part of the Tucson Mall to collapse, creating water damage in the JC Penney store.  The collapse damaged an air conditioner which caused a water line leak that led to more extensive water damage in the store.

Heavy rain of around 2 inches fell in a short amount of time in the northwest section of Willcox during the afternoon and led to flash flooding by early evening. Saguaro, North Fort Grant and Stewart Road were all closed due to flooding and one vehicle became stalled in flood waters. The flood waters caused a fissure to open up on Saguaro Road.

Flash flooding closed several roads from just south of the Tucson International Airport to Green Valley.  Franco Wash flooded Summit Street and Old Vail Connection Road.  Portions of Old Nogales Highway were also closed. In addition, Whitehouse Canyon Road east of Green Valley was flooded.

Heavy rain over 2 inches in less than an hour caused extensive urban flash flooding in parts of the Tucson metropolitan area from Drexel Heights to Casas Adobes to Oro Valley. Area fire department responded to nearly a dozen incidents involving vehicles stranded in flood waters and performed several six swift water rescues. A mother and child were rescued from 2 feet of flowing water at River Road and First Avenue. Two vehicles were stuck in flowing water on Camino Del Cerro Road under Interstate 10. Four teenagers were rescued from an SUV on South Oak Tree Drive. Another rescue was performed on two occupants of a stranded vehicle near Ina and Silverbell. Numerous roads were closed due to flood waters into the night.

Heavy rain over and adjacent to the Monument Fire burn scar caused flash flooding in the Sierra Vista and Hereford areas. Numerous roads were covered with flood waters, mud, boulders and other debris. A vehicle was stuck in the flooded intersection of Bloomfield Road and Kings Ranch Road.  Two people were caught up in flood waters at the Carr Canyon Campsite. A 22 year old male managed to escape up the bank of the wash but a 16 year old female was swept downstream and not located until 4 hours later. Both suffered minor injuries. An elderly couple were rescued from the roof of their vehicle stuck in flood waters at the intersection of Ramsey Road and Burrow Drive.
Thunderstorm winds knocked down 6 power poles along Wilmot Road south of Interstate 10 leaving 2500 customer without power.
Thunderstorm winds uprooted a tree in Amado.
Thunderstorm winds blew down a tree in Rancho Sahuarita.
Thunderstorm winds blew down a tree at East Shoreline Drive and North Sabino Canyon Road.
Houghton Road and Wentworth Road were both closed near Andrada Road due to flash flooding.
Flash flooding forced the closure of Highway 85 between Why and Organ Pipe National Monument.

A microburst caused extensive damage to a mobile home park east of Interstate 10 and south of Cortaro Farms Road. An awning was blown over one home, causing part of the roof to peel off, which fell on a vehicle. Other homes suffered skirting, awning and minor roof damage and one tree were uprooted. Another tree was uprooted farther north near Bald Eagle Road and Condor Drive.

Flash flooding closed Desert Ridge Drive in Green Valley as well as Mission Road near Twin Buttes Cemetery.  Farther north, a car became stuck in flood waters near Ajo Highway and Sandario Road. In Avra Valley and Picture Rocks, Manville Road was closed between Sanders and Trico Roads due to flooding as well as Twin Peaks Road between Sandario and Sanders Roads.

Flash flooding closed streets in far southeast Tucson and in the Vail area including Old Spanish Trail, Collossal Cave Road, Escalante at Atterbury Wash and Harrison at the Pantano Wash.  Several cars were stranded in flood waters on Houghton Road between Bilby and Valencia Roads.
Heavy rain over the Monument Fire burn scar resulted in flash flooding of canyons and the closure of several roads including Ramsey Road, Coronado Memorial Road and Stone Ridge Road.

Heavy rains earlier in the afternoon and persistent moderate rain into the early evening resulted in a tributary of the Brawley Wash flowing over Cocio Road near White Eagle Road.  A motorist was rescued from his vehicle which had been washed downstream.
Thunderstorm winds downed a tree at Fox Hollow Cabins.

Heavy rain on Tucson's east side lead to urban flash flooding. Tanque Verde Loop Road was closed at the Tanque Verde Wash and a swift water rescue was conducted of a person trapped in their vehicle at Paseo Aquimiri, near Craycroft Road south of Sunrise.

Heavy rain in the northwest part of the Tucson metropolitan area caused extensive urban flash flooding. Portions of Shannon, Magee, La Cholla and Sandario Roads were closed.  A person was rescued from their vehicle stranded in flood waters on Sandario Road in Marana.

Heavy rain continued across Tucson's west side causing extensive urban flooding. Numerous swift water rescues were conducted for motorists in vehicles stranded in flood waters. Rescues were performed on Orange Grove, West Anthony and Silverbell Roads. A large portion of Silverbell Road between Sunset and Ina Roads was completely washed out. One motorist managed to escape her vehicle with her 12 year old and 4 month old baby before the vehicle was swept downstream.  Several motorists had to be rescued by helicopter in this area. In addition, some residents of Picture Rocks were trapped in their homes because of flood waters. No injuries occurred.
Lightning struck an apartment complex near Wrightstown Road and Pantano Road. The roof started on fire and three residents of one apartment had to be evacuated.

Flash flooding forced the closure of roads south of Sierra Vista as well as the Hereford and Tombstone areas. A man was rescued from his vehicle that was stuck in flood waters on Three Canyons Road west of Hereford.  Flood debris blocked part of Moson Road.
Thunderstorm winds blew down a power pole near Bowie. About 2000 people lost electrical power.
Thunderstorm winds blew apart a carport in Whetstone.
Lightning struck and destroyed a generator that provided power for Huachuca City Police Department telephone lines.

Extreme drought (D3) continued in portions of Pinal County throughout July. The overall D3 area remained unchanged from June. While most areas received about one inch of rain, it was not enough to make up for months of drought conditions. Since the impacts of this drought began with the winter of 2010-2011, most have already been mitigated. The extent of the dry weather was manifested in dust storm events that occurred on at least five dates during July. Thunderstorm outflow winds that kicked up dust, ultimately developing into haboobs. These large areas of blowing dust rolled northward across portions of Pinal County on several occasions during July, reducing visibility to less than one quarter of a mile at times along Interstate 10.

Extreme drought (D3) continued in portions of Pinal County in August but enough rainfall occurred for conditions to improve to the severe drought or (D2) category during the latter half of the month. Since the impacts of this drought began with the winter of 2010-2011, most have already been mitigated. Rainfall amounts generally totaled between 0.75 inch and 1.5 inches. Despite the rain, dry antecedent conditions contributed to several dust storm events as thunderstorm outflow winds kicked up dust, which ultimately developed into haboobs. These large areas of blowing dust rolled northward across portions of Pinal County on at least three occasions in August.

Thunderstorm winds knocked down 15 power poles along Alvernon Way between Valencia Road and Benson Highway. As storms moved northwest, a church roof was damaged near 36th and Country Club, numerous trees were downed or uprooted in central and east Tucson and a carport was destroyed on the east side of the city. Another power pole was downed near 5th and Country Club while three others were downed near Prince and Campbell.  About 12,000 residents lost power as a result.
Thunderstorm winds downed a tree in Catalina.
Thunderstorm winds downed a large tree and damaged a pool canopy at the Green Valley Recreation Club.
Lightning struck a palm tree near Tangerine and Twin Peaks Road causing it to ignite.
Thunderstorm winds snapped several power poles southwest of Sells and damaged homes in Big Fields. Three of the homes sustained major roof damage.
Thunderstorm winds caused roof damage to one residence and damaged several sheds at Diamond Bell Ranch.  An eight inch brick wall was blown over on to a car.
The AWOS at Pinal Air Park (KMZJ) recorded a gust to 67 mph.
Thunderstorm winds registered a gust to 66 mph at the Nogales Airport then caused major roof to a home on the eastern side of the city along Royal Road.

Thunderstorm winds ripped off a 50 foot section of the roof at the Huachuca City School.  Part of the roof landed on a power line causing a power outage for area residents.  One tree was also uprooted, damaging a chain link fence.  The ASOS at Libby Field on the Fort Huachuca base measured a gust to 62 mph as storms moved through.
After thunderstorm winds ripped a 50 foot section of the roof off the Huachuca City School, heavy rain infiltrated the building, damaging six classrooms.
Spotters in Hereford measured thunderstorm wind gusts to 62 mph and reported shingles blown off the roof of one house.
Thunderstorm winds damaged several trees in Oro Valley, Marana and Casas Adobes on the northwest side of the Tucson metro area. A spotter near Oracle Junction measured a wind gust of 60 mph.
Thunderstorm winds downed power lines in far northeast Tucson leaving over 3000 residents without power.
Thunderstorm winds ripped off about 40 feet of the roof to the auditorium at the Organ Pipe National Monument Visitor Center.
Thunderstorm winds downed a tree at Mission Manor Park in Tucson and flipped over a loosely anchored small metal shed at San Joaquin Road and West Milky Way Drive.
Thunderstorm winds downed a tree at Catalina Regional Park.  The tree fell on a park shelter, damaging the roof.
Thunderstorm winds damaged two homes in Hickiwan.  One home sustained considerable roof damage.
Thunderstorm winds damaged three homes and a cellular tower near Menager's Dam.

Thunderstorm winds damaged 33 homes in Santa Rosa. Two homes had the entire roof blown off and had at least one wall damaged severely. Nine other homes sustained major damage. Some of these had a portion of their roof blown off while others were trailer homes that were completely blown off their foundations.  One villager sustained minor injuries inside one of the homes.  The rest of homes that were damaged either had shingles blown off or had broken windows.  Electrical service was out for seven hours.
Thunderstorm winds damaged roofs to two homes in Ventana.

Between two and four inches of rain fell across parts of Santa Cruz County. Several motorists were rescued from their vehicles in Nogales and Rio Rico as water ran across roads to depths over three feet in some spots. Another swift water rescue occurred at the Potero Wash along South River Road. In addition, Nogales Wash came out of its banks and flooded nearby businesses in Nogales.

Thunderstorms produced between 2 and 3 inches of rain in less than one hour in Nogales. Rainfall totals reached over 4 inches in some locations. The result was severe urban flooding with water as deep as three feet in the streets of Nogales. Several motorists were rescued from the flood waters in the city and at least one home was flooded with a foot of water. The Nogales Wash briefly topped its banks, covering the railroad tracks which halted all rail traffic into Mexico. Flood waters caused a 20 foot retaining wall to collapse. Debris flew threw a window, crushing an air conditioning unit and allowing water and mud inside the home. Flood waters also damaged an underground telephone cable leaving about 200 customers without telephone service.

Heavy rain caused flash flooding along Interstate 10 west of Mescal and ponding of water three feet deep in the Marsh Station Road underpass. One person was injured in a crash on the interstate after the driver lost control of the vehicle in the flood waters.

Heavy rain of nearly 3 inches fell on parts of the Chiricahua National Monument, much of which was affected by the Horseshoe 2 Wildfire in 2011. Flash flooding and a 2 to 3 foot debris flow damaged trails and the Bonita Canyon Campground. Bonita Canyon Drive was also covered by the debris flow. The area was subsequently evacuated.  The campground remain closed until August 30th.
Heavy rain caused Hickiwan Wash to overflow its banks. Two homes near the wash were flooded and several roads were closed.
Thunderstorm winds downed a six inch tree branch near Drexel and Houghton Roads.

Heavy rain from numerous thunderstorms caused several roads to be closed due to flash flooding across the Tucson metropolitan area, including Snyder Road near the Ventana Wash, Redington Road, West Valencia Road  and the Stone Avenue underpass. Three vehicles became stranded in flood waters near Pima and Country Club Roads.

Heavy rain and runoff from earlier rain caused flash flooding on the west and northwest side of Tucson, forcing the closure of several roads. One vehicle was washed away at Sunset and Silverbell Roads and several vehicles were stranded in the intersection.
Heavy rain flooded and closed several roads near Santa Rosa.
Heavy rain caused most washes that cross Indian Road 19 to flow rapidly.  Motorists were rescued from their vehicle near South Komelik.
Heavy rain caused flash flooding and the closure of several roads just west of Tucson including Pump Station and El Tiro Roads.
Heavy rain caused flash flooding in Santa Rosa where at least two homes were flooded.
Thunderstorms winds toppled trees near Grant and Oracle Roads. One tree fell on top of a car.
Two to four inches of heavy rain caused flash flooding of streets and homes in Covered Wells.

Heavy rain which totaled between three and five inches began the previous afternoon and continued into the night in the Quijotoa Mountains. Pisinimo Wash filled and flooded parts of the downstream community of Pisinimo, although sandbagging helped prevent major damage.  Flood watesr continued down San Simon Wash and when combined with runoff from Gu Vo Wash, flooded areas south toward the international border, including Route 18.

Very heavy rain that began the previous afternoon and continued through the night, totaled 3 to 5 inches upstream near the Quijotoa Mountains.  Runoff in Santa Rosa Wash damaged a berm along Route 15 causing water to flow across and close this road near North Komelik.
Thunderstorm winds downed a tree near Skyline Drive and Pontatoc Road.
Thunderstorm winds downed a tree which fell on to power lines near Grant Road and Columbus Blvd.
Thunderstorm winds downed a tree on the median along Campbell Avenue near 6th Street.
Heavy rain caused flash flooding near Topawa. Two people were rescued from a vehicle that was caught in flood waters along Indian Road 19.
Heavy rain east of Sierra Vista caused flash flooding of washes that cross Moson Road resulting in closure of the road from the Charleston Road intersection south to near Hereford Road.
Heavy rain produced flash flooding in Saint David. One bridge on a county road was washed out and flood waters entered one home, damaging the laundry room.

During the morning hours, brief but heavy rain fell on saturated ground, causing washes to quickly fill and flow across roads. Portions of Camino Del Sol and Mission Roads were closed due to flooding in and near Green Valley.

The second heavy rain of the morning overwhelmed a roof drain system on Continental School in Green Valley. Ceiling tiles collapsed from the weight of the rain and carpets were damaged. In addition, a motorist lost control of a vehicle in heavy rain along Interstate 19 near Green Valley.  The vehicle left the roadway and crashed into a small tree, injuring the driver.

Very heavy rain caused extensive street flooding in Ajo. Cedar Road was washed out by rapidly flowing flood waters 2 to 3 feet deep. a community health center and a school were also flooded.  Farther south, Ajo Mountain Drive in Organ Pipe National Monument was closed as well as part of nearby Highway 85.
Very heavy rain collapsed ceiling tiles in an Ajo business, damaging some of the goods inside.
Flash flooding caused the Sahuarita Road to become impassable near Ocotillo View.
Thunderstorm winds downed a tree near Ajo and Camino Verde Road.
A vehicle became stranded in flood waters on Arivaca Road.

Thunderstorms produced 2 to 3 inches of rain in about 90 minutes causing many roads to be inundated by rapidly flowing flood waters on the southwest side of Tucson.  AT least ten vehicles were caught up in the flood waters. Two people were rescued from vehicles at Sandario Road and Kinney Road while three more were rescued from a tree after their vehicle was washed away.  Another five motorists in five separate vehicles were stranded near Ajo Way and Kinney Rpad.  Bopp Road northwest of Ajo Way was washed out which caused Banks Elementary School students to become stranded in school until a detour around the washed out road could be fashioned.  In addition, Gates Pass Road at Via Roma was flooded in the Tucson Mountains. No injuries occurred to any of the motorists.
Thunderstorm winds blew down an open ended Quonset hut outbuilding and a trailer in Hunter Estates near Duncan. Another trailer sustained considerable roof damage.

Up to three inches of rain fell in Duncan, causing flash flooding of most streets in Duncan's Hunter Estates where one home was also flooded. A wash that parallels and but remains just northwest of Carlisle Road climbed to a depth of about 8 feet, flooded Fairgrounds Road. Trees and other debris in the flood waters caused minor surface damage to the bridge at Fairgrounds Road before the waters entered the Gila River.

Heavy rain caused flash flooding on the southwest side of Tucson.  A small wash that crosses Valencia Road overflowed, causing closure of the road between Viviana and Camino Verde. Several yards in the area were also flooded.

Heavy rain of two to four inches occurred the previous afternoon on Tucson's west side near Ajo Way and Kinney Road and directly over the Brawley Wash just west of Sandario Road. In addition, two to three inches of rain fell in the Sierrita Mountains west of Green Valley.  By the time the runoff from the Sierrita Mountains reached the west side of Tucson many hours later, Brawley Wash overflowed its banks. During the overnight hours, five vehicles drove into the flood waters and became stranded along Manville Road just west of Sandario Road. Around 2 am, one man escaped his vehicle before it was washed downstream only to be swept several yards away himself.  He suffered a leg injury. His vehicle was found 200 yards downstream, upside down. The man's wife was found in the vehicle, drown.  Rain redeveloped around daybreak allowing flood conditions to persist through mid morning.

Daily rounds of heavy rain created high flows in Vamori Wash, causing it to leave its banks and flow across Indian Road 21, keeping the road inundated for several days. The peak flow occurred during the afternoon of September 11th.
About 17 inches of snowfall occurred at the top of Mt. Graham with this winter storm.

events.cz_name: WHITE MOUNTAINS OF GRAHAM AND GREENLEE COUNTIES
events.event_narrative: About 16 inches of snowfall occurred at Hannagan Meadow in the White Mountains of Greenlee County at an elevation around 9000 feet.
Three to Eight inches of snow occurred in Southern portions of Eastern Cochise county including the Douglas area westward to Naco.
About 8 of snow occurred in the Bisbee area of Cochise County.

events.cz_name: UPPER SANTA CRUZ RIVER AND ALTAR VALLEYS
events.event_narrative: Two to four inches of snowfall occurred across the lower elevations of Santa Cruz county and the Altar Valley in Southern Pima County.

Widespread low elevation snowfall occurred across the Tucson Metro area with anywhere from 1 to 4 inches across the region. Tucson International Airport received 2 inches of snowfall. The Tucson airport briefly diverted flights headed to Tucson. A major golf tournament in Marana was suspended due to the snow.
Widespread low elevation snowfall occurred in Southeast Pinal County above 2500 feet. The Oracle area at about 4500 feet had about 6 inches of snowfall.
Widespread snowfall occurred across the valleys of Western Cochise County with 2 to 4 inches across the region.
Widespread snowfall occurred across the valleys of Eastern Cochise County with 2 to 4 inches across the region.

events.cz_name: UPPER GILA RIVER AND ARAVAIPA VALLEYS
events.event_narrative: Snowfall occurred across the Aravaipa Valley with 5.5 inches in the Klondyke area.
Widespread snowfall occurred the Galiuro and Pinaleno Mountains with 16 inches at Mt. Graham.
Widespread snowfall occurred across the Chiricahua Mountains with around 6 inches in the lower elevations and around a foot in the higher terrain.
Widespread snowfall occurred across the mountains of Cochise County including 6 inches in the Bisbee area. The Mule Pass Tunnel on Highway 80 was closed due to the snow.
Widespread snowfall occurred across the Catalina and Rincon mountains with 12 inches on Mt. Lemmon.
Widespread snowfall occurred across the Baboquivari Mountains with 6 inches on Kitt Peak.

events.cz_name: WHITE MOUNTAINS OF GRAHAM AND GREENLEE COUNTIES
events.event_narrative: The White Mountains of Greenlee County received significant snowfall with the Hannagan Meadow SNOTEL receiving 16.
The Pinaleno Mountains received significant snowfall with a foot of snow accumulating on Mt. Graham.

Very cold temperatures in the teens and lower 20s affected the Tohono O'Odham Nation for several consecutive nights causing frozen pipes to burst in a few locales. Temperatures dropped as low as 17 degrees in Sells the morning of January 15th.

events.cz_name: UPPER SANTA CRUZ RIVER AND ALTAR VALLEYS
events.event_narrative: Low temperatures in the teens for several consecutive nights caused several water pipes to freeze and burst in Nogales and other areas. Nogales was as cold as 10 degrees on January 15th.  A pipe burst in the Early Learning Center in Arivaca, flooding four rooms and causing $15,000 in damage.

Low temperatures in the teens or lower 20s for several nights caused numerous pipes to burst in the Tucson metropolitan area.  The Tucson International Airport dropped to 15 degrees on the morning of January 15th. Most of the frozen pipes exposed to the cold were on the roofs or sides of homes.  Also, citrus fruits were damaged by the hard freeze, which meant that local food banks could not glean unpicked fruit to supplement their food donations. Total damage was estimated at $100,000.  Additionally, two house fires were indirectly related to the cold weather.  A mobile home caught fire when the owner attempted to thaw frozen pipes with a propane torch. Another home caught fire after residents placed a heat lamp and blankets on a patio overnight to keep pets warm. No one was injured in either fire.

Several nights of cold temperatures in the teens caused several frozen pipes to burst in the Eloy area.  Temperatures on the morning of January 15th were as cold as 13 degrees at nearby Arizona City and 19 degrees at Picacho Peak.

Several nights of cold temperatures in the teens caused frozen pipes to burst in portions of western Cochise County. Temperatures dropped to 13 degrees in Sierra Vista and Benson, and 14 degrees in Tombstone the morning of January 15th.
Several nights of cold temperatures in the single digits and teens caused frozen pipes to burst in eastern Cochise County. Temperatures dropped to 7 degrees in Douglas and Willcox on January 13th.

Very cold temperatures in the teens affected eastern Pinal County for several consecutive nights. A death due to exposure occurred the morning of January 16th east of Dudleyville, in the southwest corner of the San Carlos Apache Reservation. The deceased was not a member of the tribe.

A motorist lost control of their vehicle when they encountered black ice that had formed on Interstate 19 near the San Xavier exit. The result was a ten vehicle accident. One person suffered minor injuries.

While much of southeast Arizona benefited from near or even slightly above normal precipitation in December of 2012 into January of 2013, valleys of Cochise, Graham and Greenlee Counties remained on the dry side.  February and April totals were less than 50% of normal in these areas, and they fared only marginally better during March.  By late April, extreme drought (D3) conditions developed over the northeast three quarters of Cochise County and the southern halves Graham and Greenlee Counties, essentially east of a line from Clifton to Fort Thomas to Benson to Bisbee. One impact was an increase in the wildfire danger in these areas.

Southwest winds were sustained at times between 35 and 45 mph with gusts around 60 mph.

Southwest winds were sustained between 40 and 50 mph with gusts around 65 mph.

Strong southwest winds around 30 mph with gusts to 50 mph led to areas of blowing dust across Interstate 10 in Pinal County. Visibility was restricted to less than 100 feet at times. Two semis jack-knifed and were involved in an accident with two other passenger vehicles near Picacho and Milepost 213. Four minor injuries resulted.  Another multi-vehicle chain-reaction accident on westbound Interstate 10 occurred near Milepost 212 resulted in less serious damage and no injuries.
A nearly translucent, but powerful dust devil damaged the roof to one home on Tucson's east side.
A powerful dust devil removed several dozen roof tiles from two homes in Green Valley. Wind speeds were estimated at 65 mph.  A stove vent was also blown off one roof.

The human-caused Benson 1 Fire started near Interstate 10, just west of Pomerene, AZ along the dry San Pedro River bed and spread through timber and brush near the river bottom. Since it was difficult to access, moderate winds caused this fire to spread up the banks where it destroyed a small trailer at an RV park.  As a precautionary measure, a two mile stretch of Interstate 10 was closed briefly on the day the fire started, and about 25 mobile homes were evacuated.
Thunderstorms produced wind gusts of 58 to 68 mph across southern sections of Tucson. While no damage was reported, blowing dust reduced visibilities to less than a quarter mile in spots.
Thunderstorm winds blew down a 20 foot flag pole in Three Points, Arizona. The winds also produced areas of blowing dust that restricted visibility to less than a quarter mile.

Extreme drought (D3) conditions persisted across the southern halves of Graham and Greenlee Counties and the northeast two thirds of Cochise County in June. These dry conditions were exacerbated by very hot temperatures throughout the month. While modest rain fell over western parts of this drought area on the 15th and the 30th, little if any rain occurred elsewhere.  The effects of prolonged drought were manifested when the Gila River in Graham County ran dry for the first time in a number of years.  Farmers have been relegated to using what little well water remains.

Two to five inches of rain fell along Highway 92 between Sierra Vista and Bisbee.  Some areas received up to 7 inches of rain over a 3 hour period.  Vehicles became stranded on roadways in water up to 3 feet deep, necessitating several swift water rescues. Several roads were closed, including Highway 92, which was shut down for about 90 minutes.  Also, a large concrete culvert under a private road collapsed near Palominas.  Several residents were isolated due to the collapse.

These dry conditions were exacerbated by very hot temperatures throughout the month. While modest rain fell over western parts of this drought area on the 15th and the 30th, little if any rain occurred elsewhere. The effects of prolonged drought were manifested when the Gila River in Graham County ran dry for the first time in a number of years. Farmers have been relegated to using what little well water remains.

Thunderstorm winds knocked down 15 power poles on the west side of Tucson.  One pole fell on a vehicle.  One residence sustained damage to a porch, and one tree was knocked down. 13,000 customers lost power, some for up to 2 days. Several roads were closed due to downed power lines.
RAWS station at Muleshoe Ranch reported a wind gust of 81 mph.
Thunderstorm winds picked up a storage container and blew it into a gas main.
A thunderstorm wind gust of 70 mph was recorded by the Horse Camp RAWS station.
Thunderstorm winds downed large tree limbs near Benson.  Also, a field of planted rye was mostly flattened.
A 64 mph gust was recorded at Davis-Monthan Air Force Base.

Thunderstorms produced 1 to 2 inches of rain in less than an hour over parts of Eloy. Without sufficient drainage, water quickly ponded, flooding streets and yards.  Water was a foot deep in some streets, stranding several vehicles.   Damage due to flooding of homes was minimal, but extensive areas of mud were left on streets and in yards.
One inch diameter hail was reported at Rose Canyon Campground.
Thunderstorm winds peeled a metal roof off a residence and damaged several small outbuildings and trailers near Sonoita.
Thunderstorms winds downed a tree at Esperanza Estates in Green Valley.

Thunderstorm winds downed two dozen power poles in southern Tucson, mainly along Valencia Road between Park and Campbell Avenues and near the intersection of Golf Links and Pantano Roads. Around 8,000 customers were without electrical power at one point. Thirty mobile homes were damaged by winds or downed trees near Benson Highway and Valencia Road. One tree fell on a car. In addition, two hangar doors were blown off and two trees were downed at the Tucson International Airport where a wind gust to 74 mph was measured at 205 p.m. MST.
Thunderstorm winds downed a power pole in Benson.
Thunderstorms winds downed trees in Rita Ranch.

Drought eased markedly across Cochise County during July as monsoon rainfall of mounts of 3 to 10 inches, representing 125 to 250 percent of normal, fell across the region. By July 23rd, all extreme drought (D3) was removed from Cochise county. The northern third of the county improved to the severe drought (D2) category while the remainder of Cochise County, where the heaviest rain fell, improved to either the D0 or D1 drought category. The Bisbee-Douglas International Airport recorded 10.12 inches of rain, the most ever measured there in one calendar month.

events.cz_name: UPPER GILA RIVER AND ARAVAIPA VALLEYS
events.event_narrative: The area under extreme drought (D3) conditions shrank only slightly in southern Graham and Greenlee counties as the bulk of monsoon rain fell both to the north and south of the Gila River Valley. Most locations received between 1.5 and 2.5 inches of rain during July, which is near or slightly below normal. The Safford airport received just 1.49 inches of rain.  Some of the effects on the cotton crop have been mitigated by farmers leaving half of their fields idle this season.  Mandatory water restrictions adopted by the City of Safford in August of 2012 have helped mitigate the city's supply to some extent, but due to the prolonged drought, the low water table caused the city to shut off four of the city's eleven wells. This in turn prompted the city to approve higher water rates to fund the drilling of new wells and building of pipelines. In nearby Thatcher, mandatory water restrictions were ordered and stricter water conservation standards have been adopted for new construction.
