Thunderstorms winds caused damage along a two mile long and 2.5 mile wide path along Fort Grant Road northwest of Willcox. Four homes were damaged, a pump house was destroyed, a center pivot irrigation system was flipped and the trunk of a 40-foot high tree was snapped near the ground. A trained spotter measured a wind gust of 78 mph and one member of the public reported winds in excess of 68 mph for fifteen minutes.

Very heavy rain caused flooding in southern parts of Tucson. Several roads were closed including Park Avenue between Valencia and Drexel Roads. Two adults and two children were rescued from their vehicle which was caught in flood waters on Houghton Road near Valencia Road.
Heavy rain caused Ocotillo Road northwest of Benson to become flooded. A motorist was rescued from a vehicle in flowing water 2 feet deep. Roads were also flooded in the Mescal area.
Heavy rain caused Purdy Lane to become flooded in Naco. Flood waters entered one home near the roadway.

Thunderstorms winds blew roofs off several buildings at the state prison near the Bisbee-Douglas International Airport. One outbuilding was blown into a van, causing damage to the vehicle. Several power poles were downed causing a power outage which lasted for seven hours.  The ASOS at KDUG measured a gust to 58 mph before power was lost.  The strong winds also generated areas of blowing dust which briefly restricted visibility to near one half of a mile.

The Shipman Fire began when a lightning strike sparked a fire in the Gila River bed which was thick with salt cedar trees just southeast of Kearny.  About 200 homes were evacuated and Highway 177 was closed for a short time as a precaution.  One home and two other small structures were destroyed by the fire.

A severe thunderstorm produced large hail as it tracked westward across rural portions of southern Santa Cruz County. The largest hail reported by spotters was the size of golf balls at Kino Springs. No damage was reported.
A wind gust to 58 mph was measured at the Nogales International Airport.
Spotters reported hail up to the size of quarters in Palominas.

Thunderstorm winds knocked over irrigation sprinklers, destroyed a barn, tore roofs off several other buildings, including a business in the Pearce-Sunsites area. The damaging winds also downed trees and power poles and blew a semi-tractor trailer onto its side.
A vehicle windshield was broken by large hail near Kings Ranch Road.

Thunderstorm winds downed several trees and power poles at Fort Huachuca and in Sierra Vista. In addition, several homes sustained roof damage and one had the roof completely blown off. A wind gust to 82 mph was measured by the Libby Field ASOS.

Thunderstorm winds downed several power poles in Mammoth. Evaporative coolers were blown off roofs and trees were downed, some of which caused minor damage to nearby homes. Some residents of Mammoth were without power for just over 24 hours. Thunderstorms winds also blew down a fence in Oracle.
One inch diameter hail was reported in Mammoth.
Penny size hail was reported in Winkelman.
Thunderstorm wind gusts to 60 mph were reported in Winkelman.
Penny size hail was reported in Elfrida.

Heavy rain for the second evening in a row caused flash flooding near Highway 92 from Palominas to near Nicksville and the foothills of the Huachuca Mountains. Several roads became inundated with flowing water two feet deep.
Penny size hail was reported in Marana.
A wind gust to 59 mph was measured at the Bisbee-Douglas Airport.
Quarter size hail was reported southeast of Cochise.
Heavy rain caused flash flooding of Highway 80 in the Saint David area.
Penny size hail was reported west of Pirtleville.
Penny size hail was reported at Summerhaven.
Heavy rain caused flash flooding of Mount Lemmon Highway and other roads in Summerhaven.

Thunderstorm winds downed several trees including three 45-year old eucalyptus trees. Some trees fell onto houses causing minor roof damage and one ruptured a roof-mounted gas line. Another downed tree shattered a patio wall. Several 16 foot garage doors on newer homes were damaged or destroyed because the side of garage was constructed with an opening to a gated patio between the house and attached garage. The fire station at Esperanza Blvd. and La Canada Drive also sustained minor roof damage.
Several trees were downed in Rita Ranch.  One tree crashed into the living room of a home, while another smashed a cinder block wall and yet another fell onto a truck.
Thunderstorm winds downed 34 power poles in along Anway Road between Magee and Avra Valley Roads, leaving about 2000 people without power for several hours.
Thunderstorm winds downed a power pole and damaged a roof of a residence near the Gunsight Cemetery.
Thunderstorm winds downed a tree near 29th Street and Houghton Road and downed power lines at Irvington and Houghton Roads.
Thunderstorm winds downed a large tree near Congress St. and Scott Avenue.
Heavy rain caused flash flooding of Ash Creek, which partially eroded Twin Oaks Road.

Heavy rain of around one inch in less than 30 minutes caused flash flooding across portions of the Tucson metro area.  Tucson���s southeast side was hit hard along Houghton Road from Sahuarita Road north to Golf Links Road then west to around Wilmot Road.  Motorists became stranded in vehicles and several people were trapped in washes when the normally dry stream beds began to flow rapidly. One person was injured after being washed downstream in Rose Hill Wash on Tucson���s east side. Other swift water rescues occurred in the Pantano Wash near Golf Links Road and the Rillito River near La Canada Drive. In addition, a motorist was rescued from his vehicle near Creek Street and Bonanza Avenue. The vehicle was later swept away. Near the Tucson International Airport, six inches of pavement depth along a section of South Sears Boulevard near the was completely washed away. Tucson���s southwest side also received heavy rain totaling 1 to 2 inches, especially along Valencia Road from Campbell Avenue westward to near Ryan Field.  Several cars were stranded along San Joaquin Road and sections of Snyder Hill Road and Old Ajo Highway were closed due to flash flooding.

Thunderstorm winds caused minor roof damage to several structures in Thatcher and Pima, and downed four power poles east of Fort Thomas. The wind knocked a travel trailer off its block, which in turn damaged a nearby cinder block wall.
Penny size hail was reported in Sierra Vista.

Nearly three inches of rain fell in less than an hour over the upper reaches of Bonita Canyon within the burn scar of the 2011 Horseshoe 2 Wildfire. Significant mud and debris flow, rock slides, downed trees and flood damage to the Bonita Canyon Drive roadbed and Bonita Canyon Campground occurred in the upper reaches of the canyon.  Up to 18 inches of water and mud damaged the historic campground restroom facilities . Downstream, the visitor center parking lot was also flooded. The lower portion of the roadway reopened the next day while upper reaches remained closed for several weeks.
Quarter size hail was reported on Highway 191.
Lightning struck a pair of Palm Trees near 22nd Street and Sarnoff Drive, igniting them and burning one to a cinder. Another palm tree was ignited by lightning near Golf Links Road and Prudence Road.

A severe thunderstorm moved through southern Tucson, damaging parts of the roof of Van Buskirk Elementary School and downing several power poles in the area. Power poles were also blown down at the intersection of Irvington Rd. and Campbell Ave. A total of 9,000 customers were without power for a short period of time. Additionally, several trees in the area were downed by thunderstorm winds.
A thunderstorm wind gust of 61 mph was recorded by a trained storm spotter.  A few tree branches were snapped and one tree was blown down along Tangerine Rd.

Heavy rain from a severe thunderstorm infiltrated wind-caused roof damage at Van Buskirk Elementary school. Seven classrooms were flooded causing water damage, and were not ready for the beginning of the school year.
Heavy rain caused flooding along Silverlake Road and Euclid Avenue near downtown Tucson. Vehicles became stalled in the floodwaters and the road was then closed to traffic.
Heavy rain caused washes to flow strong as they entered northeast sections of Oro Valley. A fifteen year old walking amid Big Wash was rescued after becoming surrounded by flood waters.
Heavy rain caused small washes to flood flowing northward into the Tanque Verde Wash in far east Tucson.  Speedway Blvd. was flooded near Harrison Road.
Heavy rain flooded Houghton and Wilmot Roads between Tucson and Corona De Tucson.
Sabino Creek rose 1 to 2 feet as it flowed through Sabino Canyon Recreation Area.
Heavy rain on and downstream from Sierrita Road caused flooding of washes flowing northwest toward Three Points. Sierrita Mountain Road was flooded near Guy St.
A funnel cloud extended briefly from a thunderstorm southeast of Sonoita.
Heavy rain caused flash flooding on the west side of Tucson.  Four people were rescued from a vehicle in 2 to 3 feet of water flowing across Manville Road near Anway Road in Picture Rocks.

Thunderstorm winds downed a large tree near Speedway Blvd. and Stone Ave.
A spotter measured a thunderstorm wind gust to 58 mph northwest of Hereford.
A spotter west of Hereford reported nickel size hail.

Two inches of rain fell in less than 30 minutes on the southwest slopes of the Mule Mountains and in Old Bisbee causing extensive street flooding of the historic district. A retaining wall collapsed due to the force of the flowing water. The wall fell on a vehicle, creating dents and breaking the windshield. Flooding also left debris covering Highway 92 near the San Pedro River.
Bisbee-Douglas Airport ASOS recorded thunderstorm wind gust of 64 mph.
The Tucson International Airport ASOS recorded severe thunderstorm wind gust of 61 mph.  An eight inch diameter tree branch was downed near the intersection of Sunrise and Skyline Drives.
A trained spotter reported quarter size hail north of Glenn St. and Alvernon Way.

Lightning struck the roof of an apartment building near 29th Street and Craycroft Road. The lightning penetrated the roof's asphalt shingles and caused damage to the cinder block wall below the roof's eave. A nearby palm tree was also ignited by the strike. One resident was knocked over even though he was in a different room, but no one was injured.
Lightning struck the house of a trained spotter in Vail, resulting in electrical damage.

events.cz_name: UPPER GILA RIVER AND ARAVAIPA VALLEYS
events.event_narrative: Strong outflow from a light rain shower collapsed part of a crudely supported porch attached to a house southwest of Pima, AZ. A nearby carport was undamaged.

Two to three inches of rain in less than an hour caused flash flooding northwest of Willcox. The home of a family of four was flooded.  As they attempted to escape in their sport utility vehicle, water was nearly waste high.  They drove toward Willcox but became stranded in flood waters along Old Stewart Road and needed to be rescued. The next day, another vehicle became stranded in standing water in the same location. The man was able to swim to safety. No injuries were reported in either incident.
Brief heavy rain caused mud to slide downhill, temporarily closing Highway 191 in Clifton near the old train depot. Debris was up to four feet deep across the roadway.

Heavy rain of 2 to 3 inches fell along the Hickiwan Wash between 2 and 4 pm and downstream along the San Simon Wash between the between 4 and 6 pm. The San Simon Wash flowed rapidly across Highway 86, and Indian Routes 28 and 21 downstream, causing all these roads to be closed.

Flooding continued overnight along the San Simon Wash from Santa Cruz downstream due to heavy rain that fell during the late afternoon hours. Indian Road 21 remained closed due to high water until early morning.
A wash running through Vail flooded near the intersection of Calle Rinconado and Andrada Road. Water flowing across the road was over one foot deep.

A thunderstorm dropped nearly an inch of rain in 20 minutes. The heavy rain caused drain spouts on the roof of a supermarket to break, sending water into the attic, which collapsed the ceiling. The store was evacuated but no one was injured.
Heavy rain filled many normally dry washes in parts of northwest Tucson.  Orange Grove Road had 2 feet of water flowing across it near Interstate 10.
Thunderstorm winds downed several trees on Tucson's northwest side.  In addition, an adobe chimney was toppled onto its side.
Thunderstorm winds downed several trees on Tucson's northwest side. One tree branch damaged three cars when it fell. Additionally, a small greenhouse was damaged by the wind.
Thunderstorms produced gusty winds at Saguaro National Park East with a 63 mph gust measured near Old Spanish Trail and Freeman Road.
Up to 2 inches of rain in less than an hour led to flash flooding along Valencia Road in southwest Tucson.

events.cz_name: UPPER GILA RIVER AND ARAVAIPA VALLEYS
events.event_narrative: The area under extreme drought (D3) conditions in southern Graham and Greenlee Counties was downgraded to severe drought (D2) conditions my mid September. The D2 area also contained northern portions of Cochise and Pima as well as southern Pinal counties. Between 1 and 3 inches of rain fell in early September across the D3 area, with some locations near Safford receiving nearly twice the normal monthly rainfall amount during this time period. The Safford Airport received 2.66 inches of rainfall from September 6th through the 16th. In addition, very heavy rains in western New Mexico and along the Mogollon Rim filled the Gila River during September. Stretches of the Gila River actually rose to above bank full for several days.  While the shorter term drought issues were eased, long term drought remains a concern.

During the late evening hours of September 9th, three to four inches of rain fell along the east slopes of the Baboquivari Mountains and northern portions of the Buenos Aires National Wildlife Refuge along a 10 mile length of the Altar Wash 20 to 30 miles south of Three Points, Arizona.  The flow peaked downstream at Three Points along the Brawley Wash at about 7500 cubic feet per second around 5:00 am MST on September 10th. While this represented a rise of more than six feet, only a small portion of this flow  poured over the banks downstream of this gauge, flooding a sub-division with 8 to 12 inches of water.  Roads were eventually closed although first responders were able to evacuate residents from ten mobile homes.  The residents were unable to return until the following day.  Minor damage occurred to several vehicles and mobile homes.
A funnel cloud was observed and photographed by a member of the media northeast of Mescal.

Thunderstorm winds blew the roof off an open-walled hay barn near Tanque Verde Road and Tanque Verde Loop Road. Part of the barn roof struck a moving vehicle, denting the car and breaking its windshield. No injuries occurred. A tree was also blown over near Tanque Verde Loop Road south of Speedway Blvd.
Thunderstorms winds blew the lightly-nailed wooden roof off a church at Ak-Chin Village. Two other structures had portions of their roofs blown off.
Wind gusts to 60 mph were recorded north of Ajo, but no damage was reported.
Thunderstorm winds blew off a portion of a roof in Nogales.

Thunderstorm winds downed nine power poles near Pima Mine Road and Nogales Highway. The downed poles caused 11,000 customers to be without power for several hours and both roadways were closed through the night. A roof was blown off a building at the Sahuarita waste-water treatment plant.  In addition, the roof was ripped off a mobile home on East Lumber Street near Old Nogales Highway. Several other mobile homes sustained minor damage in that area and one tree was uprooted.
Thunderstorm winds downed or bent several power poles on Valencia Road west of Casino Del Sol.
A thunderstorm wind gust of 64 mph was measured at Horse Camp Canyon RAWS.

During the evening of September 13th, heavy rain occurred along the Campbell Blue Creek near the headwaters of the Blue River in Arizona, which was an area that was affected by the 2011 Wallow Fire. Heavy rain also fell along Turkey Creek in Arizona and the Dry Blue Creek in New Mexico.  Runoff continued downstream to the confluence of the Campbell Blue and Dry Blue Creeks, which forms the Blue River.  In addition, heavy rain occurred during the evening of the 14th in Arizona and New Mexico, swelling the tributaries of the Blue River upstream of the community of Blue, Arizona.  Multiple crests in the Blue River two to four feet above flood stage resulted. Sections of Blue River Road were washed out, isolating residents of the community.  The Campbell Blue Bridge, which is a 30 foot concrete bridge just across the state line in New Mexico, was completely washed out. Electrical and telephone lines were damaged by the flooding. A utility company truck rolled into Turkey Creek after the adjacent flood-compromised road gave way.  The driver was able to escape the six foot deep flowing water without injury.

events.cz_name: WHITE MOUNTAINS OF GRAHAM AND GREENLEE COUNTIES
events.event_narrative: In Northern Greenlee County, the Beaver Head SNOTEL received 20 of snowfall and the Hannagan Meadow received about 12 of snowfall for this event.
Heavy snowfall occurred with about 18 inches at the higher elevation of the Pinaleno Mountains including Mt. Graham.

Antecedent dry conditions along with gusty winds of about 20 to 25 mph produced localized dense blowing dust that reduced visibility to near zero in parts of Pinal County. This localized blowing dust resulted in a multiple vehicle chain-reaction accident along Interstate 10 near Picacho at mile marker 214. The accident involved 19 vehicles and resulted in 3 fatalities and 12 injuries.  The interstate was closed to traffic in both directions until around 10 pm MST.
Heavy snowfall occurred on the higher peaks of the Pinaleno Mountains. 12 to 24 of snowfall occurred on Mt. Graham at elevations between 9000 and 10,000 feet.

Severe drought (D2) conditions present over much of southeast Arizona deteriorated into the extreme drought (D3) category in eastern Pinal, western Graham, extreme northeastern Pima and much of northern Cochise counties by mid February. These  counties were among those listed as primary natural disaster areas by the USDA. The growing season had not yet started, so vegetation impacts were minimal, but soil moisture conditions were generally less than 30 percent of normal and San Carlos Reservoir was a less than 14 percent of capacity. Fuel dryness levels were drier than the long term average for February and significantly drier than in February 2013.

A non-thunderstorm wind gust of 58 mph was measured at Ryan Airfield. Around the same time, shingles were blown off of a roof about 3 miles to the east north east of Ryan Airfield, with sustained winds of 37 mph (measured) gusting to approximately 55 mph.

Heavy rain was determined to be the cause of a 1-vehicle accident involving two women at Kilometer 15 on 1-19 in Rio Rico. The car drifted to the left into the center median at approximately 1215 MST and struck a tree. One woman was killed and the other was seriously injured.

Strong winds estimated at about 50 mph brought down a 30-foot tall saguaro on top of a carport at a residence in Green Valley. One of the cactus arms rolled into the street and another landed against a neighboring house. Heavy rain of more than one inch during the previous 24 hours likely loosened up the soil enough that the wind blew the cactus over. There was extensive damage to the carport, and 3 vehicles, including a golf cart, an SUV, and a vintage Cadillac.

Multiple periods of heavy rain which fell during the late afternoon and evening hours causing flash flooding near Apache Springs Ranch. Law enforcement reported fast moving water that was 35 feet across flowing near Forest Service Road 4084. There was also a report of several people stranded on the other side of this flowing water in Gardner Canyon.

Extreme drought (D3) category persisted in eastern Pinal, western Graham, extreme northeastern Pima and much of northern Cochise counties through March.  One precipitation event brought up to 150% of normal monthly precipitation in one day over parts of southern Graham and northern Cochise counties on March 1st, but the remainder of the month was dry. Soil moisture conditions were generally less than 30 percent of normal and San Carlos Reservoir was at less than 11 percent of capacity. Fuel moisture levels remained very low causing wildfire concerns.

Trained spotter reported 1 inch hail which accompanied a thunderstorm moving through the Douglas area.

Southwest winds gusting to between 60 and 70 mph were common during the afternoon hours in Santa Cruz and Cochise counties. The observatory at Mt. Hopkins in the Santa Rita Mountains reported several gusts as high as 66 mph. The KALK and FKHU ASOS at Fort Huachuca and the ASOS at Bisbee-Douglas Airport all measured  maximum gusts from 58 to 61 mph between 1300 and 1430 MST. The strong winds fanned a small 75 acre wildfire west of Sierra Vista. The human-caused Aerostat fire was attended to quickly and contained by 1900 MST that evening. No injuries or damage were reported.

events.event_narrative: The Skunk Fire was started around 1415 MST on Saturday April 19, 2014 by lightning, approximately 14 miles east of San Carlos. The fire had little growth throughout the remainder of the month of April, mostly toward the northwest on the San Carlos Apache Reservation. Total burned area on April 30, 2014 was 63 acres. No injuries, fatalities, or damage were reported in April.

events.event_narrative: The Skunk Fire was 63 acres on May 1, 2014. Rapid fire growth began on May 14, 2014, and due to prolonged periods of strong winds and low relative humidity, the total burned area increased to 43,370 acres by May 31, 2014. Most of the burned area occurred on the San Carlos Apache Reservation. Near the end of the month, the fire spilled over from northern Graham County into extreme southeastern Gila County. No injuries, fatalities, or damage were reported in May.

Extreme drought (D3) category persisted and actually expanded slightly in eastern Pinal, western Graham, extreme northeastern Pima and much of northern Cochise counties through April. Two meager precipitation events occurred on the 19th and 26th of the month but only managed to produce between 10 and 50 percent of the monthly average rainfall in the majority of the drought area. These two light rain events did produce lightning strikes that sparked a number of wildfires, including the Skunk Fire in northwest Graham County. Soil moisture conditions were generally less than 20 percent of normal and San Carlos Reservoir was at less than 9 percent of capacity.

Spotter reports a tree down across North Rancho Vistoso Road near the intersection of Moore Road in Oro Valley. Thunderstorm outflows created a wall of dust near Marana that progressed northwest along Interstate 10 beyond Eloy. Visibilities were limited to near a quarter mile.
A lightning strike to a power pole near Ina Rd. and Oracle Rd. left about 25 residents without power.
A trained spotter reported wind gusts up to 61 mph, which broke several small tree branches.
NWS employee reported two trees uprooted near Starr Pass. Around the same time, broadcast media reported trees down at Silverbell Rd and Grant Rd.
Thunderstorm winds snapped six power poles and downed trees along Old Spanish Trail from Irvington to Golf Links Roads. Over 1600 homes were left without power southeast of Houghton Escalante Roads.

A spotter measured a wind gust of 60 mph at Tucson Mall. Thunderstorm winds downed trees near Limberlost and First Avenue, one of which fell on a car, while another fell on a mobile home. A tree also fell on a jeep at Magee and Oracle while other trees were downed near River and La Cholla. About 1300 customers lost power due to downed power lines in the Flowing Wells neighborhood.

Heavy rain falling at the rate of 0.5 in 15 minutes caused flash flooding as storms moved northwest across the east side of the Tucson metro area. Houghton Rd. was flooded south of the Pima County Fair Grounds. In addition, two people who were trapped on top of their SUV in Alamo Wash, at Yale Dr. and Kenyon Dr.  were rescued. Another car was stranded in flood waters near Stella and Harrison Rd.

Heavy rain of over 2 inches in less than one hour fell in Nogales, Sonora, Mexico, causing catastrophic flooding there. Runoff crossing the border combined with brief heavy rain in Nogales, Arizona caused flooding and the closure of the DeConcini Port of Entry until 10 pm MST for the first time in history. Runoff into Nogales Wash burst from manholes into Nogales, Arizona. As the the Nogales Wash emerged above ground, it over-topped its banks and caused street flooding.

Very heavy rain in excess of 1.5 inches in a short period of time caused flash flooding in Corona de Tucson. Businesses, homes, and roads were flooded. The fire department was needed to help stalled cars and stranded drivers near Sahuarita Road and Houghton. Sahuarita Road near Alvernon was closed for a short time.
Railroad Wash over-topped its banks onto highway 70 resulting in the road being closed.
Thunderstorm winds snapped power poles south of Arizona City, closing three county roads.

Route 77 about 3.7 miles north of Mammoth, AZ was closed at mile marker 117 due to flash flooding. Rainfall in excess of 0.75 inches fell in a short period of time with a slow-moving thunderstorm, causing the road to flood. The same storm produced a storm total of 3.5 inches in Dudleyville, AZ.

A severe storm with multiple microbursts moved through the Kansas Settlement area, just south of Willcox in Cochise County. One home on E. Sulphur Springs Rd was severely damaged, and the family displaced. Pieces of a tin roof were blown off with insulation littering the ground outside the house. Rain then continued and damaged many items inside the home. Neighbors claimed to have found pieces of the roof up to two miles away on Birch Road. Several small trees and tree branches were blown down as well. There were reports to the sheriff's office of some downed power poles in the area as well.
A photo of nickel-sized hail was received from Picture Rocks.

Thunderstorm wind gusts up to 61 mph were reported at the Safford Airport. At Solomon, the roof of a shed was blown off, damaging nearby vehicles. Localized blowing dust reducing visibilities to less than a quarter mile were reported along Highway 70 near Safford.
Lightning incinerated a palm tree in Saddlebrook.

Back to back days of heavy rainfall caused major flash flooding in downtown Sierra Vista, with rainfall amounts of just over 1 in Hereford to 2.49 in Sierra vista. 2,000 cfs of flow was measured at the Charleston Bridge on the San Pedro River. Moson Road and Hereford Road both had to be barricaded because they were impassable due to flooding according to local law enforcement. Also, there were newspaper reports that a taxi took on flood waters on 7th street just north of Willcox Drive. The main gate of Fort Huachuca was closed from 2030 on Friday until 0015 on Saturday due to flooding in the area. Traffic had to be re-routed to the east gate.

Extreme drought (D3) category persisted across eastern Pinal, western Graham, extreme northeastern Pima and much of northern Cochise counties through May. Virtually no rain fell in the drought area.  Levels at San Carlos Reservoir fell to about 6 percent of capacity by the end of the month.

Heavy rain across Cochise County resulted in further flooding in parts of Sierra Vista. Early in the day, normally dry washes were still running from the previous day's rainfall, and storm debris (mainly rocks) remained on Willcox Drive and Buffalo Soldier Trail. After storms rolled through during the evening hours, law enforcement reported Moson Road closed yet again, this time at mile post 5, and Kings Ranch Road near Highway 92 was flooded over. The storm also washed out the only access for residents living along South Paloma Trail in Palominas, stranding several families.

Heavy rain in the Tucson area caused flash flooding on the southeast side of town. Flash flooding was reported I-10 and Wilmot Rd. and at Kolb and Irvington Roads where water was 1-2 feet deep. Broadcast media reported that numerous cars got stuck in flowing water. Tucson Fire Department was called to rescue one adult and one child, who climbed a tree to escape quickly-flowing waters in a wash near Escalante Rd. and Camino Seco Blvd. No one was injured.

Thunderstorm winds downed multiple trees, power poles and lines on Tucson's east side on and around Davis-Monthan AFB, leaving over 10,000 customers without power. Two trees landed on vehicles. One tree near Stella and Wilmot fell on a house, causing major damage. Several power poles were downed near Benson Highway and Campbell Ave. Five telephone poles were snapped near Irvington and Pantano Roads and roofs were blown off two houses near Escalante and Pantano Roads. A retired, 40-thousand pound F-16 was flipped over on top of another retired jet at the Davis-Monthan AFB boneyard. Strong winds punctured holes in the sun shades in a few of the aircraft shelters. Operational aircraft did not sustain any damage. The ASOS on base a mile away from the boneyard measured a peak gust of 66 mph.
Spotter reported quarter size hail in Oro Valley.
Quarter size hail was reported at two locations near Sierra Vista. The first report was from a trained spotter just south of Sierra Vista near highway 92. The second report was in Ash Canyon.

Heavy rains impacted the Tucson metro during the morning hours, causing the Rillito to flow at Camino de la Tierra near River Rd and Shannon Rd at about 6-8 inches deep. Several other roads on the west side of Tucson were closed due to flood waters.  A swift water rescue occurred at Silverbell Rd and Ina Rd. Rescues of persons from cars stranded in flood waters occurred near Ina Rd and La Cholla Rd, and near Drexel Rd and Country Club Rd. A report from first responders indicated water was above the rear bumper of the vehicle.
Thunderstorm winds downed power poles near Sunrise Drive and Sabino Canyon Road.
Thunderstorm wind gusts downed trees, blew over a gasoline pump and part of the roof of a business in Corona De Tucson.
Lightning struck and burned a pair of palm trees in Green Valley.
Thunderstorm winds uprooted a tree at Three Points.
A metal three-sided hay barn was flattened by thunderstorm winds at an exotic bird sanctuary in Cascabel, AZ.
After microburst winds ripped the roof off a home at Kansas Settlement, heavy rain damaged or ruined much of the interior of the home as well as its contents.
Heavy rain caused flash flooding near the intersection of Twin Peaks and Sanders Roads.
Heavy rain caused flooding of 30 homes near Menager's Dam and two in Gunsight. Water was up to one foot deep. Gunsight Wash overflowed its banks and washed out Indian Road 5 near Gunsight.

Extreme drought (D3) category persisted across eastern Pinal, western Graham, extreme northeastern Pima and much of northern Cochise counties through June. By the middle of the month, extreme drought (D3) expanded into south central Pinal, northeast Graham and northern Greenlee counties.  Virtually no rain fell in the drought area. Levels at San Carlos Reservoir fell to about 3 percent of capacity by the end of the month. Soil moisture remained at less than 20 percent of normal. Ranchers continued to be affected by the depletion of rangeland forage vegetation throughout the dry spring. The Skunk Fire perimeter was contained early in the month with over 73,000 acres consumed.  Due to the dry conditions, lightning was able to easily ignite other wildfires during June, the most notable of which was the Oak Fire in the Galiuro Mountains.  This became an actively managed fire that burned over 13,000 acres.

events.cz_name: UPPER GILA RIVER AND ARAVAIPA VALLEYS
events.event_narrative: The Skunk Fire was started around 1415 MST on Saturday April 19, 2014 by lightning, approximately 14 miles east of San Carlos. Rapid fire growth began in mid May, and due to prolonged periods of strong winds and low relative humidity, the total burned area increased to 43,370 acres by June 1, 2014. Most of the burned area occurred on the San Carlos Apache Reservation in Graham County, but also spread into extreme southeastern Gila County. The fire perimeter was contained on June 3rd, after a series of back burns and after a total of 73,682 acres were consumed. Interior pockets of the fire continued to smolder for several days. The fire was officially contained on June 8th. No injuries, fatalities, or damage were reported during the duration of this wildfire.

A dust devil blew shingles off a roof and an awning into a neighboring property, damaging the cover of a pickup truck.

Extreme drought (D3) category persisted across southern and eastern Pinal, northern and western Graham, extreme northeastern Pima and much of northern Greenlee and Cochise counties through July. A small portion of Graham and Greenlee counties was reduced to the severe (D2) category due to above average rainfall. The remainder of the extreme drought area received either near normal July rainfall or as little as 50 percent of normal. Levels at San Carlos Reservoir continued to fall, bottoming out at close to 1 percent of capacity by the end of the month. Soil moisture remained at less than 20 percent of normal. Ranchers continued to be affected by the depletion of rangeland forage vegetation.

Levels at San Carlos Reservoir continued to fall, bottoming out at close to 1 percent of capacity by the end of the month. Soil moisture remained at less than 20 percent of normal. Ranchers continued to be affected by the depletion of rangeland forage vegetation.

Ranchers continued to be affected by the depletion of rangeland forage vegetation.

Flash flooding occurred along Red Rock and Harshaw Creeks. Streets in Patagonia were impassable where flood waters crossed up to 2 feet deep.
A 17-year old undocumented boy was struck and killed by lightning near Windmill Drive near Sonoita, Arizona.

Thunderstorm outflow winds flowed into air vents causing a section of drywall to fall into a breezeway, where it struck four people waiting for appointments at an office in a strip mall. Three of the four sustained minor injuries.
A thunderstorm wind gust of 58 mph was measured at the Guthrie RAWS.
Thunderstorms wind gusts damaged a railroad arm in Pima and downed two trees that in turn, fell on and damaged a fence.
Thunderstorm wind gusts downed two utility poles in Nogales.

Heavy rain on both sides of the International Border caused strong flows in Ephraim Wash. An unopened gate along the International Border fence collapsed sending an additional surge of water through Ephraim Wash which topped the Leyva Bridge and spilled onto Western Avenue in Nogales. Five people were rescued from a vehicle as they tried to flee the area. A total of 10 people from two homes were evacuated. The homes were flooded to a depth of three feet while 8 vehicles were damaged by flood waters.

Heavy rain in both Nogales, Sonora and Nogales, AZ caused flash flooding in several locations. Up to 0.75 inches of rain in 20 minutes along with pea-size hail were reported. Many businesses sustained water damage along Hohokam Drive when the Nogales Wash over-topped its banks. One car was swept down Nogales Wash near the Grand Ave/Hohokam Drive bridge with nobody inside.
Thunderstorm winds downed two utility poles along Central Highway northwest of Douglas.
Penny size hail was reported north of Douglas.
Thunderstorm winds downed large tree limbs north of Douglas.
Over 1.5 inches of rain in less than 30 minutes caused flash flooding along Leslie Canyon Road on the northwest side of Douglas.
Several power poles were blown down as well as a fence in Tubac due to severe thunderstorm winds.
Sasabe RAWS recorded a 66 mph wind gust.
Thunderstorm winds downed more than a dozen trees on the northeast side of Douglas. One tree on Frederic Drive fell on a neighboring house and damaged two cars and a motorcycle.

Heavy rain resulting in flash flooding near Arivaca began around 1430 MST when several low water crossings were reported as impassable. Law enforcement reported that Indian Road 19 just north of South Komelik had to be closed around 1500 MST. Heavy rain amounts such as 1.25 inches in 1 hour and 2.75 inches in 2.5 hours were reported by spotters. Both Sapo Tank and Yellowjacket Wash came up in a short period of time and flowed quickly throughout the afternoon.
Heavy rain caused flash flooding in Hickiwan Village where four homes were flooded. Nine people were rescued from a vehicle stuck in flood waters.

Thunderstorms produced very heavy rainfall that flooded five homes in Bowie, some with up to a foot of water. The courthouse also sustained minor damage from an inch of water entering the building. High water also caused the temporary closure of a short stretch of Interstate 10 from Mile Marker 365 to near 366. Multiple car accidents occurred in that area, forcing the closure of both the eastbound and westbound lanes of Interstate 10 for about an hour. Apache Pass and Roberts Farm Road were also closed in Bowie.

Strong thunderstorms brought heavy rainfall to the Tucson area. Rainfall rates of over 2 inches per hours and storm totals of between 1.5 inches and 2.0 inches resulted in flash flooding of the streets of central to south Tucson.
Flooding occurred south of Gu Vo. Many roads including Indian Route 1 were impassable.
Spotter originally found quarter size hail, but later called back when he found pieces that were the size of half dollars.

Local law enforcement reported that a maintenance worker was struck by lightning while outside the middle school in Sells. The individual was flown to a Tucson area hospital and later succumbed to injuries sustained from the strike.

Thunderstorm winds downed a tree at Broadway Blvd. and Harrison Rd. A porch roof was blown off a house a mile west on Broadway at Camino Seco.  A palm tree was also downed at that location. In between, near Bluefield St. and Porter Ave, a 50 foot pine tree was downed and part of a roof was blown off a house.
Two spotters in Oracle reported a maximum hail size of one inch, mixed in with smaller pieces. Hail fell for about 20 minutes.

A high based, short-lived funnel cloud was seen over Babocamari Ranch around 1315 LST. Photo was received from the public via local media. The captain at the Sierra Vista Fire Department confirmed the funnel never touched the ground.
Ryan Field AWOS measured a wind gust to 59 mph.
Local media reports a portion of a roof was blown off of a residence on the 300 block of North Schrader Lane.
Local law enforcement reports water flowing over Route 35 at mile marker 6.

Emergency Management reported that Sandario Road was closed near Snyder Hill Road. Water up to 2 feet deep was flowing over the road causing it to be impassable. Swift water rescue occurred late in the evening at this location when a woman drove into a wash and got stuck. At the time of the rescue, no barricades were up to indicate road had been closed.

Law enforcement reported three road closures due to flash flooding around 1500 LST: Tangerine Road between Dove Mountain and I-10; Moonfire Road at Silverbell; and Silverbell Road south of Ina. At 1645 LST, broadcast media reported that a swift water rescue occurred at Snow Leopard Drive south of the intersection of Linda Vista and Camino de Oeste.
Over 2 inches of rain fell on the spotter's property. This caused sheet flooding which washed out fences on the property.

Flash flooding occurred on Sahuarita Road near Davidson Rd that was about 40 feet wide and 1 foot deep. Debris in the water consisted of small branches and rocks. Spotter expected, from a historical perspective, that flooding would be worse on Sahuarita Road further to the west.

Heavy rain of one half inch in less than 30 minutes over the Tucson area resulted in early morning flash flooding. A car was swept down the Alamo Wash at Calle Betelgeux near 22nd St. and Kolb Rd. Two occupants of the vehicle were rescued without injury.

Multiple reports of a car stuck on Sahuarita Road west of Houghton due to flash flooding were relayed via Twitter. Pima County Sheriff's office later confirmed that Sahuarita Road was impassable in multiple locations due to water over the roadway. Rainfall amounts of between 0.75 and 1 inch fell in 30 minutes.

Photos were received of a landspout tornado which occurred just northwest of Willcox. It was on the ground for 6 minutes. No damage or injuries occurred. EF rating, path length, and path width are estimated based off radar data and information from a photographer. No storm survey was conducted.
Water flowed over a foot deep over the Frontage Road at Interstate 10 near Red Rock.
Over 2 inches of rain caused significant flooding of route 286 about halfway between Three Points and Sasabe, near mile post 24. Roads were also flooded near and west of Arivaca.

Thunderstorms produced over an inch of rain in less than 30 minutes in Tucson causing extensive street flooding in midtown. Some areas affected include Seneca and Country Club Roads, Grant Road between Swan and Campbell, as well as Tucson Boulevard between Speedway and Grant. A swift water rescue occurred at Fort Lowell Rd at Tucson Blvd for a vehicle stalled in flood waters. Water was up to 2 feet deep in some spots.
Heavy rain of up to 1.5 inches in less than one hour lead to areas of flash flooding in the Sierra Vista/Nicksville area. Local streets and low-lying areas became flooded and impassable.

Three inches of rain in less than an hour caused flash flooding in Duncan.  One home was flooded with water up to 3 feet deep and damage was sustained to a car wash structure. Two to three feet of water cover part of Highway 70 on the northwest edge of Duncan.

Flash flooding occurred along and near the Babocamari River north of Huachuca City in the Presidential Estates area.  A woman and three dogs were rescued from a mini-van which was submerged in 3 feet of water on Bowers Road.
Heavy rain caused significant street flooding on Tucson's east side. A woman was rescued from her sedan in flood waters 1 to 2 feet deep at Broadway Blvd and Camino Seco.
Several roads were flooded in the Arivaca area.

events.cz_name: WHITE MOUNTAINS OF GRAHAM AND GREENLEE COUNTIES
events.event_narrative: By early August, extreme drought (D3) conditions were reduced to the severe (D2) category across the White Mountains of Graham and Greenlee counties and the northern Chiricahua Mountains as a result of significant late July and early August rainfall.

By early August, extreme drought (D3) conditions were reduced to the severe (D2) category across the White Mountains of Graham and Greenlee counties and the northern Chiricahua Mountains as a result of significant late July and early August rainfall.

By mid August, extreme drought (D3) conditions were reduced to the severe (D2) category across the San Pedro River Valley in extreme northeast Pima and northwest Cochise Counties as a result of significant late July and early August rainfall.

Extreme drought (D3) category persisted across southern and eastern Pinal and western Graham Counties through August. Precipitation in these areas ranged from 25  to 125 percent of normal during August. After bottoming out at around 1 percent of capacity  early in the month, levels at San Carlos Reservoir rose slightly to about 2 percent of capacity by the end of August. Soil moisture did increase to greater than 30 percent of normal, but ranchers continued to be affected by the depletion of rangeland forage vegetation.

By late August, extreme drought (D3) conditions were reduced to the severe (D2) category across north central Cochise County as a result of significant August rainfall.

By early September, extreme drought (D3) conditions were reduced to the severe (D2) category across the much of south central and parts of southeast Pinal County as a result of significant early September rainfall. Much of the rain was a result of increased moisture from the remnants of Hurricane Norbert.

Extreme drought (D3) category persisted across far eastern Pinal and western Graham Counties through September. While some portions of the extreme drought area received up to 150 percent of normal rainfall during the month, a significant area near the Pinal/Graham County line received as little as 50 percent of normal rainfall in September. Levels at San Carlos Reservoir rose to about 6 percent of capacity by the end of September, the highest level since May. Soil moisture also improved, rising to around 70 percent of normal. However, ranchers continued to be affected by the depletion of rangeland forage vegetation.

Heavy rain caused flash flooding along Peck Canyon. Two males were rescued from Peck Canyon just outside of Rio Rico. Neither were injured.
Heavy rain of over two inches in less than two hours flooded parts of Arivaca Road, causing it to be closed to traffic.

Thunderstorm winds damaged 6 warehouses at the cotton-storage facility STS Land Holding in Eloy. Four warehouses were listed as a 30 to 50 percent loss. The other 2 buildings were still marginally usable. The warehouses, covered in tin, were mostly empty at the time. A few minutes later, 39 out of 107 cars on a Union Pacific train were derailed near the Interstate 10 Picacho exit. The freight containers were empty at the time. No one was injured. Extensive damage to the tracks also resulted causing the rail line to remain out of service until repairs were completed, three days later.
A severe thunderstorm south of Patagonia produced a brief funnel cloud. Multiple reports and pictures were received both from the public and broadcast media.
KOLS ASOS recorded a severe wind gust of 59 mph.
One inch diameter hail was reported south of Green Valley.
Thunderstorms in the area of Rio Rico caused the overflowing of several washes which rendered parts of Pendleton Drive impassable.

Torrential rain associated with moisture from the remnants of tropical system Norbert caused extensive flooding of Tucson's east side.  Many streets were inundated with 1 to 2 feet of water, stalling numerous vehicles.  Several swift water rescues occurred including the rescue of driver of a truck near Pontatoc Road and River Road.  Additionally, a female driver on East Calle Betelgeux drove into the lower water crossing of Alamo Wash.  Flood waters swept her car against a pedestrian bridge where it was hung up when first responders arrived. Before they could reach the woman, the current pulled the car under the bridge and under water 12 feet deep.  When the car was found less than a quarter mile downstream, near 22nd Street just west of Kolb Road, the driver had drown.

Heavy rain which occurred near the headwaters of the San Pedro River in Mexico and also over Cochise County due to Tropical Depression Odile caused significant rises on the San Pedro River. Water eventually made its way north through Mammoth, where the river overflowed it banks. Three homes and rural roads were flooded. Other residences were evacuated as a precaution. Residents were allowed back in their homes in the morning as the water receded. No injuries occurred.
Heavy rainfall caused flash flooding in Pinal County. Saddlebrooke Wash came out of its banks near Saddlebrooke, while several washes overflowed into the streets of Oracle, rendering them impassable.

Heavy rainfall from Norbert extended into the early afternoon hours. Several additional  swift water rescues occurred. One occurred in the Pima Wash on Rudasill Rd between 1st Avenue and Oracle Road, where a single occupant was successfully rescued after his vehicle was swept off the road by quickly flowing water. Around the same time but further north, a swift water rescue occurred near Hardy Rd and Northern Ave in Oro Valley. Yet another rescue occurred when a 69-year old man and his 76-year old wife got caught in flash flood waters near Highway 79 in Oracle Junction. The couple attempted to drive through flood waters near Suizo Road when their Honda Accord began floating down Cadillac Wash. They both exited the car and the man made it to dry land, but his wife was regrettably swept down the wash and perished as she was unable to swim.
Flash flooding in Sierra Vista caused several streets to be rendered impassable.

Significant rises on the Santa Cruz River in Tucson earlier in the day flowed northward. In the Avra Valley area, where bank protection is minimal, the river came out of its banks. During the late evening hours, a woman and her son were rescued from the top of their Jeep just south of the bridge near Trico Rd and Hardin Rd. The woman had attempted to cross flood waters when the vehicle was swept off the road and became stuck under the bridge. Both were successfully rescued with no injuries.

Graham County dispatch reported that Ash Creek was flowing rapidly which resulted in the closure of Cluff Ranch Rd. Eventually, Ash Creek came out of its banks and began running into a residential area in the town of Pima. At least 1 home was flooded, and 6 people were air lifted out of Ash Canyon due to loss of road access and flooding concerns. No one was injured.
Graham County Sheriff's Office reported 4 homes in Solomon area flooded between 1650 and 1710 LST when a wash came out of its banks.

Flash flooding in Nogales occurred late in the evening as Ephraim Wash flooded over Washington Ave, with 2 homes flooded and several families evacuated off of Western Ave around 2200 LST. Nogales Wash also overtopped its banks from Doe St. downstream to Chula Vista Lane. In addition, concrete slabs within the wash were damaged, leaving the International Outfall Interceptor (IOI) that carries 9-12 million gallons of raw sewage from Sonora, Mexico to Rio Rico, exposed. In Rio Rico, Sonoita Creek flooded Pendleton Drive.

Multiple road and bridge closures occurred in response to heavy rainfall across much of Cochise County. Increased flows on the San Pedro River eventually over-topped both the Highway 92 bridge in Palominas and the Hereford Bridge, causing both to be closed for a period of time. The Hereford Bridge sustained damage, and it did not re-open until nearly a month later on October 16, 2014. Further east, rainfall in the Old Bisbee area weakened a portion of a hillside. Falling soil and rock collapsed a retaining wall which fell onto a vehicle, while another residence sustained damage. The bridge at Cave Creek Road near Portal which leads to Cathedral Rock cabins was completely washed out. Water rushed around several buildings up to 2 feet deep in some locations but little damage occurred. One resident was evacuated from her home as a precaution. Additionally, many roads in rural Cochise County were closed for a time due to areal flooding.
Heavy rain caused flash flooding along Highway 70 near mile marker 377.  Flash flooding also occurred at mile marker 380 where Rainville Wash overtopped the roadway.

Heavy rain from the remnants of Odile previously saturated soils in Cochise County. Monsoon thunderstorms then brought another round of heavy rain to the Bisbee area, where a concrete retaining wall along a wash collapsed.

A 7-month old girl succumbed to her injuries after she was left in the back seat of a car. Her father realized she was unconscious only after he had been driving, and called 911 at 1720 LST. She was taken to Arizona Medical Center where she was pronounced dead a short time later. It is not clear how long the baby was in the car, but it may have been as long as 8 hours. The high temperature was 89 degrees with a relative humidity of 26%.
Spotter report of hail with some pieces as big as quarters along interstate 19 near Tubac.

Tucson Electric & Power reported that thunderstorm winds downed several power poles and lines in an area bounded by River Road, Swan Road, Fort Lowell Road and Alvernon Way. About 1100 customers lost power.

Extreme drought (D3) category persisted across far eastern Pinal and western Graham Counties through October. While there were small signs of improvement, even bountiful rainfall was insufficient to significantly ease drought conditions. Ranchers continued to be affected by the prior depletion of rangeland forage vegetation. Precipitation during the month ranged from 75 to 150 percent of normal, and soil moisture increased slightly, to nearly 80 percent of normal. Levels at San Carlos Reservoir rose slightly to about 7 percent of capacity by the end of October, the highest level since early May.

Extreme drought (D3) category persisted across far eastern Pinal and western Graham Counties through November. After a small improvement in conditions in October, very little rainfall occurred in the extreme drought area during November with totals ranging from 0 to 50 percent of normal. Soil moisture decreased slightly, to around 70 percent of normal. Levels at San Carlos Reservoir continued to slowly rise in November, to 8 percent of capacity by the end of the month, the highest level since April. This was mainly due to decreased irrigation usage after the growing season came to an end.

Heavy rainfall of over 1 inch in less than 45 minutes caused flooding of roadways and washes in the Tucson metro area. One car got stuck in the flood waters of Arcadia Wash south of Speedway on Tucson's east side, while Tanque Verde north of Catalina Highway had to be closed for a time due to flash flooding. Many city streets were covered with several inches of water.

Heavy rain in excess of 2 on the Tohono O'Odham Nation caused several road closures for an extended period of time. Highway 86 became impassable in several locations between mile markers 76 and 106. One motorist was rescued from flood waters near mile post 79 after attempting to cross them with their vehicle.  High flows on the Hickiwan Wash near its confluence with the San Simon Wash near Highway 86 were exacerbated by the compromise of several earthen berms designed to protect the highway. High flows along the San Simon Wash continued downstream from there to the confluence with the Vamori Wash near Santa Cruz, where Indian Route 21 was impassable, then south to the International Border. High flows occurred on the Santa Rosa Wash from Highway 86 downstream into Pinal County causing the closure of Indian Route 15 at North Komelik. Water levels finally receded during the evening hours of October 9th.

The Hopkins RAWS, located at 7100 feet in a saddle area in the Santa Rita Mountains, measured sustained east winds at 40 to 60 mph and gusts of 65 to 75 mph during the overnight hours of November 5th.  A peak gust of 88 mph was measured at 12:19 am MST on November 6th.
Five inches of snow occurred in Oracle at an elevation of about 4200 feet.

Heavy snow fell in the Santa Catalina Mountains New Year's Eve. By the time snow ended early on January 1st, 2015, just over a foot of snow accumulated on Mt. Lemmon above 8000 feet.
Snow began in the Santa Catalina Mountains on New Year's Eve and became heavy.  By the time snow ended early on January 1st, 2015, just over a foot of snow accumulated on Mt. Lemmon above 8000 feet.

Levels at San Carlos Reservoir also remained nearly steady, around 8 percent of capacity.

events.event_narrative: About 20 of snow fell in the higher elevations of the White Mountains including the Hannagan Meadow area.

Sustained south and southwest winds of 25 to 35 mph affected much of Tucson metro area during the afternoon hours of March 2nd. Higher gusts were associated with light rain showers and virga. Tree damage occurred at Speedway and Tucson Boulevard, and in Three Points area. Ryan Airfield reported a maximum wind gust of 43 mph between 1:45 MST and 3:45 pm MST, while Davis-Monthan AFB recorded a maximum gust of 46 mph. Two other locations, reported gusts to 47 mph, including Tucson International Airport at 1:20 pm MST.

Extreme drought (D3) category persisted across parts of far northeast Pinal and west central Graham Counties, including the Santa Teresa Mountains, through February. Less than a quarter inch of precipitation fell in the extreme drought area. Soil moistures dropped slightly, to between the 70th and 75th percentiles. However, upstream runoff from late January heavy precipitation caused levels at San Carlos Reservoir to climb to about 16 percent of capacity by the end of February, the highest levels since September 2010.

Soil moistures remained nearly the same, between the 70th and 75th percentiles. Levels at San Carlos Reservoir remained at around 16 percent of capacity throughout the month.

events.event_narrative: Extreme drought (D3) category persisted across parts of far northeast Pinal and west central Graham Counties, including the Santa Teresa Mountains, through March. |Between a tenth and three quarters of an inch of precipitation fell in the extreme drought area, but this was only 10 to 50 percent of normal for March. Soil moistures remained nearly the same, between the 70th and 75th percentiles. Levels at San Carlos Reservoir remained at around 16 percent of capacity throughout the month.

Extreme drought (D3) category persisted across parts of far northeast Pinal and west central Graham Counties, including the Santa Teresa Mountains, through March. |Between a tenth and three quarters of an inch of precipitation fell in the extreme drought area, but this was only 10 to 50 percent of normal for March. Soil moistures remained nearly the same, between the 70th and 75th percentiles. Levels at San Carlos Reservoir remained at around 16 percent of capacity throughout the month.

Several vineyards near Elgin may have lost between 40 to 60 percent of their harvest due to freezing temperatures, although the exact amount of loss won't be known until harvest. Temperatures dropped as low as 23 degrees in a few places, although most spots only dropped as low as 29 degrees for 4 hours or more. This freeze was especially damaging because of above average March temperatures, which caused an early budding of many crops.

Extreme drought (D3) category persisted for much of April across parts of far northeast Pinal and west central Graham Counties, including the Santa Teresa Mountains, but were reduced to the severe (D2) drought category by month's end. Soil moistures remained around the 70th percentile while levels at San Carlos Reservoir dropped slightly, to around 13 percent of capacity by the end of the month.  However, between one half inch and one inch of rain fell in the extreme drought area on the 25th and 26th, which meant that some areas received more than their monthly normal during those two days, thus prompting the easing in the drought category.

A strong dust devil caused structural damage to 2 homes in northwest Tucson. Part of a roof was torn off of a home and traveled about 100 feet. Some pieces of the roof were over 200 pounds. The entire roof will need to be replaced. Two people narrowly missed being hit by the flying debris, but no injuries occurred. The dust devil then impacted a second home, causing damage to some gutters and to an air conditioning vent. Public report was relayed via a NWS Flagstaff employee.

The U of A Coop Extension specialist for Santa Cruz County documented significant damage to apple, pistachio, and pecan trees in the Sulphur Springs Valley. This freeze was especially damaging because of above average March temperatures, which caused an early budding of many crops.

Sustained southwest winds of 15 to 25 mph affected much of Tucson metro area during the afternoon hours of May 18th. Higher gusts were associated with modest cloud buildups and virga. Two carports were damaged near Flowing Wells High School.  One landed on top of a nearby mobile home.

The human caused Kearny River Fire occurred in the dry Gila River bed near Kearny, AZ. The fire started just southeast of Kearny, prompting the evacuation of the Stephens Trailer Court and about 300 residents of Kearny. State Route 177 was briefly closed to traffic due to smoke. All but the residents of the trailer court were allowed back in their homes within 48 hours. The riverbed was overgrown with salt cedar, which burned intensely and allowed for wildfire growth northwest, or downstream, to a significant bend in the river near the community of Riverside. Three homes, two outbuildings and one vehicle were damaged or destroyed in the Stephens Trailer Court near the point of the fire's origin.  One of the outbuildings contained numerous tools and equipment used to maintain the mobile homes. In total, the wildfire consumed 1428 acres.

A Recreational Vehicle that started on fire along Highway 83 about 10 miles north of Sonoita, ignited nearby brush and was quickly spread over complex terrain by gusty winds. The highway was closed in both directions between Sahuarita Road and Sonoita for about 24 hours.  The wildfire consumed 2,023 acres before firefighters gained control.

High temperatures ranging from 108 to 115 degrees were common August 14-16 across the lower deserts of southeast Arizona, essentially at elevations below 3000 feet in Pima and south central Pinal County. The hottest of the three days was the 15th when record high temperatures were set at Tucson, Ajo, Organ Pipe National Monument and Picacho Peak State Park. The high temperature at Tucson International Airport of 110 degrees, broke a record set in 1915. The new record high temperature established at Organ Pipe National Monument on August 15th was 112 degrees.  There were at least a dozen people who were treated for heat-related illnesses throughout the three day period in Tucson.  The hot temperatures caused high demand for power and electrical equipment outages, which resulted in up to 1700 customers to lose power in Tucson.
Thunderstorm winds downed 5 power poles down on the 3500 block of east US-70. A wind gust of 61 mph occurred at the Safford Airport.
Thunderstorm winds uprooted a tree and caused minor damage to a mobile home on Tucson's east side. A wind gust to 60 mph was measured at the Tucson International Airport.
Thunderstorm winds uprooted trees in Lions Park and Apache Park in Benson and ripped a roof off a patio from one residence on Dragoon Street.
Quarter to golf ball size hail fell in the Sahuarita area causing damage to vehicles and motor homes.
Hail up to the size of golf balls damaged several ultralight aircraft an airport near Picture Rocks.
Thunderstorms winds uprooted several trees in the Rita Ranch.

Large hail up to golf ball size occurred in a swath across Tucson from the Catalina Foothills through midtown's Amphi area southwestward to the Tucson Estates area.  Hundreds of vehicles sustained hail damage ranging from dented hoods to broken windshields and many homes suffered damage to skylights and roofs.
Thunderstorm winds downed a tree near Fry Blvd. and El Camino Real.

Thunderstorm winds downed several trees in Tucson, including one at Catalina High School and another at Lantana Apartments.  One tree near Oracle and Grant fell on top of a car while another tree elsewhere in the city fell onto and damaged a porch and awning.
Wind gust to 67 mph was measured at Casino Del Sol.

Thunderstorm winds knocked one unoccupied mobile home off its foundation, tore the roof off another and blew windows out of several others in the Sullivan Park neighborhood of East Sahuarita. Several trees were also uprooted.
Lightning struck a house and ignited a small fire on the second story of a Sahuarita home.  The lightning also caused a water pipe to burst which subsequently led to ceiling damage.
Lightning struck and killed a man who was walking along a dirt road.

Power poles, power lines, and multiple tree limbs 3-4 in diameter down between Country Club and Tucson Blvd between Broadway and Speedway with over 200 customers without power. One tree was down near the intersection of Campbell and Broadway.
A dust devil was stretched into a small landspout tornado by a passing thunderstorm near Safford. No damage was reported.
Duncan Valley Electric reported a power pole down in Franklin.
A heavy wooden tree house was damaged by thunderstorm winds near Avra Valley Rd.

Thunderstorm winds caused damage along Sanders Road. A large dead tree fell on a mobile home which sustained some damage. Multiple power poles blown down with almost 100 customers without power for a time. An abandoned large commercial building also sustained damage. Trees in the median of Interstate 10 in Marana were blown down which partially blocked lanes and caused traffic backups.

Thunderstorm winds downed four towers of a center pivot which was full of water at the time to tip over. The storm then blew the wood and metal roof off a commercial produce building for an apple orchard, with multiple pieces found up to three fields away. Four power poles, several trees and a tent were also blown over.
Thunderstorm winds blew over and severely damaged a metal hay barn at a horse rescue which was full of bales. Some of the hay bales suffered water damage.
Heavy rain in Nogales, Sonora caused strong flows in Nogales Wash. The Doe Street Bridge in Nogales was closed for a time as the Nogales Wash over topped its banks.

Thunderstorm winds downed a power pole was also knocked down near the airport, which resulted in electrical wires on top of vehicles. A few shallow-rooted trees were also downed near Drexel and Country Club.

A swift water rescue of two adults occurred after their vehicle was swept away in Rodeo Wash. The vehicle eventually stopped when it became pinned under the Rodeo Wash Bridge near Interstate 19. Both occupants escaped the vehicle and were able to crawl partially up the side of the wash where they were rescued. They were not injured.

A woman and her dog became trapped in their truck when she attempted to drive through a flooded wash crossing Cascabel Road. The woman did not realize that water had washed the road away. When she attempted to cross the wash, the vehicle dropped 3 feet into the water before it was pushed downstream about 200 yards. Cascabel fire personnel and civilians were able to rescue both the woman and her dog. The woman was transported to a nearby hospital and treated for severe hypothermia.

Heavy rain of 2 inches in an hour caused flash flooding in San Manuel, which caused severe road damage. Public works estimated hundreds of thousands of dollars in damage to Avenues A, B, G, and Webb Drive.
Heavy rain caused the San Luis Wash to flow across Route 232 near the village of San Luis to a depth of 1 to 2 feet.

KALK reported wind gusts of 61 mph and 67 mph at 1213 LST and 1216 LST, respectively.
Thunderstorm winds knocked down a tree and broke a tree limb 6 inches in diameter along Irvington in southern Tucson.

Road closures occurred due to flash flooding in the northwest Tucson metro, including Overton Rd at the Canada del Oro Wash, Thornydale Rd at Freer Drive and Oasis Drive, and Linda Vista between Thornydale Rd and Camino de Oeste.
Water flowing across Linda Vista Blvd west of Hartman Lane caused at least 1 vehicle to become disabled.
Thunderstorms produced heavy rain on top of ground saturated from storms earlier in the day. Runoff caused 3 vehicles to become stranded due to high water near Sunrise and Pontatoc Roads.
Thunderstorm wind damage occurred at the Greenlee County Fairgrounds. One power pole was knocked over and the horse stalls building sustaining significant roof damage.
Thunderstorm winds downed nine power poles near Manville and Reservation Roads.
A power pole was knocked down near the intersection of Camino de Oeste and Lambert Lane.

Thunderstorm winds damaged a gas station awning near Houghton and Valencia. Several large trees were damaged with at least 4 power poles snapped along the west side of Houghton between Valencia and E Rita Road, closing the road for several hours and leaving nearly 3500 customers without electricity.
Thunderstorm winds downed multiple trees along Sunrise Road between Swan and Via Palomita. Several trees were also blown over at the Quail Ridge Apartment complex, and part of a carport was damaged.
Thunderstorm winds uprooted and knocked over a 40 foot tree that fell onto a home near Oracle Rd and 1st Ave in Oro Valley. Several other trees were blown over in Oro Valley.
Thunderstorm winds snapped branches 4-5 inches in diameter near Campbell and Roger Roads.
Nearly two inches of heavy rain fell in a short time period and caused significant flooding of streets and small washes in northwest sections of Sierra Vista.
Thunderstorm winds downed power poles and lines down near W. El Camino del Cerro and N. Tortolita Rd. Approximately 1400 customers lost power.

Thunderstorm winds downed power poles and lines down along Whittier St. between Alvernon Way and Columbus Blvd. About 100 customers lost power. A shallow-rooted tree was uprooted near Swan Rd. and Timrod St.

Thunderstorm winds uprooted and knocked down a large palo verde tree near the entrance of Orange Grove Estates on Orange Grove Rd. just east of Thornydale Rd. Additional damage occurred in the complex as the gates around an outdoor recreational area were blown away.
A lightning strike shattered a 30-ft tree in the Orange Grove Estates complex.
A 45-year old tree was struck by lightning. It landed in a woman's backyard when it fell, and no other damage occurred.
A faint and likely weak landspout tornado spun up from  a dust devil before attaching to the cloud base near Interstate 10 and Houghton.
A lightning strike ignited a fire at a residence on N Oracle Rd. in Catalina.
A man was struck and injured by lightning near Three Points.

Thunderstorms over Nogales produced 1 to 2 inches of rain, which resulted in heavy flows in Nogales wash. The Doe Street Bridge was closed for a time after flood waters breached the wash banks and over-topped the roadway.
Thunderstorm winds downed 20 power poles down along Marana Trico Road and Luckett Road. A chicken coop in Marana sustained some damage as well.
A palm tree was struck by lightning near the 3500 block of S. Austin Place. This resulted in multiple windows blown out of a nearby duplex.
Local police report a tree was struck by lightning near Benson.

Downed power lines in Marana resulted in multiple road closures, and up to 1000 customers without power. At least 20 power poles were knocked over by wind on Twin Peaks Road alone, which trapped 6 vehicles and 11 people in their cars for a period of time. In addition, a 51 kt wind gust was measured at Marana Airport.
A pepper tree was uprooted by thunderstorm winds in Green Valley.
Thunderstorm winds downed tree limbs near Golf Links and Swan and near 6th Ave and 26th St.  Another tree limb 1-1.5 ft in diameter snapped and fell onto a car near 4th Ave and 7th St.
One inch hail occurred in St. David with minor car damage.
SR-80 was closed at Apache Powder Road due to flash flooding. A few pieces of asphalt broke off into the flow as water over-topped the roadway.
Street flooding of 1-2 feet deep occurred near Park Ave and Pennsylvania St. Some minor flooding of businesses occurred near 12th Ave. and Lincoln St.
Snyder Rd. between Kolb and Sabino Canyon Road was closed for a time due to the flash flooding of Ventana Canyon Wash.

Persistent showers and thunderstorms caused to up to 2 inches of rain in the Redington Pass area, including the Tanque Verde and Agua Caliente Washes. Redington Pass Road became flooded and impassible.
A mesonet station measured a wind gust to 61 mph at Saguaro National Park East and a tree was blown down near 22nd and Harrison.
Thunderstorm outflow winds blew a tree down near Wrightstown and Camino Seco and downed tree branches and damaged a chimney top near Wrightstown and Pantano.
A brick wall and several fences were blown down by thunderstorm winds.
Thunderstorm winds uprooted a tree in the Gladden Farms complex in Marana.
Multiple trees down in Oro Valley Marketplace Shopping Center, and in Catalina near Wilds Road.

A mesonet station recorded a wind gust to 62 mph in Safford. Thunderstorm winds blew down several power poles and power lines resulting in closures along Highways 191 and 70 between Solomon and Safford. One car suffered damage when power lines fell on it, temporarily trapping the driver. Additionally, damage to a local farmer's cotton crop was reported.

A woman in her vehicle was swept into flash flood waters when attempting to cross a wash on High Knoll Rd east of Sierra Vista. Rescuers found the car had been swept downstream, but were unable to locate the driver.
A brief tornado touched down north of St. David.
Off duty NWS meteorologist estimated a wind gust of 60 mph at this residence.

One to four inches of rain fell near and especially southwest of Safford causing canals and washes to overtop their banks and flow over roadways. Water was a foot deep on parts of Highway 191 south of Safford. A vehicle on Lebanon Rd. had to be towed out of mud and rushing water.
Heavy rain caused Florida Canyon to overflow its banks near the Santa Rita Mountains.
Thunderstorm winds broke a 10 inch diameter tree limb near Orange Grove and Oracle Roads.
Thunderstorm winds downed a large dead tree branch, which fell on top of a residence near Speedway Blvd and Swan Rd, causing roof damage.
Heavy rain caused extreme flows in Davidson Wash, which was flowing 300 ft across.  The wash flowed across Empire View Road, stranding residents on either side of it.
Thunderstorm winds uprooted trees and snapped branches in the Rancho Del Lago neighborhood in Vail.
Heavy rain caused the driver of a small pickup truck to skid off Interstate 19.  The vehicle sustained moderate damage but the driver was not injured.
A power pole was snapped off at the base. In another area, power lines were snapped and were dangling from their poles.
Thunderstorm winds blew down trees on Tucson's east side near the intersections of Ft. Lowell and Swan Roads and Kenyon and Sarnoff Drives. Some of the downed trees damaged power lines.
A cold air funnel was viewed from the NWS office on the southwest side of Tucson. It was also photographed by a local TV meteorologist.
Lightning struck a house in the 12000 block of North Lost Shadow Court, damaging the roof. The fire which was ignited caused minor smoke damage, mainly in the attic. No one was home at the time.

Poor visibility and slick roads due to heavy rainfall during a severe thunderstorm caused a multiple-vehicle rollover accident at the intersection of Oracle Rd. and Orange Grove Rd. The 3 occupants of the vehicle were airlifted to a nearby hospital with minor injuries. In the same area, the rain leaking through the roof at a Bed, Bath and Beyond caused water damage and sparking in the electrical room. The store was evacuated and remained closed into the overnight hours for repairs. There were no injuries.
Firefighters responded to a woman who was stuck in a pickup truck which was submerged in water near Bear Canyon Rd and Bear Paw Pl. She was uninjured.
A cyclist who tried to cross Alamo Wash which was flowing over a low water crossing on El Calle Betelgeux was rescued by first responders. He was not injured.
Multiple reports and pictures were received of 1 inch diameter hail occurring near Thornydale Road from the intersection its intersection with Cortaro Farms Road north to  Overton Road.

Heavy rain near Marana High School fell on already saturated ground and caused a quick rise in small washes crossing Twin Peaks Road just west of Sandario Road. Three vehicles became stuck in a foot of water and mud that was crossing the road.
Twitter photo of a cold air funnel near Avra Valley was received.

events.cz_name: WHITE MOUNTAINS OF GRAHAM AND GREENLEE COUNTIES
events.event_narrative: Reports of 12 to 14 inches of snow were common across Northern Greenlee County including the Hannagan Meadow area.
Eighteen inches of snow occurred on Mt. Graham in the Pinaleno mountains of Graham County.
Heavy snow of 12 to 18 inches occurred on Mount Lemmon including around the village of Summerhaven.

Strong wind gusts occurred especially in the Sierra Vista area with a measured gust to 65 MPH near Hereford. There were also numerous gusts of 58 MPH or higher including the Canelo area and Pioneer airfield. These strong wind gusts resulted in seven downed power poles near Sierra Vista along Highway 92 and closed the highway for several hours. One house had a portion of its roof torn off by the wind.
The automated surface observation at Douglas-Bisbee airport recorded a wind gust to 58 MPH.

An ultrasonic anemometer on Mt. Lemmon recorded a wind gust to 105 MPH before the instrumentation iced up. This resulted in many trees downed on Mt. Lemmon. In addition, a total snowfall of 5 inches occurred which resulted in brief blizzard-like conditions. This event continued into February 1.

An ultrasonic anemometer on Mt. Lemmon recorded a wind gust to 105 MPH before the instrumentation iced up. In addition, snowfall of 5 inches occurred which resulted in brief blizzard-like conditions. This event began on January 31.

events.event_narrative: The Guthrie RAWS recorded a wind gust to 75 MPH.

events.cz_name: WHITE MOUNTAINS OF GRAHAM AND GREENLEE COUNTIES
events.event_narrative: The higher elevations of Northern Graham and Greenlee County received 6 to 12 inches of snow combined with wind gusts in excess of 50 MPH. This event continued into February 1.
