events.cz_name: UPPER SANTA CRUZ RIVER AND ALTAR VALLEYS
events.event_narrative: Heavy snow fell during the early morning hours of January 2nd in Santa Cruz and far southeast sections of Pima County.  Snow reports were generally in the 2 to 5 inch range in Vail, Corona De Tucson, Rio Rico, Nogales and Patagonia.  However an isolated report of 6 inches was received from Nogales and Kino Springs reported 7 inches. State Route 82 was closed between the Nogales Airport and Patagonia after several vehicles became stuck in the snow, including a jackknifed semi truck.

Heavy snow fell during the early morning hours of January 2nd in Santa Cruz and far southeast sections of Pima County.  Snow reports were generally in the 2 to 5 inch range in Vail, Corona De Tucson, Rio Rico, Nogales and Patagonia.  However an isolated report of 6 inches was received from Nogales and Kino Springs reported 7 inches. State Route 82 was closed between the Nogales Airport and Patagonia after several vehicles became stuck in the snow, including a jackknifed semi truck.
Snowfall began early in the morning January 2nd. Sierra Vista recorded 3 inches, Benson recorded 3-4 inches, and Huachuca City recorded 3 inches. Several minor accidents were reported.

Snowfall began the afternoon of January 1. 3 inches of snow was common across the area with Willcox reporting 4 inches, Portal 7 inches, Douglas 3 inches, and Paradise 3 inches. There were also reports of accidents on I-10 involving cars or semi's sliding off the road as well as minor crashes.

events.cz_name: UPPER GILA RIVER AND ARAVAIPA VALLEYS
events.event_narrative: Snowfall began the afternoon of January 1st and continued into the afternoon of January 2nd. Safford reported 3 inches and Klondike reported 5.5 inches of snow. The snow caused several accidents on Highway 70 between Bylas and San Carlos and was eventually closed.
Accumulating snow began early in the morning of January 1. By the morning of January 2 estimated snowfall totals in the Chiricahua Mountains above 7000 feet were one foot or greater.
Accumulating snow began on the afternoon of December 31. By the morning of January 1 estimated snowfall totals in the Catalina and Rincon Mountains above 7000 feet were one foot or greater.
Accumulating snow began in the afternoon of January 1 and continued into the afternoon of January 2. By the morning of January 2 the Canelo area had received 4 inches of snow.

events.cz_name: WHITE MOUNTAINS OF GRAHAM AND GREENLEE COUNTIES
events.event_narrative: Snow began falling on the morning of February 21st and continued into the 22nd. SNOTEL observations reported 25 at Hannagan Meadow and 21 at Beaver Head.
Snowfall began the morning of February 21st and continued into the 22nd. By the evening of February 21 estimated snowfall totals in the Pinaleno Mountains above 5000 feet were one foot or greater.

Snowfall began the morning of the February 21st and continued into the 22nd. By the morning of February 22 estimated snowfall totals in the Santa Rita, Huachuca, Mule, and Dragoon Mountains above 5000 feet were one foot or greater.

Snowfall began the morning of the February 21st and continued into the 22nd. By the evening of February 21 over a foot of snow had fallen in the Santa Catalina Mountains. Summerhaven reported a storm total of 30.5 inches and Willow Canyon reported 27 inches.

Snowfall began the morning of the February 21st and continued into the 22nd. By the evening of February 21 estimated snowfall totals in the Baboquivari Mountains above 5000 feet were one foot or greater.

Snowfall began late in the evening of the February 21st and continued into the 22nd. The Oracle area recorded 11-13 inches of snow by the evening of February 22 with multiple road closures and minor accidents also reported.

Snowfall began in the early evening of February 21st and continued into the 22nd. By the afternoon of February 22 estimated snowfall totals in the Chiricahua Mountains above 5000 feet were one foot or greater.

events.cz_name: UPPER GILA RIVER AND ARAVAIPA VALLEYS
events.event_narrative: Snowfall began late in the evening of February 21st and continued into the 22nd. By the morning of February 22 estimated snowfall totals across the southwest portion of the zone were greater than 3 inches.

Snowfall began late in the evening February 21st and continued into the 22nd. Sonoita received 10, Elgin 9, Sierra Vista 3-4, and Huachuca City 4. There were reports of multiple road closures in Sierra Vista and a crash on I-10 about 7 miles east of Benson which the east-bound closed lanes of I-10 for a couple of hours.
Snowfall began late in the evening February 21st and continued into the 22nd. Dragoon reported 3.5 and Douglas reported 3.

Snowfall began the morning of the February 22nd and continued into the early evening. Green Valley, Vail, and Corona de Tucson reported 3-7 of snow. There was an accident on I-10 eastbound near Vail. There were also multiple accidents along I-19 including a rollover near Duval Mine Road. Snow fell in the city of Tucson for several hours, with visibility reduced to less than a mile at times. While several inches of snow accumulated on non-paved surfaces, city streets remained wet or saw light slush accumulations.

Heavy rain fell on the mountains near Tucson beginning the morning of February 14th and continuing into the early morning hours of February 15th. The Santa Catalina Mountains recorded 3-7 of rain. This caused flooding downstream along Sabino Creek, Tanque Verde Creek, and the Rillito River. Flooding also occurred along Rincon Creek from runoff down the Rincon Mountains.  Multiple roads needed to be closed due to flooding and multiple swift water rescues were performed. Mount Lemmon Highway was also closed due to several rock slides.

Snow melted as it fell on December 29th, but refroze after dark as one to two inches of new snow accumulated after dark. A single vehicle rollover accident occurred on icy roadways shortly after snow had ended on State Route 92 near Hereford. The pickup truck's only occupant was not wearing a seat belt, was ejected from the vehicle, and died at the scene.

events.cz_name: UPPER SANTA CRUZ RIVER AND ALTAR VALLEYS
events.event_narrative: Six to seven inches of snow fell in Patagonia, causing downed tree branches and power lines, and a loss of power for several hours. Snow reports in the Rio Rico area ranged from 2 to 5 inches.

events.cz_name: WHITE MOUNTAINS OF GRAHAM AND GREENLEE COUNTIES
events.event_narrative: Snow began falling early in the afternoon of March 11th and continued into the 13th. SNOTEL observations reported 12 to 18 of snow at Hannagan Meadow.

Snow began the evening of the March 11th and continued into the evening of the 12th. By the afternoon of March 12 a foot of snow had fallen in the Santa Catalina Mountains. Mount Lemmon Highway was closed to everyone but residents for a time due to heavy snow.
Thunderstorm outflow winds lifted a carport and a portion of the roof that was attached to the house, causing significant damage.

events.cz_name: UPPER GILA RIVER AND ARAVAIPA VALLEYS
events.event_narrative: Freezing temperatures between 29 and 32 degrees occurred in parts of the Sulphur Springs Valley. The average duration was around 1 hour, with up to 3 hours in isolated locations. Minor crop damage was observed to corn, cotton and peppers.

Freezing temperatures between 29 and 32 degrees occurred in parts of the Sulphur Springs Valley. The average duration was around 1 hour, with up to 3 hours in isolated locations. Minor crop damage was observed to corn, cotton and peppers.
Thunderstorm outflow winds damaged several trees in Bisbee.  Two shallow-rooted tree were blown down completely. Winds also peeled back roofing material on the patio of one house.

Multiple swift water rescues were performed on the west side of Tucson. Locations included Airport Wash near 6th and Bilby, near 36th St. and Mission Rd, I-10 and Prince, San Juan Wash at La Cholla and King Ave.

Small tree limbs and power lines were downed in the vicinity of Grant and Stone. The limbs and lines also knocked down some fencing. Wind-driven small hail damaged a house's skylights and shade structure near Speedway and Greasewood.

Runoff from heavy rain in Sonora caused flash flooding in the Nogales Port of Entry. Water was flowing 8-10 inches deep through the checkpoint area. Flash flooding was also reported at Potrero Creek near near Meadow Hills Drive.
Multiple trees down near intersection of Western Ave and N Bautista St. The window in a house was also blown out just north of the intersection.
Seven power poles were knocked down in the Kansas Settlement area.
Several homes suffered roof damage in Upper Covered Wells, Covered Wells, Lower Covered Wells, and Mountain Village.
Multiple homes suffered roof damage in Pisinemo, and the window was broken in 1 home. Two outbuildings were also damaged.
One home in Hickiwan suffered roof damage.
Thunderstorm winds downed four power poles near Larson and Moson Rds in Sierra Vista.
Thunderstorm winds downed six power poles in two different locations on Old Sonoita Highway.
Sasabe RAWS measured a gust to 67 mph.
Davis-Monthan ASOS reported 66 mph gust. Thunderstorm outflow winds also toppled a mesquite tree near Wilmont Rd and Stella Rd.
Gust of 65 mph was recorded at Black Hills RAWS. Twenty minutes later a 71 mph gust was recorded at Horse Camp RAWS.
Thunderstorm winds downed a power pole near Nebraska St. and 12th Ave.
Heavy rain caused a partial ceiling collapse along with water damage near Dakota St. and 12th Ave.

Thunderstorm winds broke a window in Fresnal, downed tree branch that fell onto Highway 86 between mile posts 136 and 137, then caused roof damage to one house in Sells and three houses in Big Fields.
Near Picture Rocks Rd and Sandario Rd a tree was snapped at its base, a portion of a wooden fence was blown down, and an evaporation cooler was blown off a roof.
Thunderstorm winds knocked down several power poles south of Safford along Lebanon Rd and in Thatcher along Hoopes Ave in Daley Estates.
Lightning ignited a palm tree near Fort Lowell and Alvernon. The burning fronds spread to a vehicle and apartment building causing additional damage.

A garage door was partially blown in and small tree downed near Bajada Dr and Tortolita Rd. Dozens of trees were uprooted or damaged in Dove Mountain. Two power poles were down at Wentz and Grier. Ten power poles and several trees were down along Tangerine between I-10 and Moore Rd. There was a semi-truck rollover on I-10 just south of Marana Rd. exit. A weather station near I-10 and Tangerine measured a wind gust of 60 mph.
Blowing dust caused visibility to fall to �� mile near Avra Valley.
A wind gust of 60 mph was recorded near Arivaca.
Wind gust of 59 mph measured at Black Hills RAWS. Same line of storms took down trees in Fort Thomas, Pima, and Thatcher. A camp trailer was blown off its jack in Pima.
A large tree was downed in San Jose.
A foot of water was flowing across Sanchez Rd forcing it to be closed.
Heavy rain and flash flooding caused a rock slide that closed SR 366 at MP 131.
Lightning started a fire in several palm trees near Prince and Cherry.
A large mesquite tree was downed near Ali Chugk. Power was out to the village for several hours.
Flash flooding made Rt 1 between Gu Vo and Ali Chuk impassable at mile post two and mile post 7.

About 2.5 inches of rain caused flash flooding on the east side of Tucson. The intersection of 22nd and Kolb as well as the intersection of Irvington and Pantano had over a foot water running through them. Numerous vehicles were stranded in the flood waters and several water rescues were performed in the area. An 11-year old child was rescued after falling into a swift flowing Alamo Wash near Bellevue St.
About 2.5 inches of rainfall in less than two hours caused the roof of a historic building to collapse in Ajo. Residents of the building, which used to be the Curley School, were displaced.
A Southwest Airlines pilot reported a funnel cloud in a PIREP in a storm to the south of the flight path over the Tohono O'odham Nation.
A child was injured while swimming in Cluff Lake after lightning struck the water.
Heavy rainfall of 2.5 inches caused flash flooding in Ajo with water over 1 foot deep flowing across many streets.
Lightning struck an orthodontist office in Tucson near Pima and Alvernon causing damage to some computer equipment in the office.

Thunderstorm outflow winds well removed from the dissipated thunderstorms created a wall of dust that reduced visibility to less than a quarter mile in south central Pinal County, west of the Interstate 10 corridor.

Very hot temperatures occurred on July 15th and 16th with respective high temperatures of 110 and 111 degrees at Organ Pipe National Monument, 109 and 108 at Sells, 108 and 110 (tied record) at Tucson International Airport, and 109 both days at the Safford Airport.

Very hot temperatures occurred on July 15th and 16th with respective high temperatures of 110 and 111 degrees at Organ Pipe National Monument, 109 and 108 at Sells, 108 and 110 (tied record) at Tucson International Airport, and 109 both days at the Safford Airport.

events.cz_name: UPPER GILA RIVER AND ARAVAIPA VALLEYS
events.event_narrative: Very hot temperatures occurred on July 15th and 16th with respective high temperatures of 110 and 111 degrees at Organ Pipe National Monument, 109 and 108 at Sells, 108 and 110 (tied record) at Tucson International Airport, and 109 both days at the Safford Airport.
Power poles were downed near mile marker 85 on state route 86.
A mesonet station in Bisbee measured wind gusts to 58 MPH.
KALK ASOS station measured a wind gust of 62 mph.
Numerous trees uprooted in Douglas. One shed was moved off its foundation, a cooler was blown off of a roof, and a stop sign was uprooted.

Between 2 and 3 inches of rain in one hour caused flash flooding in Rucker Canyon. This forced closure of Rucker Canyon road and washed a trailer and a tent with two people in it downstream. Five people were rescued in all. In Elfrida, Mormon road was closed between Jefferson and Whitewater School Roads.
Between 1 and 2 inches of rain in around one hour between Mammoth and San Manuel caused flash flooding at Copper Creek Road along the San Pedro River.

One inch of rain in less than an hour caused flash flooding of several roads in the Safford area. One vehicle was swept away near First Avenue in Thatcher.  The wash intersecting Lebanon Road and 191 also overflowed.
Thunderstorm winds downed a shallow rooted tree in Green Valley on West Moorwood Street. The tree fell against the house causing minor damage.
Two to three inches of rain in a 2 hour period caused flash flooding in the Washington Camp area in the Patagonia Mountains.
Around three inches of rain fell in a 2 hour period causing Blanco Wash to flood over Tucker Road, making it impassable.
Around an inch of rain in the northern Mule Mountains in less than an hour caused Davis Road to become closed due to flooding flooding near mile post 13.
ASOS station KDUG recorded thunderstorm wind gust of 64 mph.
KFHU and KALK ASOS weather stations measured thunderstorm wind gusts of 66 mph.
Around 2 inches of rain in 1 to 2 hours flooded many yards and several homes in the St. David area.  Some vehicles became stuck in floodwaters.
Landspout tornado formed north of Three Points and persisted for 3 minutes.
Trees were downed and uprooted at Ajo and Alvernon as well as near Pantano Rd and Seneca St. About 7000 customers lost power in Tucson. KDMA ASOS also recorded a 76 mph wind gust.
Five power poles were downed north of Via Vo Farms.
Horse Camp RAWS recorded wind gust of 61 mph.
Several large trees snapped at the base in Saint David. Two windows were blown out and minor roof damage occurred to one structure. A 73-foot tall antenna was snapped in 3 places.
One inch diameter hail was reported in southern Green Valley.
A funnel cloud was reported near the intersection of Magee Rd and Oracle Rd.
Penny sized hail was reported south of Vail.
Nickel sized hail was reported in Whetstone.
A pocket of 1 to 2 inches of rain fell in less than an hour in Ironwood Forest National Monument.  This caused 2 to 3 feet of water to flow across West Silverbell Road.

Well above normal and very hot temperatures occurred on August 5th with high temperatures of 110 degrees at Ajo, Picacho, and Organ Pipe National Monument, 108 at Sells, and 109 at Tucson International Airport (record high).  The Pima County Medical Examiner confirmed that heat was the primary cause of death for one adult male and one unidentified male between Pisinemo and Sells on the Tohono O'odham Nation.

Very hot temperatures occurred on August 14th through the 16th with respective high temperatures of 110, 113 (record) and 115 (record) degrees at Ajo, 109, 109 and 108 at Picacho, 110, 111, and 106 at Sells and 114 degrees on all three days (all were records) at Organ Pipe National Monument.

Very hot temperatures occurred on August 20th and 21st, with respective high temperatures of 111 and 113 degrees at Ajo, 109 and 111 degrees (both records) at Picacho, 111 degrees on both days at Sells, 113 degrees on both days (both were records) at Organ Pipe National Monument, 109 and 110 degrees (both records) at Tucson International Airport, 105 and 107 degrees (both records) at Sasabe, 104 and 103 degrees (both records) at Nogales International Airport, 107 degrees on both days (both were records) at Safford airport, and 109 and 108 degrees in the Gila River Valley on the San Carlos Apache Tribe reservation.  The Pima County Medical Examiner confirmed that heat was the primary cause of death for one adult male north of Arivaca on the 21st.

Above normal temperatures were recorded in western Pima County on April 25th. Organ Pipe National Monument reached 97 degrees. The Pima County Medical Examiner confirmed that heat was the primary cause of death for one adult male.
Two power poles were downed in Ali Chugk.
Lickskillet Lane and Michelob Rd were flooded in Avra Valley. There was a report of 3.87 inches of rainfall in the area.
Power pole was downed on Puerto Blanco Dr just west of Highway 85.
The Horse Camp RAWS measured a wind gust of 65 mph.

Well above normal temperatures occurred on the Tohono O'odham Nation on May 5th and 6th.  Sells recorded a high temperature of 102 degrees on both days. The Pima County Medical Examiner confirmed that heat was the primary cause of death for one adult female east of Sells.

Well above normal temperatures occurred in the San Pedro River Valley of Cochise County May 16th through May 18th.  The hottest day was May 17th when a high temperature of 96 degrees was recorded at Tombstone and 97 degrees at Saint David.  The Pima County Medical Examiner confirmed that heat was the primary cause of death for one adult male near the San Pedro River north of State Route 90.  The exact date that the fatality occurred is not certain, but likely occurred within this three-day time period.
Thunderstorm winds progressed northwest across western Pima County to the south and west of Ajo.  A station 16 miles west of Ajo measured a wind gust to 60 mph.

At least 3 cars were stranded in flood waters 1 to 2 feet deep and six homes had at least minor flooding in Douglas from 2 to 4 inches of rain which fell on the east side of the city.  A retaining wall was washed out near 8th St. and Washington St.  Much of the runoff drained into a baseball field, filling it with water 3 to 4 feet deep.

Thunderstorm winds caused damage in Eloy. The sheet metal roof and a wall of a tire shop was blown off near Sunshine Blvd and Frontier St. and a nearby power pole was damaged. A tree was blown onto power lines near 5th and D streets and an empty semi trailer was blown on its side near Santa Cruz Ave. and 1st St.
Landspout tornado developed in remote terrain to the south of Chuichu ahead of developing thunderstorms.
Flash flooding occurred in the Chuichu area.
Flash flooding caused the road to become impassable at Dead Man's Corner in Picture Rocks.
Wall of dust moved through south central Pinal County and reduced visibility to less than a quarter mile in the Eloy area.
Thunderstorm winds generated a wall of dust, or haboob, which moved through Eloy and continued south towards Marana reducing visibility to near zero.

Dozens of trees were downed, there was damage to several residences roofs and  fences.  At least two vehicles were damaged from falling trees and limbs, and at least one road sign was bent over from the strong winds.

Straight-line wind damage occurred in and around Willcox. Damage to multiple structures along with multiple downed power poles. Many trees were downed as well. A fifth wheel trailer was tipped over with two occupants inside.  Both suffered non-life-threatening injuries.
Hail up to 1.5 inches was reported in the Willcox area.

A tornado touched down near Cox and Hamilton Rd, and moved northeast for approximately 1.7 miles causing extensive damage. One mobile home was lifted and moved off its foundation. Five people inside, including three children sustained minor injuries. The roof of another mobile home was ripped off and power poles were snapped. Two other homes were damaged along with a large machine shed-type storage building and several trees were snapped in half or uprooted. The damage survey concluded that peak wind speeds from the tornado were between 90 and 100 mph.

Heavy rain of 2 to 3 inches in less than 6 hours caused Wetstones Rd, Calle Rinconado, and Wentworth Road in Vail to become flooded and impassable. There was also flooding in Corona de Tucson and debris from flooding on Sahuarita Rd. A motorist was rescued from floodwaters near Old Vail Road and Wilmot Road.
A swift water rescue was performed at Harrison Rd and Pantano wash after a teenager became stranded trying to walk across flood waters.
Heavy rain of around 2 inches in less than 6 hours caused several roads to become flooded in Saint David, Huachuca City and Sierra Vista.
Thunderstorm winds damaged power poles in Bylas.

Well above normal temperatures occurred on the Tohono O'odham Nation on June 3rd and 4th. Sells recorded a high temperature of 107 degrees on the 3rd and 104 on the 4th.  The Pima County Medical Examiner confirmed that heat was the primary cause of death for one adult male east of Sells. The exact time of death was not determinable, but very likely occurred on June 3rd.

Well above normal temperatures occurred in southeast Arizona on June 13th.  Several new record high temperatures were established including 110 degrees at Picacho, 109 at Safford Airport, 107 at Duncan and 105 at Sasabe. Other high temperatures included 107 at Sells. The Pima County Medical Examiner confirmed that heat was the primary cause of death for two adult males, one west of Ajo, and another in northwest Santa Cruz County.

The Pima County Medical Examiner confirmed that heat was the primary cause of death for two adult males, one west of Ajo, and another in northwest Santa Cruz County.

The Pima County Medical Examiner confirmed that heat was the primary cause of death for two adults, one west of Ruby in Santa Cruz County on the 22nd and another on the Tohono O'odham Nation in southwest Pinal County on the 23rd.

Well above normal temperatures occurred in Cochise County on June 26th. A temperature of 107 degrees occurred at Cascabel with 100 at Benson and Willcox. The Pima County Medical Examiner confirmed that heat was the primary cause of death for one adult male west of Dragoon.

High temperatures from July 5th through July 7th were between 105 and 113 from Tucson westward across Pima County and in southwest Pinal County, which were significantly above normal. Respective high temperatures include: Tucson International Airport 111 (record), 105 and 107 degrees; Organ Pipe Cactus  National Monument 113, 113 (record) and 109 degrees; Sells 113 (record), 107 and 106 degrees; and Picacho 111, 109, 110 degrees. Thunderstorm winds downed several trees and caused roof and wall damage in parts of Avra Valley and Marana.  Additionally, an unoccupied fifth wheel trailer was blown on its side. Two power poles were also damaged near Twin Peaks Rd and Quarry Rd.

A line of thunderstorms caused extensive tree damage from the Rooney Ranch and Steam Pump Ranch area through Oro Valley Marketplace to Catalina Regional Park.  A portion of the roof to an outbuilding was blown off at Steam Pump Ranch.  The most severe damage occurred to trees within the park and in a residential area immediately to the east.  Several one-foot diameter trees were snapped off at the midpoint of the trunk while others were uprooted.  Roof damage to mobile homes farther east was also noted. A tree fell on a car at one residence.

A large tree was uprooted by thunderstorm winds near City Hall in Nogales.  A soaking rain of nearly 1.5 inches in the 24 hours preceding the thunderstorms had softened the ground around this shallow-rooted tree.

High winds, aided by saturated ground from 2 to 3 inches of soaking rain during the preceding hours, uprooted several large trees in Sierra Vista. Winds also blew a gazebo over a brick wall and destroyed it.

Around one inch of rain fell in southern Cochise County during the afternoon of November 27th with a total of 2 to 3 inches of rain by midnight.  By mid evening, several roads became impassable. This included Davis Road, King's Highway north of Route 80 and Frontier Road at Double Adobe. Route 80 was closed west of the Mule Pass Tunnel due to a rock slide.

events.cz_name: WHITE MOUNTAINS OF GRAHAM AND GREENLEE COUNTIES
events.event_narrative: Hannagan Meadow in northern Greenlee County received 14 inches of snow.

Widespread rain of 2 to 4 inches fell along the San Pedro River in southern Cochise County and upstream in Sonora on November 27th into the 28th, causing the river to rise markedly on the morning of November 29th.  The river neared flood stage at Palominas, but did not come out of its banks.  Farther downstream, the San Pedro River flooded Hereford Road on the east side of the bridge, but did not over top the bridge itself. However, the road was closed for several hours.

Three inches of rain fell in Bisbee from midday on November 27 into the morning hours of November 28.  A day later, a retention wall failed as a result.  The debris from this failed wall caused the closure of a section of Shearer Avenue in Bisbee.

Lightning started the Bighorn Fire on the west side of the Santa Catalina Mountains during the evening of June 5th.  The fire spread rapidly over the subsequent days and weeks, driven by multiple days of strong winds. Residents of Summerhaven, nearby mountain communities and those on the periphery of the mountains from the Catalina Foothills to southern Pinal County and near Redington Road were evacuated at times, but no structures were damaged by the fire. Five firefighters suffered from heat-related illness while two other personnel sustained minor injuries battling the fire during June.  By the end of the month, the fire consumed over 118,00 acres, but was only 59% contained.  The fire became fully contained on July 23rd after a total of 119,978 acres burned.

Thunderstorm outflow winds produced a gust to 67 mph at Empire RAWS.

Radar rainfall estimates of over 1 inch in the northwest Mule Mountains caused streams flowing west toward the San Pedro River to rise markedly. A vehicle became stuck in nearly two feet of water flowing across High Knoll Road.

Strong thunderstorm winds initiated a dust storm near the Willcox Playa that moved west restricting visibility to less than a quarter mile along Interstate 10 between Willcox and Texas Canyon, temporarily halting traffic.

Thunderstorm wind gusts downed six power poles in Sierra Vista near Willcox Rd. and S Carmichael Ave.  Wind gusts of 61 mph were reported at KFHU Libby Field ASOS and 79 mph at KALK Pioneer Field ASOS.
Thunderstorm winds downed a tree at the Benson Visitor Center.  The falling tree also damaged a pole-mounted gaslight.

Thunderstorms rolled northwest across the Tucson Metro area with thunderstorm outflow winds downing numerous trees and ten power poles.  Power was out for several hours for at least 12,000 customers due to downed poles and lines as well as damaged transformers.  Power poles were reported down at Broadway and Craycroft, Prince and Flowing Wells and Ina and Oracle.  Fallen trees caused damage to the Mission Palms Apartments near Orange Grove and La Cholla. Trees also fell onto a vehicle at River and Craycroft and two cars in Oro Valley. A wind gust to 59 mph was recorded at KDMA Davis-Monthan AFB ASOS.

Thunderstorm outflow winds produced blowing dust that restricted visibility to less than a quarter mile along Interstate 10 in northwest portions of the Tucson Metro area, temporarily halting traffic.
Lightning struck a house in 26th St and Camino Seco in Tucson.  Lightning only caused a small hole in the roof, but fire caused considerable damage to at least one room in the house.
Lightning started an attic fire in a house near Dove Mountain and Golden Barrel.
Thunderstorm winds downed several mesquite tree branches in Saint David.
A thunderstorm wind gust of 67 mph was recorded at Empire RAWS.

A debris flow of mud, ash, branches and brush was caused by rainfall between 0.75 and 1.25 in less than 1 hour on the northern part of the Bighorn Fire burn scar. A flow of nearly 5 feet was measured at the upper reaches of the Canada Del Oro Wash and a debris flow as deep as 3 feet was observed downstream crossing Edwin Road.

A debris flow of mud, ash, branches and brush was caused by rainfall between 0.75 and 1.25 in just over 30 minutes on the northern part of the Bighorn Fire burn scar. A flow of around 2 feet was measured at the upper reaches of the Canada Del Oro Wash and a debris flow as deep as 2 feet was also observed downstream crossing Edwin Road.

A debris flow of mud, ash, branches and brush was caused by rainfall between 0.75 and 1.25 in just over 30 minutes on the northern part of the Bighorn Fire burn scar. A flow of around 2 feet was measured at the upper reaches of the Canada Del Oro Wash and a debris flow as deep as 2 feet was also observed downstream crossing Edwin Road.

Thunderstorms produced heavy rain of 1 to 2 inches in one hour in northern Tucson and the Catalina Foothills. At Glenn and Craycroft Rd. flood waters were 2 feet deep causing stalled vehicles. Alamo Wash experienced a nearly 3 foot rise near Glenn St. and the Rillito at Dodge rose 2 feet.

Around an inch of rain in 30 minutes fell during the early morning hours near the headwaters of Pima Wash and Ventana Canyon Wash, within the Bighorn Fire burn scar area. Additional heavy rain of 0.75 to 1.5 fell in the urbanized area downstream of the burn area later that morning which caused combined runoff sufficient to cause a 2 foot sooty flow in Ventana Canyon Wash at Sunrise Drive and the closure of Snyder Road.

Flash flooding occurred across a large part of central and southwest Tucson.  Around 2 inches of rain fell in 60-90 minutes from the Catalina Foothills near Alvernon Way west through Flowing Wells and south to Tucson Estates, Drexel Heights and the Pascua Pueblo. Rain totals of at least 3 to 4 inches in southwest Tucson caused numerous road closures, including San Xavier Rd near the Mission.  Interstate 10 at Sunset Road was also closed briefly. Multiple vehicles became stranded in flood waters and several swift water rescues occurred in midtown. Vehicle rescues were noted on Fort Lowell Rd. at Tuscon Blvd and Stone Ave. and also near Glenn and Fairview.  A man was also rescued from the Rillito River near the Tucson Mall.  Farther south and west, a truck became stuck in Camino De Oeste Wash at Lloyd Bush Dr.  A two to three foot wall of water progressed down the normally dry Santa Cruz River.  The Pima County Medical Examiner determined that the cause of death was drowning for a man pulled from the Santa Cruz River near Speedway.

Pockets of heavy rain on the order of 1 inch in just over an hour caused isolated areas of flash flooding in parts of Picture Rocks and Marana.  Road closures due to flooding were noted on Emigh Rd. near Sandario and Sanders.

Lightning started the Klaus Fire in the Chiricahua Mountains in southeast Cochise County on August 10th. The fire was spread by strong winds and a lack of monsoon rainfall, and consumed 4864 acres before becoming contained August 18th. Fire suppression costs tallied $377,500.

events.cz_name: UPPER GILA RIVER AND ARAVAIPA VALLEYS
events.event_narrative: Lightning started wildfires on the San Carlos Apache Tribe lands in Graham County during the last 10 days of August. The Rockhouse Fire 22 miles southeast of San Carlos on August 21st was the largest of these fires.  It spread rapidly by strong winds and a lack of monsoon rainfall before becoming fully contained September 15th after consuming 19,506 acres. Fire suppression costs totaled $546,000.  The Juniper Fire, 18 miles east of San Carlos--just east of July's Valley Fire, consumed another 2,867 acres and totaled another $200,000 in suppression costs during late August.

events.cz_name: UPPER GILA RIVER AND ARAVAIPA VALLEYS
events.event_narrative: The human caused Light Fire started on August 28th on San Carlos Apache Tribe lands between Calva and Bylas in northwest Graham County.  The fire spread through salt cedar by strong winds and burned around 1000 acres with nearly 500 foot high flames, before becoming contained August 31st. Fire suppression costs tallied $50,000.  Five homes were evacuated near Calva Road and several utility poles burned, but no homes were damaged. The fire burned under the Bylas bridge causing the bridge and Highway 70 to be closed for 16 hours.

The extreme drought (D3) category was reached in late August across most of Graham County, northern and central Greenlee County, northwest Cochise County and eastern portions of Pima and Pinal counties, including San Carlos Apache tribal lands, the White Mountains, the Pinaleno Mountains and the Santa Catalina Mountains. Below normal precipitation occurred each month from April through August of 2020 and the summer was the hottest on record in many locations. Several lightning caused wildfires and at least one human caused wildfire spread rapidly due to dry fuels, and continued into September. This included the Cow Canyon Fire in Greenlee County, which started on August 18th, but smoldered in heavy fuels with very little growth during August. Soil moisture readings were well below normal and ranked below the 20th percentile. Levels at San Carlos Reservoir fell from around 15 percent in July to less than 7 percent of storage capacity by the end of August.

Over two inches of rain fell in one hour and nearly three inches in about two hours southwest of Saint David prior to midnight, but flash flooding continued into September 9th. Over a foot of water flowed across Wentworth Road about 3 hours after the crest at Chiva Tank.

events.cz_name: WHITE MOUNTAINS OF GRAHAM AND GREENLEE COUNTIES
events.event_narrative: The Cow Canyon Fire was ignited by lightning on August 18th southeast of Blue in Greenlee County. The fire grew only minimally for several weeks until hot, dry and breezy conditions caused more rapid growth toward the end of September, which continued into October when northerly winds sent smoke plumes aloft over the communities of Clifton and Morenci at times. While the fire continued well into November, the spread of the fire was halted by October 22nd after consuming 35,371 acres. Fire suppression costs were estimated at $2,850,000.

The extreme drought (D3) category, which began in late August and expanded in September, expanded further in October to include all of the Tohono O'odham Nation and all of Santa Cruz and Cochise counties, except for the Huachuca Mountains. Extreme drought continued across all of southeast Arizona north and east of these locations and the exceptional drought (D4) category began in eastern portions of Pima and Pinal counties and western Graham County. Tucson recorded its fifth warmest October on record and while most of October was dry and warmer than normal, Tucson actually recorded its 4th earliest fall freeze on record, which was brought on by an early season winter storm that also produced low elevation snow during the last week of the month. Nevertheless, precipitation totals from this storm were generally less than a quarter inch in the valleys with around a half inch for the Mogollon Rim and some of the sky islands, and at less than 30 percent of normal precipitation for the month, were not enough to stop drought conditions from deteriorating further. The lightning-caused Cow Canyon Fire, that started in August, continued to spread in Greenlee County, consuming over 35,000 acres due to hot, dry and breezy conditions before being slowed by the early season snow. Meanwhile, several human caused wildfires took hold during October.  The largest was the Encinos Fire which consumed nearly 15,000 acres along and east of the Baboquivari Mountains in Pima County. Soil moisture readings remained  well below normal, falling to below the 5th percentile ranking in most areas, while remaining just below the 10th percentile ranking near the New Mexico state line. Levels at San Carlos Reservoir fell to less than 3 percent of storage capacity by the end of the month.

The exceptional drought (D4) category, which began in eastern portions of Pima and Pinal counties and western Graham County in October, expanded across all of Graham and Greenlee counties, northern Cochise and Santa Cruz counties and central Pima County during November. November totals across southeast Arizona were 0.5 to 1.5 inches below normal for the month, and were not enough to keep drought conditions from further deteriorating. Soil moisture readings remained below the 5th percentile ranking in most areas, and below the 10th percentile ranking near the New Mexico state line. Levels at San Carlos Reservoir remained at less than 3 percent of storage capacity throughout the month.

A modest sized tree was blown down in downtown Tucson near 1st St. and Euclid Ave. shortly after the onset of strong winds that occurred much of the day. The tree blocked one lane of traffic on Euclid for a short time.

Southwest winds sustained at 25 to 30 mph with gusts to 40 mph created a dust storm that reduced visibility to less than a quarter mile in south central Pinal County along Interstate 10 from mile posts 213 to 226 and along Highway 87 north of Picacho. State officials ordered the closure of Highway 87 between mile posts 220 and 223, but minor accidents were reported prior to the closure taking affect. No injuries were reported.
Thunderstorms produced small hail that nearly covered portions of roadways in Marana. Slick road surfaces led to several traffic accidents involving a total of least 10 vehicles on Interstate 10.
Nine to eleven inches of snow fell at the higher elevations of the Santa Catalina Mountains, which caused the closure of Mt Lemmon Highway at the base.
Heavy snow accumulations of 16 to 20 inches combined with winds gusting to 30 mph caused blowing and drifting snow on Mt. Graham.

The exceptional (D4) and extreme (D3) drought categories continued across a large part of southeast Arizona during December, with the exception of western Pima County. Precipitation totals for the month, which occurred primarily on December 9-10, totaled 0.10 to 1 inch or about 0.5 to 1.5 inches below normal. Soil moisture readings remained below the 5th percentile ranking in most areas, and below the 10th percentile ranking near the New Mexico state line. Levels at San Carlos Reservoir dropped slightly, to around 2 percent of storage capacity.

The exceptional (D4) and extreme (D3) drought categories continued across a large part of southeast Arizona during January, with the exception of western Pima County. Precipitation totals for the month totaled 0.5 to 1.5 inches, with higher amounts in the form of snow on the highest mountains. These totals were 25 to 125 percent of normal, but even where substantial precipitation occurred, were not enough to improve the drought status. Soil moisture readings improved slightly, but were still below the 5th percentile ranking across Santa Cruz and eastern sections of Pima and Pinal counties and below the 10th percentile ranking elsewhere. Levels at San Carlos Reservoir remained around 2 percent of storage capacity.

Strong south winds created areas of blowing dust in south central Pinal County. events.cz_name: UPPER GILA RIVER AND ARAVAIPA VALLEYS
events.event_narrative: The human caused Salt Fire started on April 8th on San Carlos Apache Tribe lands near Bylas in northwest Graham County. On the first day, the fire burned over 2000 acres in the Gila River bed having been spread by winds gusting to more than 30 mph. Two homes were evacuated in Bylas as a precaution, but the only structures damaged were two abandoned corrals. The fire was contained April 14th, but not before it consumed 4425 acres and came within a mile of Fort Thomas. Fire suppression costs tallied $350,000.

The human caused Margo Fire started on April 8th in the San Pedro River bed near Dudleyville. The fire was spread by gusty winds which led to the evacuation of over 200 of the town's residents.  The wildfire destroyed seventeen residences and around two dozen outbuildings and caused the closure of State Route 77. The fire consumed 1148 acres before it was contained April 11th. Property damage costs were estimated at around $2 million while fire suppression costs tallied $300,000.

The human caused Jack Fire started on April 21st in the Chiricahua Mountains of southeast Cochise County.  The wildfire was driven by wind gusts to 40 mph at times and over 1600 acres were burned in the first 24 hours.  Forward progress was stopped on April 25th and the fire was contained April 28th with a total of 1856 acres consumed. Fire suppression costs tallied just over $2 million.

events.cz_name: UPPER SANTA CRUZ RIVER AND ALTAR VALLEYS
events.event_narrative: The human caused Alamo Fire started June 20 near the International Border in Santa Cruz County. The wildfire grew quickly in hot conditions and due to occasional thunderstorm outflow wind gusts near 40 mph on both sides of the border. The fire was contained on June 28 after consuming 4953 acres on the U.S.side of the border and nearly that acreage in Mexico. Fire suppression costs in Arizona tallied over $400,000.

events.cz_name: WHITE MOUNTAINS OF GRAHAM AND GREENLEE COUNTIES
events.event_narrative: The lightning caused Bear Fire started June 16 in the White Mountains in Greenlee County. Thunderstorm outflow wind gusts in excess of 40 mph caused the wildfire to grow to more than 2000 acres on June 20 and resulted in the closure of Highway 191. Rapid fire growth occurred during the next week due to several additional days of gusty thunderstorm outflow winds with 23,480 acres consumed by June 28. Increased humidity inhibited rapid growth thereafter, and during this time of less active fire management, the final total reached 24,067 acres by July 8, when Highway 191 was reopened. Fire suppression costs tallied $200,000.

events.cz_name: UPPER GILA RIVER AND ARAVAIPA VALLEYS
events.event_narrative: The lightning caused Bottom Fire started June 28 in the Gila River Valley on San Carlos Apache tribal lands within Graham County. The fire quickly grew to around 3000 acres by the end of the month due to daily bouts of gusty thunderstorm outflow winds. The fire was officially contained July 10 after consuming 6004 acres. Fire suppression costs tallied $1.4 million.

events.cz_name: WHITE MOUNTAINS OF GRAHAM AND GREENLEE COUNTIES
events.event_narrative: The Horton Fire was the largest of four lightning caused that ignited on June 16 north of Hannagan Meadows in the White Mountains in Greenlee County. The four fires, driven by thunderstorm outflow wind gusts in excess of 40 mph at times, merged into an 11,000 acre fire by June 26 and grew to 12,263 acres by June 29. No fire growth was experienced after this date, but the fire was not officially contained until July 13. Fire suppression costs tallied $3.5 million.

The human caused Shamrock Fire started June 9, five miles north of the International Border in the Patagonia Mountains of Santa Cruz County. The wildfire grew quickly in hot and dry conditions, but was contained June 16 after consuming 1104 acres. Fire suppression costs tallied $2.38 million.

The lightning caused Walnut Fire started June 20 in the Little Dragoon Mountains in Cochise County. The wildfire grew rapidly to nearly 7000 acres in hot, dry and occasionally windy conditions by June 22, jumping Interstate 10 and prompting its closure and the evacuation of several residences and businesses in the Texas Canyon and Dragoon areas. Rain on the 23rd helped slow the fire's spread and additional rain on the 28th quashed the fire after it consumed a total of 10,667 acres. Fire suppression costs tallied $1.4 million.

events.cz_name: UPPER GILA RIVER AND ARAVAIPA VALLEYS
events.event_narrative: The human caused Pinnacle Fire started June 10 on Pinnacle Ridge in the Santa Teresa Wilderness of western Graham County. The fire grew to over 15,000 acres within a week in hot, dry and windy conditions and to 34,417 acres by June 25. No fire growth was experienced after June 25, but the fire was not officially contained until July 16. Residents of the Aravaipa, Black Rock and Klondyke communities were evacuated for about two weeks, but no structures were lost. Fire suppression costs tallied $10.5 million.

events.cz_name: UPPER GILA RIVER AND ARAVAIPA VALLEYS
events.event_narrative: The lightning caused Bottom Fire started June 28 in the Gila River Valley on San Carlos Apache tribal lands within Graham County. The fire quickly grew to around 3000 acres by the end of the month due to daily bouts of gusty thunderstorm outflow winds. Nearly daily rounds of thunderstorm winds continued during the first week of July causing the fire to grow to 6004 acres before it was fully contained July 10. Three structures in Calva were temporarily evacuated on July 6 when strong winds caused the fire to break containment lines. Highway 70 was closed for a time and a nearby Eastern Arizona railroad trestle was damaged. Fire suppression costs tallied $1.4 million.

The exceptional (D4) and extreme (D3) drought categories continued across a large part of southeast Arizona during June, with the exception of western Pima County.  Most areas only tallied 0.5 or less for the month, which is close to normal. A few locations received 1-1.5 of rain, but that was not enough to make up for record rainfall deficits over the past 12 to 15 months. Soil moisture readings remained below the 5th percentile ranking across most of southeast Arizona except around the 10th percentile ranking in Greenlee and southeast Graham counties. Levels at San Carlos Reservoir remained near zero percent of capacity. Numerous human and lightning caused wild land fires occurred, five of which grew to more than 10,000 acres during the hot, dry and windy month.

Thunderstorm outflow wind gusts of 50 to 60 mph blew across the Gila River Valley. Several power poles were downed in Pima and south of Safford. A wind gust to 54 mph was measured at the Safford Airport ASOS.

Thunderstorm winds downed two large trees, one power pole, a barn and a few small sheds in Central. One of the downed trees smashed through a brick wall. Another of the trees downed two power lines which trapped two people in separate vehicles.
Lightning struck a partially constructed home, causing it to burn to the ground.
Thunderstorm winds damaged or uprooted 35 shallow-rooted trees at Evergreen Cemetery in Tucson.

Very hot high temperatures of 106 to 119 degrees, or 8 to 13 degrees above normal, occurred in the lower elevations of southeast Arizona June 12-20, and caused the High Heat Risk category to be reached. New record daily high temperature records were established at numerous sites on several days during this period. For Tucson International Airport, this nine day period contributed to the hottest June on record and the 4th hottest temperature on record of 115 degrees occurred on June 15.  Sites that tied or broke all time hottest temperature records included Ajo with 119 degrees, Sasabe with 113, Green Valley with 112. The Pima County Medical Examiner confirmed that heat was the primary cause of death for 14 people found in the desert of Pima and Santa Cruz counties during this time period.

Very hot high temperatures of 103 to 112 degrees, or 8 to 16 degrees above normal, occurred in the lower elevations of Cochise County June 12-14, and caused the High Heat Risk category to be reached. New record daily high temperature records were established at several sites, including 112 degrees at Cascabel, 111 at Willcox, 109 at Tombstone, and 107 at Sierra Vista. The Pima County Medical Examiner confirmed that heat was the primary cause of death for 1 person found in the desert near the International Border south of Palominas on June 14.

events.event_narrative: A wet July caused the exceptional (D4) drought category and extreme (D3) drought category to cease across nearly all of southeast Arizona, with exceptional drought only remaining in far southeast Cochise County by the end of the month. The extreme (D3) drought category remained across the rest of eastern and central Cochise County, much of Graham and Greenlee counties and parts of the Tohono O'odham Nation. July rainfall varied widely from 2 to 15 inches across southeast Arizona. In areas where the drought lingered through the end of the month this equated to 75 to 125 percent of normal rainfall while areas in which the drought eased further rainfall tallied as much as 400 percent of normal. July ranked as the wettest on record for any month at the Tucson International Airport where 8.06 inches was recorded. The rainfall caused wildfire season to end and soil moisture readings to improve from below the 10th percentile to between the 30th and 70th percentiles by month's end. Levels at San Carlos Reservoir started to rise, but only reached slightly more than 1 percent of capacity by the end of the month.

Photo showed a landspout in northeast Tucson around Skyline and Kolb. No damage occurred.
A storm chaser observed a funnel cloud for 3 minutes in northeast Tucson around Swan and Sunrise.

Thunderstorm winds downed or uprooted numerous trees in midtown Tucson including several at a cemetery on Prince Rd and Oracle Blvd. One tree fell on a house near Pima St. and Columbus Blvd. and another damaged a car at River Rd. and 1st Ave. Winds also damaged a house under construction near Prince and Country Club Rd. and downed large |power poles near Tucson Mall causing the closure of 1st Ave between River and Wetmore Rds. About 6000 customers lost electricity service.
A trained spotter estimated 70 mph wind gusts in Catalina.
Thunderstorm winds blew a metal utility shed into a utility pole at Magee Rd. and La Ca��ada Dr.
Black Hills RAWS measured a wind gust of 58 mph.
Heavy rain of 1 to 1.5 fell in less that 1 hour in the Catalina Foothills. Ventana Wash rose and flowed up to 18 deep across Snyder Rd, causing its closure.
Heavy rain of 1-2 in less than 1 hour from Tucson Mt Park to Highway 86 caused the flooding and closure of Bopp Rd closed in several locations from Lead Flower Ave west past San Joaquin Rd.

One to three inches of rain in 90 minutes in the Cornfield Canyon watershed caused flash flooding. As two females, who had exited their vehicle, were viewing the stream at Ocatillo Road, an additional rise in water levels swept them downstream. One was rescued about three quarters of a mile away while the other was finally located in the San Pedro River the next morning. Both sustained minor injuries.
More than one inch of rain in less than 1 hour in upper reaches of Huachuca Canyon flooded the canyon and flowed across Burt Rd at Fort Huachuca.
Two inches of rain in less than 1 hour caused extensive flooding of Arivaca Road between mile markers 10 and 16 with additional flash flooding farther north near Keystone Peak.
More than 3 inches of rain in 90 minutes in Rio Rico Southwest caused flash flooding more than 1 foot deep across several roadways.
Thunderstorm winds downed seven power poles and damaged or destroyed several storage sheds near Moson Rd, between Dakota and Nevada Aves.
The Sasabe RAWS measured a wind gust of 66 mph.
Thunderstorm winds destroyed a dwelling at Cold Fields.
Thunderstorm winds downed a tree, which well on a vehicle at Rodeo Lane near Highway 70 in Peridot.

More than 1 inch of rain in less than 1 hour fell along State Route 286 north of Santa Margarita Road west to the Baboquivari Mountains causing a number of washes to flow east across Route 286 two to three feet deep.

Thunderstorm winds downed 10 power poles in 2 different areas between Tombstone and Huachuca City. A private weather station at Huachuca City measured a gust to 70 mph at 1704MST near the location where the roof of a store was ripped off. A wind gust to 68 mph was measured at Libby Field on Fort Huachuca at 1711MST. Two miles west at the Pioneer Field ASOS, a wind gust to 91 mph was measured at 1721MST.  Near that site, winds destroyed a large reinforced military tent.
Thunderstorm winds downed several trees and power poles in the east part of Safford.
A wind gust to 61 mph was measured in Artesia.
A slow moving thunderstorm produced several minutes of nickel to quarter size hail near Patagonia.
Hopkins RAWS, at an elevation of over 7000ft MSL, recorded a wind gust to 78 mph.

Thunderstorms winds downed 30 power poles and dozens of trees in Green Valley and Sahuarita. One of the downed trees broke a water main and other blocked streets. Around 10,000 customers were without power into the overnight hours. A CoCoRaHS observer on the southeast side of Green Valley measured a wind gust of 66 mph at 1855MST.
Thunderstorm winds downed power poles near Speedway Blvd and Tanque Verde Loop Rd. A private weather station near Escalante and Freeman Roads measured a gust to 76 mph at 1943MST.
A wind gust to 60 mph was recorded at Tucson International Airport at 1904MST. Outflow winds downed trees in midtown Tucson and in Marana.

Thunderstorm winds downed multiple trees in eastern Tucson. A wind gust to 64 mph was recorded at Davis-Monthan AFB at 1946MST and a gust to 58 mph was recorded at a private weather station near Irvington and Harrison at 1948MST.
Thunderstorm winds caused minor damage to a house in Little Tucson on the Tohono O'odham Nation.
Thunderstorm winds caused minor damage to two homes in Anegam and substantial damage to a home in Comobabi.
Thunderstorm winds damaged the roof of a storage building, an awning at a gas station and downed several trees in Eloy.
Thunderstorm outflow winds produced widespread blowing dust that reduced visibilities to less than a quarter mile from Green Valley to Marana causing traffic disruptions along Interstates 19 and 10.
Thunderstorm outflow winds produced widespread blowing dust that reduced visibilities to less than a quarter mile and caused traffic disruptions along Interstate 10 in southern Pinal County.

Thunderstorm outflow winds produced widespread blowing dust that reduced visibilities to less than a quarter mile that caused traffic disruptions along Route 15 and Highway 86 on the Tohono O'odham Nation.
Heavy rain of 2.5 in less than 1 hour at the headwaters of Tanque Verde Creek caused rapid rises of over three feet in Tanque Verde Creek downstream before the channel widens out.
Heavy rain of 2.5 in less than 1 hour at the headwaters of Tanque Verde Creek caused a 1 foot rise in water levels at Tanque Verde Loop Road, resulting in its closure.
Thunderstorm wind gusts downed several trees in western Oro Valley and Marana and downed power poles along Trico Rd.
A wind gust to 58 mph was recorded at Pinal Airpark.

Between 1 and 1.5 of rain fell in less than 1 hour in central Tucson causing widespread street flooding with water flowing across roads 1 to 2 feet deep. Swift water rescues occurred near the intersections of Grant and Tucson and Silverlake and Euclid with vehicles stranded at Mabel and 7th Ave. and the Orange Grove/I-10 underpass.  A house was flooded near Speedway and Country Club.

Between 1 and 1.5 of rain fell in less than 1 hour south and west of the Tucson Mountains to near Three Points causing widespread street flooding and street closures due to water flowing across roads 1 to 2 feet deep. A vehicle was stranded in flood waters at the intersection of Snyder Hill and Sandario. Several dirt roads were washed out in the Three Points area.
A funnel cloud was observed descending from a wall cloud near Mt. Wrightston.
A wind gust to 63 mph was recorded at the Empire RAWS.
Thunderstorm winds downed power poles near the intersection of Speedway and Painted Hills.

Heavy rain of 1 to 2 in less than an hour in the upper reaches of the Canada Del Oro Wash within the Bighorn burn scar caused rapid rises downstream. Rail North Rd along Lago Del Oro Parkway to Wilds Rd was closed to high water levels.

Strong flows continued in the Canada Del Oro Wash as a result of 1 to 2 of rain in less than an hour in the upper reaches of the basin within the Bighorn burn scar. Overton Rd. was closed due to flooding and the loop trail at Christina Taylor Green Park was flooded. More than an inch of rain in less than 1 hour also occurred from Marana to the southern Tortolita Mountains. As a result a swift water rescue was performed near Grier and Sandario and another west of Edwin and Oracle Rds.

Heavy rain of 1 to 1.5 in 90 minutes west of Interstate 10 and north of Highway 86 in Tucson resulted in flash flooding and the closure of several roads including Bopp Rd, Jamie Ave, Aldon Rd, and Sandario Rd. A vehicle was stranded in floodwaters at Sweetwater and Silverbell.
More than 1 inch of rain in less than 1 hour caused flash flooding in Cactus Forest and the closure of Quail Ridge Way near Diffin Rd.
Two inches of rain in 2 hours north of Three Points caused flooding of roadways west of Picture Rocks. A vehicle was stranded in floodwaters on Tucker Road at the Blanco Wash.
Two to four inches of rain in two hours fell over the higher terrain north of Safford and Pima. Flash flooding caused multiple road washouts of Safford-Bryce and Bryce-Eden Rds.
A wind gust to 69 mph was recorded at Safford Airport.
A wind gust of 62 mph was recorded at Safford Airport.
One hour rainfall of 0.5 to 1 on ground saturated from rain the previous day caused flash flooding northeast of Ryan Field and the closure of Snyder Hill Rd west of San Joaquin Rd.
Lightning started a small fire at a residence in the Saddlebrooke area.

One to two inches of rain in 90 minutes caused flash flooding in the Benson and St. David areas. Several washes to overtopped in the St. David area and North Miller Rd was closed due to flooding. Ocotillo Road was closed due to flooding north of Benson.
Three hour rainfall of 2.5 fell at the headwaters of Rincon Creek, causing rapid rises in stream flow and flash flooding of Old Spanish Trail.
One to two inches of rain in less than an hour caused flash flooding in the Clifton-Morenci area. One school was damaged by floodwaters.
A considerable area of more than 2 of rain fell in less than 1 hour east of Haekel Rd. in southeast Graham County. A section of the roadway was washed out by floodwaters near the Artesia Rd turnoff.
One to two inches of rain in less than 1 hour in the Sunsites area caused flash flooding and the closure of Birch Rd. near Highway 191.
One to two inches of rain in less than 1 hour south of San Simon caused flash flooding of roadways and resulted in the closing of Coyote Song Rd.
One to two inches of rain in less than 1 hour north of Willcox caused flash flooding of roadways and the closure of Hardy Rd.

Thunderstorm winds caused damage at a church complex near Broadway and Craycroft in Tucson, blowing in one 50-foot tall stained glass window and blowing out another.  An awning was damaged on the school building and the pastor's residence suffered shingle damage.  A tree was also downed which damaged an iron post fence, and the church marquis was damaged. Nearby, a tree was downed damaging the wall of a house. Several other trees were downed farther north and west and a carport was destroyed near 5th St. and Alvernon Way.
Thunderstorm winds downed more than a dozen large trees at an apartment complex near Orange Grove and Oracle Rds. The downed trees fell on carports and vehicles, and destroyed an apartment stairwell.
Thunderstorm winds downed a tree near the intersection of Speedway and Craycroft, which led to a traffic accident.
Thunderstorm winds downed a power pole and caused minor damage to a house in Chuichu.
Thunderstorm winds downed several trees and blew a metal roof off a hardware store in Douglas.

Thunderstorm winds downed 60 power poles and numerous trees and in Green Valley and Sahuarita, mostly along La Canada Dr. from Duval Mine Rd to near Anamax Rd. and near the entrance to Quail Creek. A traffic signal was also damaged in Green Valley while the wall of a townhouse was blown over in Sahuarita.
Thunderstorm winds downed a tree near Interstate 10 and Houghton.

One to two inches of rain in less than 1 hour over east central Tucson caused flash flooding along and near Alamo Wash.  A child was rescued from flood waters near 22nd and Kolb.  Farther north, Alamo Wash overtopped Speedway Blvd and Sahuara Ave.

Heavy rain of 2 to 2.5 fell in less than 2 hours between the Pinaleno Mountains and Highway 70 west of Safford. This caused flash flooding of roads in the Pima area and significant rises in Cottonwood Wash. A large SUV which was attempting to cross the wash and carrying two adults and four children was swept away in the floodwaters. A four-year old girl drown during the rescue attempt. Her body was found four days later downstream in the Gila River near Eden.

Heavy rain of 1.5 to 2.5 fell in less than 1 hour in the Douglas area causing flash flooding of streets and caused the closure of Washington Ave where several homes were flooded and a block wall was knocked down by flood waters. West of town, Kings Highway just north of State Route 80 was closed due to flooding.

A large area of 1 to 2 of rain fell in less than 90 minutes in southeast Pima County and caused extensive flash flooding from southeast Tucson and Vail southwest to Sahuarita and Green Valley. In the Vail area, three to four feet of water washed out East Andrada Rd at the Santa Rita Wash and a car was swept downstream 300 yards, but the occupants escaped unharmed.  Many roads in Saguaro National Park East were also flooded or closed.  In southeast Tucson, a person was rescued from a sandbar in the Pantano Wash near Harrison Rd. and farther south, Sahuarita and Wilmot Rds. were closed. In Sahuarita a woman was rescued from her vehicle at Beta Street and the Interstate 19 Frontage Rd.  In Green Valley, several roads were closed and homes were flooded in the Casa de Abrego neighborhood east of I-19.

Heavy rain of 1 to 1.5 fell in less than 1 hour along the entire length of the San Pedro River from San Manuel to Dudleyville and 3 fell near Dudleyville caused the river to rise rapidly, with a greater than 7 foot rise measured in one hour near Mammoth. Extensive flash flooding and severe damage to nearby roadways occurred in the San Manuel, Mammoth and Dudleyville areas.

A large area of 1 to 3 of rain fell in less than 1 hour over much of the Tucson Metro Area, including parts of the Bighorn burn scar. Around ten swift water rescues were performed during the overnight hours for motorists trapped in vehicles including near Escalante and Sarnoff. Plus, two people were rescued from the Rillito River near La Canada Dr. Also, many trails were damaged at Sabino Canyon Recreation Area and six homes were flooded in near Finger Rock Wash in the Catalina Foothills due to runoff from the Bighorn burn scar. No injuries were reported.

A broad area of 1 to 2 of rain fell in less than 1 hour from the Tucson Mountains west to Picture Rocks. Numerous streets were flooded, closed and/or damaged as a result. At least one vehicle was stranded in flood waters, on Manville Rd.

Widespread heavy rain across eastern Pima County resulted in widespread flooding of roadways and high flows along Pantano Wash and Rillito River. Significant damage to the Loop hiking and biking trail system occurred.

Heavy rains upstream in the basin late July 22 into July 23, raised water levels in the Santa Cruz River and Greene Wash in Pinal County. Several roads were washed out where the Santa Cruz becomes multi-channeled from west of Pinal Airpark to southwest of Picacho.

Heavy rain of 1 to 1.5 in less than 1 hour fell in Green Valley and caused flash flooding and the closure of several roads. Five homes were flooded in the Casa de Abrego neighborhood, some of which had just been flooded less than 48 hours earlier.
Early morning rainfall of 1 to 1.5 on saturated ground quickly resulted in flash flooding and closure of several roads in north Marana.
Early morning rain of 1 to 1.5 on saturated ground caused flash flooding, closure and damage of Camino Adelante Rd between the Picacho Peak Interstate 10 interchange to Park Link Dr.
More than 1 of rain fell on saturated ground causing flash flooding of several roadways from Sahuarita to Corona De Tucson, including Sahuarita Rd. near Wilmot Rd.

One to two inches of rain on saturated ground cause numerous flooded and closed roads in the Vail area from just east of Rita Ranch to Old Spanish Trail and south to near Interstate 10. One vehicle was stuck in floodwaters near Old Spanish Trail and Drexel Rd.

Strong outflow winds from a thunderstorm complex caused severe winds across the Douglas area. Strong winds blew down a storage shed in Douglas, knocked down several trees and caused a partial roof collapse.
Up to 1 of rain on saturated ground caused Franco Wash to rise rapidly and flood and damage several roads in the Summit area.

Widespread rain occurred on July 24 and 25 in the Santa Cruz River watershed in Pinal County and upstream in much of eastern Pima County with 48 hour rain totals of 3 to 4 inches common. High flows in the river traveled downstream into Greene Wash. A levee breached in the wash near Toltec Buttes and washed out a road, then flowed into a canal, causing damage along 3/4 mile of the canal.  Further downstream in Greene Wash, Sunland Gin Rd was also flooded and damaged. Indian Route 15 near Chuichu was also flooded and two nearby homes sustained minor flood damage.
Strong winds from thunderstorms caused a partial roof collapse to a home in the village of San Miguel.
A 6 foot rise occurred on Cienega Creek South of Vail.
Washes were running across Silverbell road near Sunset Road.
One to two inches of rain fell in less than 1 hour in Nogales and caused flash flooding of several roads and minor damage to a couple of homes near Western Ave.
A vehicle was stranded in the road at Fairview Avenue and Tipton Drive due to high water.

Around 2.5 of rain in less than 1 hour was measured near the headwaters of Sabino Creek in the Bighorn burn scar and caused a two-foot rise in the stream that crosses trails in the Sabino Canyon Recreation Area. Six hikers had to be rescued after becoming trapped by the high flows.

Heavy rain of 2.5 in less than 90 minutes occurred near the headwaters of Rincon Creek. Flash flooding occurred downstream in the Rincon Ranch Estates area. Camino Loma Alta became flooded and impassible.
A trained spotter reported 0.88 inch hail east of Benson.
Thunderstorm winds downed three power poles north of the Organ Pipe Cactus National Monument Visitor Center.
Hail up to 1.25 inches in diameter occurred in the Rita Ranch area and along Houghton Road between Valencia Road and Interstate 10.
Heavy rain of 2 to 3 in less than 1 hour at Organ Pipe Cactus National Monument caused flash flooding of roadways making them impassible.

One inch of rain in less than 90 minutes caused rapid rises in Josephine Canyon. Two teenagers swimming near a waterfall were swept downstream by a rapid rise in the water level. One teenager drowned and another escaped the floodwaters while sustaining minor injuries and was later rescued.
Thunderstorm winds downed a power pole near Nolic.
A wind gust to 67 mph was recorded at Tucson International Airport.
A trained spotter recoreded nickel sized hail near Marana.

One to two inches of rain fell in less than 1 hour northeast of the Tucson International Airport causing flash flooding of area roads. One swift water rescue was conducted for a vehicle stalled in a wash.
More than 1 of rain fell in less than 1 hour along South Wilmot Rd causing flash flooding and the closure of the roadway north of Sahuarita Rd.
One to two inches of rain in less than 1 hour from south of Ajo to east of Why. This caused flash flooding of area washes and the closure of Highway 86 east of Why and Highway 85 between Ajo and Why.
Part of a roof was lost on a home near 36th St and Kino Blvd.

Temperatures 5 degrees above normal near 110 degrees, occurred in western Pima County causing the Moderate Heat Risk category to be reached on July 6. The Pima County Medical Examiner confirmed that heat was the primary cause of death for one male found in the desert west of Ajo.

Temperatures 5 degrees above normal around 105 degrees, occurred on the Tohono O'odham Nation causing the Moderate Heat Risk category to be reached on July 6. The Pima County Medical Examiner confirmed that heat was the primary cause of death for three males found in the desert, two near Sells and one near Vamori.

Temperatures 5 to 10 degrees above normal near 100 degrees, occurred in southern Cochise County causing the Moderate Heat Risk category to be reached on July 10. The Pima County Medical Examiner confirmed that heat was the primary cause of death for one male found in the desert near Palominas and another in the Leslie Canyon area.

Temperatures 5 to 10 degrees above normal near 100 degrees, occurred in southern Cochise County causing the Moderate Heat Risk category to be reached on July 10. The Pima County Medical Examiner confirmed that heat was the primary cause of death for one male found in the desert near Palominas and another in the Leslie Canyon area.

Temperatures 5 to 9 degrees above normal of 100 to 105 degrees, occurred on the Tohono O'odham Nation causing the Moderate Heat Risk category to be reached on July 21. The Pima County Medical Examiner confirmed that heat was the primary cause of death for one male found in the desert near Ali Chugk and a contributing factor to one male found near Vamori.

A wet August caused the extreme (D3) drought category to cease in parts of the Tohono O'odham Nation and Graham, Greenlee, and much of Cochise counties--only remaining in far southeast Cochise County, where it eased from the exceptional (D4) drought category present in July. August rainfall of 2 to 8 inches in the drought-stricken areas varied from 100 to 300 percent of normal. The rainfall caused soil moisture readings to improve to the 70th percentile or greater by month's end. Levels at San Carlos Reservoir continued to rise, but still only reached around 3 percent of capacity by the end of the month.
